Wingman Handguide

Wingman Handguide

Air combat fundamentals, formation & wingman tactics, BVR & missile defense, strategy, a War Thunder vehicle guide, and weapons/sensor reference — built as a live-reference tool in training-manual order (fly first, worry about killing later), not a book to read once. Use search or Compact mode to cut straight to what you need mid-session.

How to use this guideThere's no time mid-fight to analyze a situation and plan the optimal move, or replay afterward why one choice was wrong — what actually wins fights is instinct, built beforehand, not real-time analysis. Reading a section here gets you to comprehension — you understand it, can explain it, can predict what should happen. Only repetition — flying the exercise, ideally against a training partner — gets you to application, where the right move happens without having to think it through. Treat the deepdives as something to go fly and feel, not trivia to memorize. (Framing per Mike Solyom/The Ops Center, "Learning BFM | BFM Series Intro | Part 1.")
Part I — Fundamentals
  • BFM = aircraft-handling to attain a position, deny one, or defeat a weapon — not memorized moves.
  • Governing axiom: all maneuvers are relative to the bandit — never your own heading or a compass direction.
  • Energy fighter: wins by preserving speed/altitude, staying fast in the vertical.
  • Angles fighter: wins by spending energy for a tighter turn. Know which yours is; default to its plan.
  • Corner velocity is a one-time withdrawal, not a cruising speed — turn rate & G both drop right after.
  • Instantaneous turn: max rate at corner velocity — for a break turn or snap only.
  • Sustained turn: gentler rate held without bleeding energy — fly this for anything held more than a couple seconds.
  • Common mistake: living at corner velocity like a cruising speed, then empty three seconds into a fight that was going fine.
  • Unload to accelerate: push toward zero G — biggest gain at low speed and high altitude. In a dive, the heavier or cleaner aircraft pulls away.
BFM, formallyThe US Air Force's own definition: BFM is "the efficient application of aircraft handling skills to either attain a position from which weapons may be employed, deny the adversary a position from which weapons may be launched, or defeat weapons employed by the adversary." Those three clauses map onto this Part's structure: attain a position is Offensive BFM, deny a position is Defensive BFM, defeat a weapon is missile/guns defense. None of them are canned maneuvers — BFM is aircraft-handling skill applied to a BFM problem, a specific range/angle/closure situation, not a memorized move list. (Source: Mike Solyom/The Ops Center, "How Fighter Pilots Talk About BFM | BFM Series | Part 2," quoting the USAF's own training manual.)
Governing axiom: relative to the banditEvery maneuver described in this guide — pursuit geometry, turn-circle alignment, lift-vector placement, defensive jinks, all of it — is judged relative to the bandit, not to your own heading or a fixed compass direction. "Nose ahead," "lag," "out of plane," "aligning turn circles" are all bandit-relative descriptions; the same maneuver described against an absolute heading is meaningless, since the bandit is the only reference point that actually matters mid-fight. This governs everything that follows in Part I and III — see also Lift Vector vs. Plane of Motion in High-Aspect BFM below, which works out the precise mechanics of maneuvering against the bandit's plane of motion specifically. (Per Reynard, echoing this guide's existing Mike Solyom/The Ops Center and Echo Victor source material — exact source video not pinned down.)

Altitude and speed are one budget, tradeable either direction. More of it means options — fight, disengage, reposition. Less of it means reactive by default.

  • Energy fighters — win by preserving speed/altitude, staying fast in the vertical.
  • Angles fighters — win by spending energy for a tighter turn.

Know which your aircraft is. Default to its game plan, not the opponent's.

Every airframe has two turn rates. Instantaneous — the tightest, fastest turn it can pull for a moment, at corner velocity. Sustained — a gentler rate it can hold without bleeding energy.

Corner velocity is a one-time withdrawal, not a cruising speed: turn rate and available G both drop the instant after, as speed bleeds off. Use instantaneous-max turns deliberately, for a break turn or a snap to close angle. Fly sustained-turn speed for anything held more than a couple of seconds.

Practical performance points, per Shaw

  • Unload to accelerate. Most drag at low speed and high altitude comes from making lift. Pushing toward zero G removes it: Shaw's example jet gains roughly 20–70% more acceleration this way, most at slow speed and altitude. A steep dive after unloading gives the fastest acceleration of all.
  • Weight and drag decide who wins a dive. Of two otherwise similar aircraft, the heavier one accelerates faster in a dive and reaches a higher top speed; at equal weight, the cleaner one wins. That's why a heavy fighter can often dive away from a lighter turner. Jettison drop tanks and spare ordnance when the fight starts.
  • Negative G can stop the engine. Some piston engines with float carburettors cut out under zero or negative G. In WWII, fuel-injected German fighters used steep push-over dives to escape carburetted Allied fighters. Know whether your engine and the bandit's has this weakness.
  • Props turn better one way. Engine torque and P-factor make high-powered prop fighters roll and turn better in one direction, mostly at low speed and high power, and too much the other way can cause a departure. Shaw's example: P-38s with counter-rotating props spiralled up in a full-power climbing turn while Fw 190s trying to follow spun out.

(Source: Robert Shaw, Fighter Combat, Appendix: Fighter Performance.)

Common mistakeLiving at corner velocity as if it were a cruising speed, then having nothing left three seconds into a fight that was going fine.

Corner velocity, precisely

Corner velocity is where two turn limits meet:

  • Load limit — structural/pilot G-limit; the airframe or pilot gives out first.
  • Lift limit — the wing stalls before generating more G.

Below corner speed: lift-limited. Above it: load-limited, paying drag for no extra rate. Most jets sit in the 460–740 km/h band at 3–5G — check your own aircraft's numbers, this varies by airframe.

What a lift-limited pull actually does vs. a load-limited one

Pulling back on the stick raises angle of attack, and lift with it, up to the lift limit. Past that, flow separation stalls the wing: lift drops, induced drag spikes. Which limit you hit first depends on which side of corner velocity you're on:

  • Too slow → lift-limit pull. Maximum lift the wing can generate at that energy state. Impressive instantaneous turn rate, at the direct cost of airspeed — the energy-exertion trade, spending speed for turn rate right now.
  • Too fast → load-limit pull. Flight controls (or your arm) hold you at max G, but induced drag is low at that AOA, so speed keeps building instead of bleeding off. Turn rate stays flat while turn radius keeps growing.

Neither is wrong on its own. A lift-limit pull is exactly what you want for a short, deliberate instantaneous-rate excursion. An unwanted load-limit pull, from entering a turn too fast, is how a fight that should favor you turns into a widening, losing circle instead.

Tactical rate band & energy excursions

The tactical rate band is a range of speeds that all sustain roughly the same turn rate — not one magic number. Fly at the top of it, not the bottom: that leaves speed in reserve for a deliberate energy excursion, a short above-sustained pull that buys a temporary rate or angle advantage but has to be earned back afterward.

Bleed that excursion from the top of the band and you're still inside it when you level off. Bleed it from the bottom and you're under corner speed with nothing left.

Worked example (DCS World F/A-18C Hornet, not a War Thunder figure — included only to show the shape of the concept):

  • Max-sustained-turn-rate speed: ~796 km/h
  • Rate band: ~741–852 km/h
  • Clean-aircraft max sustained rate: ~21°/sec

Fly slightly above the bottom-anchor speed, not dead-center — bank a small energy margin rather than starting every fight at the band's floor. (Source: Echo Victor, "The ULTIMATE BFM Guide," BFM-fundamentals chapter — DCS F/A-18C-specific numbers, offered here only as a worked illustration of the rate-band concept.)

Radius ≠ rate — a worked example

The tighter-looking circle doesn't automatically win.

  • Aircraft A: 491 km/h, 3.3G → 579 m radius, 13.4°/sec.
  • Aircraft B: 972 km/h, 7.5G → 991 m radius (wider), 15.6°/sec — completes a 180° turn about two seconds sooner despite the bigger circle.

Radius is distance from the turn's center, the post. Rate is angular speed around it. The two are related by G and speed together, not by radius alone — don't assume the smaller-looking loop is winning.

Specific energy vs. specific excess power

Specific energy — speed and altitude combined, per unit weight — is the budget itself. Specific excess power is how fast you can currently add to that budget: the power available beyond what's needed just to hold your current flight condition.

A jet can be fast with poor excess power at that speed/altitude/G — little left to climb or accelerate with. Or slower with plenty in reserve. When in doubt whether to trade energy now, ask "how fast can I get more back," not "how much do I have."

The EM diagram

The energy-maneuverability (EM) diagram turns this from feel into a real comparison: a plot of turn rate against speed for a given aircraft, altitude, and loadout, showing sustained and instantaneous curves at once. The US Air Force uses it as its actual combat-performance standard, not a teaching aid.

Lay your diagram against an opponent's: the curves' crossover points show directly which speeds favor which of you. That's what "knowing your energy/angles identity" means in numbers, not reputation.

War Thunder doesn't publish official EM charts, but it does have community test data: a player-run sheet that measures real in-game sustained turn rate (and the G it takes) across a speed sweep, per aircraft. That's the zero-Ps line of an EM diagram, measured rather than published — see the table below, and each Part V card's Flight Performance section for the full per-speed curve. (EM-chart framing: Mike Solyom/The Ops Center, "Learning BFM | BFM Series Intro | Part 1." Data: community "Sustained turn rate tests – War Thunder" Google Sheet.)

Reading the chart's lines

Turn rate on the vertical axis, speed on the horizontal.

  • Gold/yellow — constant turn radius.
  • Blue — constant G (e.g. ~556 km/h at 8°/sec might need 3G).
  • Green — Ps, specific excess power: energy gain/loss rate at that speed/G point. Negative Ps means descending just to hold the turn.
  • Red — the airframe's real physical limits: lift limit, G limit, speed limit.

Corner velocity: the peak point where lift-limit and G-limit lines cross. Max instantaneous, unsustainable rate, above the zero-Ps line — it costs energy to hold.

Sustained turn rate: the best point on the zero-Ps line itself. Held indefinitely, no descent or speed loss required.

One chart, one weight/altitude/throttle

An EM diagram is valid for one weight/altitude/throttle combination only, not one universal chart per airframe. Lighter, lower, and more throttle each independently shift the curves in your favor.

Altitude alone is dramatic: minimum turn radius grows from ~366 m at sea level to over 1,097 m at 9,150 m — a 300%+ increase, same weight and throttle otherwise.

Worked reference-airframe example (generic fighter, 4,540 kg / 10,000 lb, 4,570 m / 15,000 ft altitude, maximum power): ~843 km/h, ~5.75G, ~10°/sec sustained. (Reference conditions per a published generic USAF-style EM diagram: Mike Solyom/The Ops Center, "Reading an EM Diagram.")

Why a small edge compounds

A 6G pilot against a 5G-limited opponent on the same airframe: only ~2°/sec and ~244 m of turn radius apart per turn. But that edge compounds geometrically — ~56° of angular gain per full 28-second circle, a full rear-aspect position after just two circles. This is the numeric reason a small, consistently-held performance edge wins a sustained turning fight. (Source: Mike Solyom/The Ops Center, "Reading an EM Diagram.")

Turn Circles & Fight Flow

  • Turn circle: flight-path circle around a fixed "post"; size set by speed & G.
  • Bubble: you can never fly inside your own turn circle.
  • Control zone: ~760–1,370m slant range, 25–45° aspect cone — the shot-commit zone.
  • One-circle (same-direction turn): radius fight — tighter radius wins; ends in a 2nd merge.
  • Two-circle (opposite-direction turn): rate fight — higher turn rate at corner speed wins; can flip to one-circle.
  • Vertical flow: displace into the vertical, using exclusive room to deny the fight they want.

Every turn traces a circle around a notional center point: the post. How a merge resolves depends on which way both aircraft turn relative to each other and to that circle.

The post

A level, constant-bank turn traces a circle in space around a notional center point: the post. It's the fixed reference for this section's vocabulary. Radius is distance from it. Rate is angular speed about it. "Aligning turn circles" means getting your post close to the bandit's.

Turn circle, radius & rate

Officially, that circle is the turn circle (TC): an imaginary circle following the aircraft's flight path in the turn. Size is set by speed and G together — more speed at the same G makes it bigger, more G or less speed makes it smaller.

  • Turn radius — half the TC's diameter.
  • Turn rate — degrees of heading change per second on that same circle.

Same two quantities the Energy section uses, now tied to the circle they're properties of. Most of BFM reduces to visualizing these circles and exploiting what you see — the offensive fighter must align turn circles with the bandit before a shot is possible at all.

The bubble

The circle itself, and the volume an aircraft can reach at its current turn performance, is sometimes called its bubble. An aircraft can never fly inside its own bubble.

  • Outside a bandit's bubble: he can eventually turn his nose onto you.
  • Inside it: he geometrically cannot, no matter how hard he pulls, until something changes the circle's size or position.

Control point

The ideal attacking position is roughly one turn radius behind the defender, on his turn circle — called the control point.

Control zone

The control point sits inside a cone-shaped control zone: enough range and reaction time to answer whatever the defender does. The USAF training manual gives exact numbers — roughly 760–1,370 m of slant range, within a 25–45° aspect-angle cone. Close enough to be near the bandit's turn circle. Far enough to still have reaction time to refine position rather than committing blind.

The third element: the attack window

Bubble and control zone are two of three elements of a turn circle. The third: the attack window — a specific point in space where an Attack Window Entry delivers range, angles, and closure all under control at once, not one at a time.

An Attack Window Entry is mechanically an offensive break turn: max afterburner, roll to 90° of bank, pull to whichever limit (lift or load) your energy state gives you, for the maximum turn rate available right then — timed to start exactly inside that window, not early or late.

"Aligning turn circles," in other words, is maneuvering until you're standing in the attack window before you commit to that break turn. (Source: Echo Victor, "The ULTIMATE BFM Guide," BFM-fundamentals chapter — resolves this guide's long-standing "Attack Window Entry" gap.)

Misaligned turn circles — reading and using the sight picture

A misaligned turn circle shows up directly in the canopy: the target bobs up and down in the sight picture. The more it oscillates, the more misaligned the two circles are.

The fix: work out roughly where both circles' posts are, then extend at the correct point to shift yours into alignment and reset the pull. Same idea as the Energy section's corner-velocity material and the Turn Circle Extension technique below, just read visually instead of numerically.

Misalignment can also be left alone and exploited: if your positioning is otherwise sound, it will often bring the bandit to bear on its own. When that happens, just align the pipper and take the shot. (Source: Echo Victor, "The ULTIMATE BFM Guide," BFM-fundamentals chapter.)

Turning room

Turning room is space around either aircraft that can still be exploited to solve an angles problem. It's reciprocal — room available to the attacker is equally available to the defender.

  • Lateral turning room — available to either aircraft equally.
  • Vertical turning room — can be exclusive to just one of you. A bandit low on energy may not have it at all; flying too high into it risks a stall, or worse near the ground.

Passing close to a bandit without room to spare leaves no space to convert onto his tail. Opening the gap slightly before the pass — deliberately building turning room — is what makes that conversion possible afterward.

Angle vocabulary, straight from the manual

TermMeaning
Aspect angle (AA)Angle off the bandit's tail — 0° directly astern, 180° head-on (why a head-on merge is "high-aspect")
Heading crossing angle (HCA)Also called angle-off — the heading difference between the two aircraft
Antenna train angle (ATA)Usually called angle-off-nose — how far your radar has to slew from your own heading to point at the bandit
Angle-off-tail (AOT)Same measurement as ATA, taken from your tail instead of your nose — reads identically to ATA when the bandit is actually on your tail, which is why the two get used interchangeably in a defensive situation

Situational Awareness & the OODA Loop

  • SA is continuous, not occasional — it decays fastest exactly when you're task-focused mid-attack.
  • Habit loop: attack → disengage → immediate six check → re-scan → reassess → decide.
  • OODA: Observe → Orient → Decide → Act — cycle it faster than your opponent.
  • When ambiguous, default to the choice that preserves options (disengage, gain energy), not freezing for certainty.
  • Common mistake: target fixation — locking on so hard that six, altitude, and fuel all stop getting checked.
  • Scan: sweep with peripheral vision rather than staring; refocus on something distant every few seconds; move your head to see past canopy frames.
  • Spot and hide: look for shadows over light ground, contrails and smoke. Approach on a collision course against a darker background.

SA is a continuously maintained model of the fight, not something checked occasionally. It decays fastest exactly when you're task-focused mid-attack. That's also when you're most exposed. Build the habit loop: attack → disengage → immediate six check → re-scan → reassess → decide. Never chain straight from "I hit my target" into "I look for the next one" without the check in between.

Underneath every mechanical skill is how fast you cycle Observe → Orient → Decide → Act relative to your opponent. Orient is the stage this whole guide exists to improve. Two pilots can see the same picture and draw different conclusions based on what they know. When a situation is ambiguous, default to the choice that preserves options — disengage, gain energy — rather than freezing for more certainty.

Common mistakeTarget fixation — locking onto a kill so hard that six, altitude, and fuel all stop getting checked. The single most common way a winning fight turns into a loss.

Visual scan, per Shaw

Shaw puts it plainly: about nine out of ten air-to-air victims never knew they were under attack until they were fired on. Seeing first is most of the fight.

  • Sweep, don't search sector by sector. Detailed sector search is too slow to keep you safe; it suits looking for a target you already expect. For defense, sweep the eyes and head back and forth fairly quickly and let peripheral vision catch movement. The eyes only see while they pause, so let them stop briefly during each sweep.
  • Fix your focus first. Eyes staring at empty sky relax to focus a few feet away, often on the canopy. Focus on a distant cloud or ground feature, then shift your scan to the area of interest. Repeat every few seconds.
  • Cover everything regularly: above and below the horizon, forward and aft to the limits of view on both sides. Roll or turn to see past the aircraft's blind areas. Weight the likely threat sector most, but never ignore any sector for long. In a pair, each pilot scans toward the other.
  • Move your head forward and back and side to side. It clears areas hidden by canopy frames, and the brain filters out canopy spots because they move with your head.
  • Use a cue when you have one. A radar or other pointer narrows the search to a small area, which gives the earliest visual pick-up.

Spotting and staying unseen

  • A low aircraft over light, uniform ground on a sunny day leaves a dark shadow even from 600–900 m up. Watch the ground for shadows; avoid making one.
  • Contrails and heavy engine smoke can be seen from 30+ km. Stay out of the contrail level.
  • A collision-course approach makes you sit still in the enemy's view, so peripheral vision is less likely to catch you. Pointing your nose straight at him also shows the smallest profile.
  • Pick a background that matches your aircraft's shade, and when in doubt the darker one. Don't approach level against the bright horizon or a light cloud, which silhouette you. Coming out of a bright sun is the classic approach; a low, dull sun doesn't hide you.

(Source: Robert Shaw, Fighter Combat, ch.10 Tactical Intercepts, "Visual Considerations in Air Combat.")

Pursuit Geometry

  • Lead pursuit (nose ahead of his path): closes fastest, overshoots if held too long.
  • Pure pursuit (nose at him now): intuitive, but the least efficient way to close.
  • Lag pursuit (nose behind his path): gains no ground, conserves energy, hides in his blind spot.
  • Beginner default: lead to close/get an angle → pure just long enough to line up the shot → lag if overtaking too fast.

Where your nose points relative to a bandit's flight path — not his current position — decides whether the gap closes, holds, or blows past. Lead pursuit (nose ahead of his path) closes fastest but overshoots if held too long. Pure pursuit (nose at him now) is intuitive but the least efficient way to close. Lag pursuit (nose behind his path) gains no ground but conserves energy and hides in his blind spot.

Beginner default: pull lead to close and get an angle → ease to pure just long enough to line up the shot → back off to lag if overtaking too fast.

The same three variables, every time

All three geometries manage the same three variables: range, angle-off, and closure.

  • Lead pursuit: closes fastest but rapidly increases angle-off — good for a gun snapshot or when angles don't matter.
  • Pure pursuit: cuts the corner more gradually and keeps the bandit centered in a missile seeker's gimbal.
  • Lag pursuit: the only one that can reduce closure or extend range, making it the tool for avoiding an overshoot rather than causing one. Costs you nose-off (outside gun/missile gimbal limits), and held too long lets the bandit regain energy and slip back to neutral.

Hot-side vs. cold-side lag

Lag isn't one fixed position.

  • Hot-side lag: more forward separation, shows you the top of the bandit's aircraft.
  • Cold-side lag: closes tighter, sits low in his blind spot, seeing mostly his belly.

Both control the same three variables — just trading range for concealment differently.

Reading a bandit's pursuit curve visually

The same three geometries are just as readable on an attacker as on your own aircraft, useful for reading an incoming bandit on defense.

  • Pure pursuit: narrow, nose-on profile — the tell for an incoming IR shot, since a missile needs pure pursuit to keep its seeker on you.
  • Lead pursuit: shows you his belly, a good early warning he's setting up a gunshot, since guns need lead pursuit in a turning fight.
  • Lag pursuit: shows you his topside, usually paired with an LOS shift toward the aft of your canopy. Means his closure is too high or he's repositioning for a better angle.

Telling lead from pure apart can be hard and varies by aircraft. The required lead depends on gun cant angle: a dedicated air-to-air platform may cant guns up to reduce required lead, a ground-attack-optimized one may cant them down. (Source: Mike Solyom/The Ops Center, "Defensive Ranging Exercise.")

Out-of-plane pursuit

All three geometries also work out of plane — off the bandit's own plane of maneuver. Place your lift vector ahead of, on, or behind him, adjusting roll continuously to hold that geometry as he turns. It's a common last-resort way to bleed an overshoot without crossing his flight path. A weapon fired out of plane has a worse shot: a missile drifts toward its gimbal edge instead of staying centered, and guns fired out of plane have very low hit probability.

Overshoots — know which kind you just caused

Two overshoot types exist, by severity.

  • Wingline overshoot: you cross the defender's 3–9 line (his wingtip-to-wingtip line) — a full role reversal. Now you're the one who needs to defend.
  • Flight-path overshoot: less severe — you cross behind his actual flight path rather than his airframe.
  • Control-zone overshoot: a mild flight-path overshoot — you cross outside his control zone, and he continues the same turn with angles mostly intact.
  • In-close overshoot: the more dangerous flight-path overshoot — close enough, inside his control zone, that he can reverse his turn into you and force a wingline overshoot instead.

Lag pursuit and yo-yos exist specifically to stay on the right side of that line.

Show maneuver catalog (solo)
MoveTypeWhat it does
High yo-yoOffenseClosing too fast on a turning target: ease the bank, pull up and across into a new plane, bleed the excess speed, drop back in behind before overshooting.
Low yo-yoOffenseFalling behind: roll nose-low into a steeper slice below the target's plane, trading altitude for an instantaneous speed increase that closes range and improves angle without overshooting.
Lead turnOffenseTurn early into where the target's flight path is going, not where it is now — sets up the merge before he's even level with you. The core skill behind a stern conversion.
Lag displacement rollOffenseToo close or too much angle-off in lead/pure pursuit: roll away from the turn, then pull back in once your lift vector re-aligns on the bandit — brings you from lead back to pure or lag, preventing the lead-pursuit overshoot.
Barrel roll attackOffenseCounter to a defender's break turn: roll away from his break while simultaneously looping, so the combined roll+loop (a helical path) ends with your nose already pointed along his direction of travel instead of chasing his turn directly.
High-side guns passOffense"Boom and zoom" / "hit and split": dive on a lower, slower opponent using stored altitude as speed, take the shot, zoom back up to a safe perch. Favors an energy fighter against a more maneuverable target it doesn't want to turn with.
Quarter PlaneOffenseLast-resort fix for a rapid, excessive closure rate about to overshoot the bandit's 3-9 line. As range breaks about 300 m — wingspan fills half the sight ring — roll wings-level relative to the bandit ("feet on the bandit"), idle power, and pull a max-performance pull-up out of his plane of motion to arrest closure, then roll back into the turn.
Break turnDefenseSomeone on your tail: turn hard across their path (the Defensive Break Turn), using your smaller radius and higher angular rate to raise angle-off-tail fast. Briefly exposes your plan-form (a "snapshot" risk) — that's the trade for denying a stable follow-on shot.
Flat / rolling scissorsDefenseMutual-overshoot fight of repeated reversals. Flat scissors follow a low-speed horizontal overshoot — reverse and try to force the attacker out front. Rolling scissors follow a high-speed overshoot from above — reverse into a vertical climb/barrel roll, forcing him to try to follow. Only stay in it with a turn-rate edge. Judge who's winning by the vertical 3-9 line (downrange displacement), not nose position.
Guns defense / jinkDefenseRandom, arbitrary changes to your flight path — yaw, skid, slip, pitch, roll — that deliberately decouple your nose from your velocity vector, spoiling a tracking gun solution by presenting a constantly shifting target rather than a predictable one.
High-G barrel rollDefenseLast-ditch response once an attacker already has a guns solution — a much more violent version of the offensive barrel roll, flown over-the-top or underneath. Rarely causes a full wingline overshoot, but typically forces a flight-path overshoot or drags the fight into a scissors.
Defensive spiralDefenseLast resort once energy is spent: nose-low descending spiral using gravity itself to keep generating evasive turn performance, staying out of phase with the attacker. Buys time at the direct cost of altitude — watch the hard deck, since impact is a guaranteed kill (Pk = 1) that ends the trade either way.
Unloaded extensionDisengageZero the G, nose down, full throttle — the fastest way to build range once there's any separation.
Bug-outDisengageOnly when a genuinely clean escape opens up: turn away and accelerate while using brief check turns (shallow glances back) to keep eyes on the bandit as you separate — not blind running.
Sideclimb / wingoverDisengageAngled climb or a quarter-loop-over-quarter-loop reversal — rebuilds altitude and energy for another pass.

Offensive BFM

  • Lose sight, lose the fight — stay padlocked on the bandit.
  • Maneuver against the bandit's plane of motion, not your own nose or even his lift vector.
  • Manage energy deliberately — trade it for nose position only when you actually need it.
  • Kill quickly — a shot and a disengage beats a prolonged turning fight.
  • Stay offensive — don't trade a secure position for a low-probability speculative shot.
  • If neutralized, transition deliberately toward your own strengths (see High-Aspect BFM) rather than repeat a plan that stopped working.
  • Goal: drive into the control zone with range, angles, and closure all under control at once.
  • High yo-yo: trade airspeed for altitude to prevent an overshoot when closing too fast.
  • Low yo-yo: trade altitude for closure when trapped in lag pursuit and falling behind.
  • Snapshot: if the bandit reverses in front of you, fly through his flight path and take the shot early — don't match the reversal.
Core BFM axiomsThree rules sit underneath everything else in this section, offense or defense.
  • Lose sight, lose the fight: stay padlocked on the bandit — every technique below assumes you still have him.
  • Maneuver relative to the bandit's plane of motion, not your own nose position or even his lift vector — react to where he's actually going.
  • Manage energy deliberately: trade excess energy for nose position only when you actually need it, not by default.
Three tenets, before the mechanics
  • Kill quickly — a prolonged turning fight narrows your attention and burns fuel. That's exactly when a mistake or a missed six-check costs you the engagement. The goal is a shot and a disengage, not a sustained "movie dogfight."
  • Stay offensive — as long as the bandit is reacting to you rather than the reverse, he's constrained in what he can do. Don't trade a secure offensive position for a low-probability speculative shot.
  • If neutralized, transition deliberately — the instant you lose the offensive, assess both aircraft's strengths and weaknesses, then actively drive the fight toward yours (see High-Aspect BFM below) instead of continuing the plan that just stopped working.

The whole of offensive BFM reduces to one goal: drive into the control zone with range, angles, and closure all under control at once — not any one of the three alone.

Turn circle entry is where most of the above actually gets applied. Its timing is unforgiving in both directions: enter too early and you overshoot; enter too late and your circle ends up misaligned with his, costing you the angles you were trying to gain.

The high and low yo-yo are the two standard corrections either side of that window.

  • High yo-yo: trades airspeed for altitude to prevent an overshoot when you're closing too fast.
  • Low yo-yo: trades altitude for an instantaneous closure increase when you're trapped in lag pursuit and falling behind.

If the bandit reverses his turn in front of you rather than committing away — a snapshot opportunity — the answer is to fly through his flight path and take the shot early, rather than trying to match his reversal.

Reading line-of-sight rate

Line-of-sight rate is how fast the bandit moves across your canopy or HUD. It's a function of angle-off and closure, not turn rate — even two aircraft flying straight and level with lateral offset generate LOS rate. It's a useful early warning that you're approaching his bubble, though not the only one. Direction matters as much as speed.

  • Bandit crawling forward across the canopy (toward the nose): you're gaining on his turn circle, closing the angles problem.
  • Bandit sliding aft (toward the tail): the opposite — you're losing the turn-rate battle.

A LOS rate that suddenly reverses direction is usually the tell that you've just crossed the bandit's turn circle.

The vertical 3-9 line

The normal 3-9 line (wingtip to wingtip) is referenced to the lift vector. Its vertical extension is referenced to the weight vector instead. That's the more reliable read in a rolling scissors, where each aircraft's downrange displacement matters more than where its nose happens to be pointed at any instant.

Lift vector vs. plane of motion

The "maneuver relative to the bandit" axiom above has a precise meaning. Your lift vector is the line straight up out of the canopy, perpendicular to the wings — the direction the wings are actually generating lift toward. Your plane of motion (POM) is different: the direction you're actually traveling, which also depends on yaw, angle of attack, G, and airspeed. The two converge as G increases, but there's normally a real gap between them. You maneuver against the bandit's plane of motion — where he's actually going — not the line his wings happen to be pointing along at that instant. (Source: Mike Solyom/The Ops Center, "How Fighter Pilots Talk About BFM | BFM Series | Part 2," which also supplied the AA/HCA/ATA/AOT angle definitions and control-zone numbers in the Turn Circles section above.)

Closing for the gun shot — the Rule of Threes

Before pulling into a gun shot, confirm all three at once: roughly 900 m of range, roughly 30° of aspect angle (AA), and a steady, controllable closure rate.

  • Judging range by stadiametric ranging — how much of the gunsight ring the bandit's wingspan fills: a full ring ≈ 150 m, half the ring ≈ 300 m, the gap between two smaller reference marks ≈ 900 m.
  • Judging aspect with an imaginary box around the bandit's silhouette: at 90° (beam) it draws a rectangle, fuselage longer than wingspan in apparent length; at 30° it looks roughly square.

If range and closure are already good but the box still reads rectangular, ease back on the stick slightly to widen your circle and shrink aspect — an ease reposition. It's fine to go under 30° AA; the rule is to avoid going above it, since a higher aspect makes the tracking solution harder. A valid tracking shot needs the pipper held on target for a minimum 0.5 continuous seconds inside that range band. Anything shorter is a snapshot, not a tracking shot. (Source: Mike Solyom/The Ops Center, "Your First BFM Exercise — Heat-To-Guns.")

Weapon engagement zones by aspect angle (real-world USAF reference)

A companion framework to the Rule of Threes above, keyed to aspect rather than range alone. Real-world USAF employment doctrine for the AIM-9P missile family and the gun lays out three nested weapon engagement zones (WEZ), each valid only within its own aspect-angle cone.

  • Gun: widest cone, usable out to roughly 135° of aspect (well forward of the beam), but only at close range. Reference range marks sit at roughly 305 m, 610 m, and 760 m (1,000 / 2,000 / 2,500 ft); the diagram doesn't state what distinguishes the three beyond all sitting inside the gun's envelope.
  • AIM-9P+ (the product-improved, more all-aspect-capable seeker): needs the target within roughly 90° of aspect (from the beam aft), reaching out to roughly 1,370 m (4,500 ft).
  • AIM-9P (the older, less sensitive seeker): needs a tighter 45° of aspect, closer to a tail shot, but rewards it with the longest envelope of the three — roughly 2,740 m (9,000 ft).

None of these specific weapons exist in War Thunder or Ace Combat, but the underlying principle transfers directly: a weapon's real engagement envelope isn't one range number — it shrinks hard as the target's aspect angle opens up. That's exactly why the Rule of Threes above caps AA at 30° for a gun shot, and why a defender who presents high aspect denies far more of your shot envelope than range alone would suggest. (Source: Mike Solyom/The Ops Center, referencing US Air Force AIM-9P/gun weapon-engagement-zone doctrine — real-world reference envelope, not a War Thunder or Ace Combat weapon system.)

Training drills for offensive BFM

Two structured exercises worth flying deliberately rather than just reading about.

  • 900 m perch drill for the Quarter Plane maneuver above: starts inside the bandit's turn circle, bandit defensive and slower, fighter carrying deliberate excess closure to force the technique.
  • Medium Range OBFM exercise, using a 1,830 m perch that starts outside the bandit's turn circle: first task is aligning turn circles before anything else. The bandit wins by reaching 720° of total turn (two full circles) on a max-performance sustained turn before the fighter can close for the Rule-of-Threes shot. A simple way to judge 720°: start facing a cardinal heading and count passing it twice after "fights on."

Every number here — perch distance, speeds, AA limit, bandit power restriction — is a suggested, adjustable training parameter, not a fixed rule.

To cleanly end any BFM training rep over the radio, any flight member transmits the flight's call sign plus "knock it off" or "terminate." Use "knock it off" when a safety-of-flight factor or genuine doubt/confusion exists; use "terminate" for a routine, no-issue end. Every other member then acknowledges in turn with their own position number — e.g., "Iron one, knock it off," "Iron two, knock it off." (Source: Mike Solyom/The Ops Center, "Quarter Plane / Medium Range OBFM Exercise.")

PADS Setup — a US Navy training-scenario format

A second, more formal way to brief a repeatable training engagement, distinct from the perch drills above: PADS — Position, Altitude, Distance, Speed.

  • Position: the starting formation, typically Combat Spread (also called Abeam).
  • Altitude: set for both aircraft.
  • Distance and Speed: set once and flown to.

Because no two players will hit the exact numbers, allowable deviations are defined up front: ±30 m of altitude, ±185 m (±0.1 nm) of distance, ±10° of bearing, and ±19 km/h (±10 kts) of speed. Treat any of these four numbers as a template to adapt, not a fixed standard — the value of PADS is having all four agreed before "fights on," not the specific figures. (Source: Echo Victor, "The ULTIMATE BFM Guide," offensive-BFM chapter.)

Attack Window Entry, and countering a defender's Ditch

The attack window and Attack Window Entry are defined above in Turn Circles & Fight Flow: the offensive break turn, timed to start exactly inside the bandit's attack window, that delivers range, angles, and closure all under control at once.

Once you're closing for that shot, a defender may try to deny it with the Ditch: rolling 90° and pulling a maximum-rate pure nose-low pull. This denies the shot, and may force an overshoot outright. Just as importantly, it rotates his control zone up and away from you, actively denying angles rather than just running. Spot it quickly — a slow reaction here is how a should-be-easy kill turns into a lag-pursuit chase.

Counter it with a Ditch Follow:

  • Point your nose at his point of departure and drive toward it in a climb rather than following him straight down. The climb preserves your energy (banking potential energy) and hands you an altitude advantage on top of it.
  • From there, initiate a Split-S or similar pure nose-low maneuver: roll inverted, max-perform through a nose-low pull, and select IDLE throttle once pointed down so speed doesn't run past the rate band. You exit pointing the opposite cardinal direction, having traded some altitude for staying max-performing throughout.
  • Bring your nose back onto him for a tracking guns solution: place the crosshair on target and squeeze.

Timing is everything — a poorly timed Ditch Follow leaves you stuck in lag pursuit, unable to get Sensor Nose On at all. (Source: Echo Victor, "The ULTIMATE BFM Guide," offensive-BFM chapter — resolves this guide's long-standing "Ditch Follow" gap.)

Countering a defender's Radius Defence

The other escape a defender being pulled for guns may reach for is a radius defence: an oblique nose-low redefinition that trades altitude for energy to shrink his turn radius and deny you angles. If he redefines nose-low too early you'll see him come forward in the canopy, but he pays for it with a flight-path overshoot of his own.

Answer with a Radius Defence Follow:

  • The instant you identify it, extend immediately to gain energy, then drive toward his point of redefinition and re-enter the turn.
  • Done correctly, he should appear roughly 15° below the horizon with a stable line-of-sight rate. Place your lift vector slightly above him and follow him down.

From there you have two options: take an energy exertion and the shot it buys you, or simply wait for the deck to become a factor for him. The second option forces him to level out and hands you the misaligned-turn-circle exploitation described in Turn Circles above. (Source: Echo Victor, "The ULTIMATE BFM Guide," offensive-BFM chapter — resolves this guide's long-standing "Radius Defence Follow" gap.)

Snapshot on a reversing defender — the full sequence

If a defender commits what one source calls "the cardinal sin" — reversing his turn directly in front of you rather than committing away — don't try to match the reversal. Immediately reposition for a snapshot instead. The gun pipper will begin rapidly transiting toward him. Fly the pipper through the target rather than chasing it onto him: squeeze the trigger just before the pipper reaches the target and release as soon as it passes through, to avoid wasting rounds on either side of the brief window. The sequence isn't finished when the trigger is released. Immediately transition into lag pursuit, then re-enter the turn, to hold the positional advantage the reversal just handed you rather than letting a one-off shot be the whole plan. (Source: Echo Victor, "The ULTIMATE BFM Guide," offensive-BFM chapter — enriches this guide's earlier, partial coverage of this maneuver.)

D1Heat-To-Guns — the Rule of Threes
  • Aim: confirm all three Rule-of-Threes conditions before pulling into a gun shot — about 900 m of range, 30° of aspect or less, and a steady closure rate.
  • Setup: the starting geometry is not recorded in the material this guide holds. ?
  • Fly it: judge range by how much of the gunsight ring the bandit's wingspan fills (full ring about 150 m, half the ring about 300 m, the gap between two smaller marks about 900 m). Judge aspect with the imaginary box: rectangle means aspect is too high, roughly square means about 30°. If range and closure are good and only the box is still a rectangle, ease back slightly on the stick (an ease reposition).
  • Pass (suggested by the source): a valid tracking shot — pipper on the target and trigger held at least 0.5 s continuously inside the range band — within 180° of turn after the Fox-2 shot, counted on the compass heading. Missing it flags a gap to work on; anything shorter than 0.5 s is a snapshot, not a pass.

(Source: Mike Solyom/The Ops Center, "Your First BFM Exercise — Heat-To-Guns." Every number is the source's own suggested, adjustable training parameter.)

D2Quarter Plane — stopping a runaway closure
  • Setup: the 3,000-ft perch — start about 1,830 m apart and call "fights on" at about 915 m. Bandit defensive, both aircraft start at about 650 km/h and the bandit ends at about 585 km/h by "fights on"; the fighter is faster to create closure (his exact speed is garbled in the source). ?
  • Fly it: resist the urge to slow down early — keep the closure high so you can practice the move, gun side on the bandit. When range is about to break 305 m (the bandit's wingspan fills half the gunsight ring): roll wings-level relative to the bandit, set idle power, and pull a maximum-performance pull-up out of his plane of motion. Once closure is arrested, roll back into a turn with him and keep fighting.
  • Pass: the source states no pass/fail test. It is a last-resort move to drill until it is instinctive, not the normal way to manage closure.

(Source: Mike Solyom/The Ops Center, "Quarter Plane / Medium Range OBFM Exercise." Every number is the source's own suggested, adjustable training parameter.)

D3Medium Range OBFM — the offensive "final exam"
  • Setup: the 6,000-ft perch, which starts outside the bandit's turn circle — begin about 2,745 m apart and call "fights on" at about 1,830 m, both aircraft holding about 650 km/h. Start facing a cardinal heading and check-turn 45° left to build the perch.
  • Bandit's job: fly a maximum-performance sustained turn (hold the best sustained-turn speed from the EM chart, track accumulated turn on the heading indicator). For a beginner fighter, limit the bandit to military power with no afterburner and remove that limit as you improve.
  • Fly it: (1) find the bandit's turn circle — a sudden shift in line-of-sight rate marks it; (2) reposition into the control zone, with the bandit just above the canopy bow; (3) confirm the Rule of Threes (about 900 m, 30° aspect or less, steady closure); (4) ease the pipper up and hold the trigger at least 0.5 s.
  • Pass: a valid gun shot before the bandit reaches 720° of turn — he gets there when he passes the starting cardinal heading two more times after "fights on."

(Source: Mike Solyom/The Ops Center, "Quarter Plane / Medium Range OBFM Exercise." The two earlier exercises in that video used a passive bandit; this is the first with an actively evading one. Every number is the source's own suggested, adjustable training parameter.)

Defensive BFM

  • Assume the bandit is at least as good as you, probably better.
  • Priority order: survive first → deny him a sensor (a stable firing solution) → defeat the shots he does get off.
  • Survival is winning, not delaying — drag a fight to 2 circles (~72s) and every friendly within ~23km can join.
  • Read his entry, then pick: force a bad shot, prolong to buy time, or neutralize and escape — no fixed playbook.
  • Bug-out only on a genuinely clean opening — accelerate away using check turns, not blind running.
  • A reversal is a bet: right moment flips you to neutral/winning; wrong moment hands him an easier shot. If in doubt, don't.
  • Force a low-speed overshoot and you're in a flat scissors — win it on your tightest sustained turn, not by out-accelerating him.
  • Against guns: a max-performance break turn toward the attacker, then jink to spoil his tracking solution.
  • Behind on angles: aim for neutral first, not straight for offense. Fix angles before energy. A break turn is wasted when a hard turn will do.
  • You had the advantage and lost it? The trend rarely reverses — bug out while it's still neutral.
  • Your hard deck outranks the fight itself — impact is a guaranteed kill (Pk = 1) regardless of who was winning.
Mindset & defensive axiomsDefault assumption going in: the bandit is at least as good as you, probably better. Plan for his best game, not his average one. Three axioms, in strict priority order:
  • Survive first, above every other consideration.
  • Deny him a sensor: don't let him get a stable firing solution — this matters more than any single evasive maneuver.
  • Only once those hold, defeat the shots he does get off.

Why survival ranks first, in numbers: a fighter in a sustained turn takes roughly 36 seconds per circle, and a friendly at Mach 1 covers about 11 km in that time. Drag the fight out two circles (72 seconds) and every friendly within about 23 km can join. Staying alive is winning, not just delaying losing.

The sequence: the Defensive Break Turn buys the first bit of angle and time. What you do next depends entirely on how the bandit answers it. Read his entry into your turn circle, then pick from three broad options.

  • Force him into a bad shot or a follow-on you can exploit.
  • Prolong the fight to buy time or altitude.
  • Actively work to neutralize and escape.

None of those is automatically correct — which one's available is set by his entry, not by a fixed playbook.

Bug-out. If a clean escape opportunity actually opens up, take it deliberately — turning away and accelerating while using check turns (brief glances back through a shallow turn) to keep eyes on the bandit as you separate, not just running blind.

Change the fight to suit you rather than just surviving the fight he started. Every reversal, yo-yo, or plane change is a chance to re-present a different problem than the one he planned for. A reversal specifically is a bet: done at the right moment it can flip you from losing to neutral or winning; done at the wrong moment — too early, while he still has the angle and energy to punish it — it just hands him an easier shot. If in doubt, don't reverse.

If you do force a low-speed overshoot, you're now very likely in a flat scissors — the fight to force him out in front, using your own tightest sustained turn rather than trying to out-accelerate him.

Against a guns solution specifically, a maximum-performance break turn toward the attacker rotates him into your forward hemisphere, increasing his angle-off-tail and denying the easy stern shot. The jink itself is about rolling to present as slim a profile as possible while forcing the attacker to continually adjust his own plane of motion just to stay tracking. Every correction he has to make is time his gunsight isn't settled. Altitude is a resource here too, not just a background number. Impact is a guaranteed kill (Pk = 1) regardless of who was winning the turn a second earlier, so know your hard deck and treat it as a harder limit than the bandit is.

Starting at a disadvantage — Shaw's method

Assess first. An angular disadvantage is easy to see: whoever's nose is closer to pointing at the other has it, and the gap is the difference in turn each needs to point. An energy disadvantage is harder. Assume the higher aircraft has more energy unless you know you're much faster. Nose-to-nose turns are the best speed check: when similar aircraft both pull hard, the slower one ends up inside the faster one's flight path. Zooming to zero airspeed settles it, but only do that if you're sure, because the loser is in serious trouble at the top.

Once a trend sets in 1v1, it rarely reverses without a real mistake by the winner. If you had the advantage and lost it, you're losing even while still neutral, so that is the moment to bug out.

  • Angular disadvantage: don't panic, and don't try to go straight from defense to offense; aim for neutral without being shot. Use only the reaction the situation needs. Against an out-of-range bandit, an in-plane turn hard enough to bring him to your nose by the time he reaches range is enough.
  • He drifts to lag pursuit: keep pulling just hard enough to deny your six, using a shallow nose-low turn if needed. If that turn would have to be steeper than about 10–15° nose-low, reverse instead, level or slightly nose-low. A nose-high reversal usually leads to a zoom contest or a rolling scissors, neither of which suits you until you know his energy. Meet him head-on, level with or below him, at or below corner speed, with no more than about a quarter turn radius of altitude difference.
  • He goes out of plane (high yo-yo, barrel roll): stop the defensive turn and make an unloaded, nose-low extension while holding your bank angle, so he can't read it. As his climb angle peaks and he pulls back in, either escape if you have the separation, or turn hard back toward him in the closest direction with your lift vector on or slightly below him.
  • He starts more than about 90° ahead: defend against his weapon first. Against guns, make a hard in-plane turn toward him until he nears firing parameters, then go out of plane to spoil his aim. If a missile is possible, start a break turn toward him now, lift vector slightly below him, to hold him outside rear-quarter missile limits and keep speed for missile defense.
  • Energy disadvantage: escaping is an honourable choice. If you stay, work below him, make him come down to fight and keep the fight horizontal. Fly nose-to-nose turns at about minimum sustained-turn-radius speed, roughly 1.5× power-on stall speed for most jets and slower for props, where a similar bandit can't out-turn you whatever his speed. That speed is well below corner, so it's risky with other threats around. If he passes well above you, zoom to within about a quarter of a turn radius of his altitude just before the pass to deny him an overhead attack.

(Source: Robert Shaw, Fighter Combat, ch.3 One-versus-One Maneuvering, Similar Aircraft.)

The four defensive axioms, precisely

A second, more actionable framing of the mindset callout above, keyed directly to what you're actually seeing on the bandit.

  • First, survive: deny him "sensor nose" (a stable nose-on tracking position), then defeat whatever shots he does get off, in that priority order.
  • Second, if he's moving forward in your canopy toward your nose, maintain your current pull. It's working — keep bringing him forward.
  • Third, if he's becoming thinner in profile, he's pulling lead for a guns shot. ("Thinner in profile" means his target aspect is reducing toward pointing straight at you.) Immediately increase your pull to hold his nose off — this may mean deliberately bleeding speed toward the bottom of your rate band for a momentary instantaneous-rate boost. If he still holds the lead position after that, jink to defeat the shot itself rather than trying to out-turn it.
  • Fourth, if he's within about 60° of your tail, not moving forward in your canopy, but still reducing target aspect, redefine the fight. Transition to a nose-high fight if you have high excess energy, nose-low if you don't. Continuing straight ahead on that flight path leads to an eventually-unavoidable guns hit.

Two terms this framework leans on: line-of-sight rate is how fast the opponent moves forward or aft in your canopy; target aspect is the angle between his nose and you — zero when he's pointed straight at you, negative once he starts pulling past that for lead. (Source: Echo Victor, "The ULTIMATE BFM Guide," defensive-BFM chapter.)

Shaw's break-turn-and-roll sequence

Shaw's own defensive-maneuvering advice against guns still holds up. A maximum-performance break turn toward the attacker rotates him into your forward hemisphere, increasing AOT and denying the easy stern shot. If he still holds a firing position, roll roughly 90° either direction into a maneuver that inscribes something close to a circle around the shooter's own aircraft rather than away from it. The modern "high-G barrel roll" is the same idea.

Target-aspect angle (TAA) and why it matters to a gunsight

How much lead a gun shot actually needs comes down to target-aspect angle (TAA): the angle between your velocity vector and his line of sight to you. TAA is zero flying straight at him, 90° flying past him abeam. The closer to abeam you present, the more lead his gunsight has to compute. That's part of why a jink that keeps changing your aspect is so effective against a human eye or a fixed sight.

Recognizing a reversal opportunity

A good reversal picture, per the USAF manual: a high heading crossing angle (HCA) combined with close range, and/or a high LOS rate. Ask "does it look like he'll cross behind my tail with a little help from me?" A steady, pure-pursuit bandit is a no.

Execute with an unloaded roll: quickly reduce backstick pressure, roll to the other side, then resume pulling once established in the new turn. It's unloaded specifically because rolling under G burns energy you want to save.

  • Place your lift vector on the bandit if he's still far away, to use the turning room available.
  • Place it above or below him if he's already close, to actively build turning room.

A correctly executed reversal lands you in a scissors — not ideal, but neutral-or-better, which beats staying defensive.

Cross-checks & the floor

Three variables control your turn rate and deserve constant cross-checking alongside the bandit: lift vector, G, and airspeed — the same three the EM diagram above turns into a real number. A fourth belongs in the same habit: altitude. With altitude to spare, you can trade it for turn performance by lowering the lift vector below the horizon (borrowing above the zero-Ps line). Once you reach your chosen floor — a minimum altitude standing in for the ground — that trade is no longer available, and you must fly the sustained, zero-Ps turn and no higher.

Close-range defensive tools: Tighten Down, Out-of-Plane, the Jink

Tighten Down (TD): pull back on the stick while already in a sustained turn, cashing in saved energy for a temporary, unsustainable turn rate. This pushes your vulnerable rear quarter outside the bandit's ~45° AA weapon-employment zone and raises his heading crossing angle. The sudden speed loss also creates a high-closure problem that forces him to reposition — watch for the resulting reversal picture above.

Out-of-Plane (OOP): an unloaded roll (under 1G, never negative) to reset the lift vector off the bandit's shared plane of motion, then a smooth pull onto a new plane in either direction. Costs little energy and can be repeated in alternating directions. Assess for a reversal opportunity after each one.

The Jink: a genuine last resort, combining both of the above. Only once the bandit is actually pulling lead for a gun solution: go idle power, unload, set the lift vector below the bandit, then execute a maximum-onset two-hand pull into the lift vector, held to the edge of an aerodynamic stall. This drastically slows you and forces the bandit to reposition, at the cost of real altitude each repetition — use caution once within a few hundred meters of your floor. If no reversal appears, repeat to the opposite side rather than giving up. (Source: Mike Solyom/The Ops Center, "How To Survive A Close Range Dogfight.")

Guns Defence "Jink" — three quicker, explicit methods

A second source describes the same guns-defense jink as three distinct, quicker roll-based techniques rather than the sustained stall-edge pull above. Worth having all three in reserve rather than treating the Jink as one fixed move. The aim in every case is the same: present as slim a target profile as possible, and defeat the attacker's already-computed lead angle by forcing him to reposition for a new plane of motion.

  • Method one — roll and pull nose high: roll to place your inside wing on the target, then pull hard upward. The attacker has to react quickly and re-roll to retake the shot.
  • Method two — roll and pull nose low: roll to place your outside wing on the target, then pull hard downward. Effective, but watch the deck — it becomes a factor fast.
  • Method three — roll and bunt: roll to place your inside wing on the target, then immediately push forward on the stick rather than pulling. The least intuitive of the three but can be the most effective: the roll direction alone can fool the attacker into expecting an upward pull (and pitching his own nose up to chase it) right as you're actually unloading downward.

(Source: Echo Victor, "The ULTIMATE BFM Guide," defensive-BFM chapter.)

Radius Defence and The Ditch — the defender's own escape tools

Two further defensive options, both built to buy a 2-circle energy advantage or collapse range on your own terms rather than just absorbing pressure.

  • Radius Defence: roll to overbank 45° to the horizon with the lift vector facing down, then a lift-limit pull at maximum thrust. It's an oblique nose-low redefinition that minimizes your turn radius while gaining energy for a 2-circle fight down near the deck, using gravity ("God's G") to pull your nose around faster than the attacker can match. Done well, it forces the bandit outside your bubble, regaining angles back, and displaces you enough below the horizon that he has to choose between a weapon shot and following you into more BFM. With luck, he overshoots out in front and hands you a snapshot. (This is the maneuver the Radius Defence Follow counter in Offensive BFM above is built to answer.)
  • The Ditch: a pure nose-low maneuver to rapidly collapse range — roll inverted and pull through. Selecting IDLE throttle on the way down is what actually forces the overshoot: unless the attacker also goes to idle and recognizes what you're doing, he'll overshoot and you can line up a guns shot of your own. (This is the maneuver the Ditch Follow counter above is built to answer.)

(Source: Echo Victor, "The ULTIMATE BFM Guide," defensive-BFM chapter.)

Bug-Out — full procedure and success criteria

When a genuinely clean escape opportunity opens (most commonly right off a merge, bugging toward the bandit's own 6 o'clock), the procedure is specific, not just "turn and run":

  • Select maximum thrust (afterburner if fitted).
  • Enter a dive while unloading — unloading is what actually gives the most acceleration.
  • Keep sight of the bandit at all times, dipping a wing if needed to do it.
  • Do at most two check turns of about 30°, so you don't inadvertently put the bandit back on your own 6 o'clock.

A bug-out has succeeded once you're further than about 1.85 km from the bandit with more than 90° remaining on his turn. At that point he can no longer employ guns, and your rate of separation is enough to complete the escape. Both of those have to be judged visually, not read off an instrument, since you won't know the exact range in a real fight. If the escape doesn't pan out, don't keep running blind: place the lift vector back on the target, re-enter a maximum-rate turn, and go back to working Defensive BFM until the next opportunity actually appears. (Source: Echo Victor, "The ULTIMATE BFM Guide," defensive-BFM chapter.)

Lost Sight Gameplan

Losing sight of the attacker is not the same emergency as losing sight of a wingman. It needs its own immediate answer, since a bandit you can't see is one second away from a shot you won't see coming. If you know roughly where he is, max-perform the aircraft toward that direction anyway. Even if he isn't exactly where you thought, an aircraft actively max-performing is a much harder target to hit than one flying predictably while you search.

  • If you're already down near the deck when sight is lost, reorient your lift vector regularly rather than settling into one predictable turn, to stay unpredictable and defeat any gun shot already being tracked.
  • If you're high, the better answer is to keep turning the direction you were already going and roll into a nose-low dive all the way down to the deck. An aircraft silhouetted against the sky from below is considerably easier to reacquire than one blended into ground clutter from above.

(Source: Echo Victor, "The ULTIMATE BFM Guide," defensive-BFM chapter.)

Training drill: Medium Range DBFM

The defensive mirror of the OBFM drill above: same 1,830 m perch, same 720°/two-circle survival target. The fighter's only job is to survive. The initial move is the Defensive Break Turn, precisely: max afterburner, lift vector on or slightly below the bandit, pull to 5–5.5G. This settles you onto the sustained-rate turn. Against a MIL-power-only bandit, simply holding the sustained turn is often enough to win outright, since he has to spend all his energy chasing a shot he can't quite get.

D4Defensive Ranging — reading the bandit and using the floor
  • Setup: the 6,000-ft perch; call "fights on" at about 650 km/h and about 1,830 m range, in a slowly descending turn, and the defender wants the bandit to turn toward him in the initial check turn. Suggested altitudes: start at about 4,570 m with a floor at about 3,050 m (the floor stands in for the ground).
  • Bandit's job: close to a 305 m "safety bubble" he may not enter, showing pure aspect and calling "Fox 2" whenever an IR-missile shot opens up. Inside about 760 m go pure then lead pursuit for a gun shot, calling "snapshot" or "tracking," then fall back into lag to rebuild range. End with "terminate" or "knock it off."
  • Defender practices: reading the bandit's pursuit curve (pure shows a narrow nose-on profile, lead shows his belly, lag shows his topside and slides the line of sight toward the aft canopy), cross-checking lift vector, G, airspeed and altitude, and trading altitude for turn rate by lowering the lift vector below the horizon until you reach the floor — then you are on your sustained turn.
  • Pass: the source states no pass/fail test; use the debrief.

(Source: Mike Solyom/The Ops Center, "Defensive Ranging Exercise." Every number is the source's own suggested, adjustable training parameter.)

D5Reversal — recognizing the one good window
  • Setup: the 3,000-ft perch, chosen because it starts the defender slower than the attacker and so produces the overtake a good reversal picture needs.
  • Realistic bandit: comes into gun range quickly and pulls lead for a gun attempt; you answer out of plane, which may make him overshoot and give you the picture. It does not always work and is hard for beginners.
  • Training-only bandit (recommended by the source as more reliable, and explicitly not realistic): after "fights on" he deliberately over-pulls lead until you drift below his nose, which forces the reversal picture every time.
  • Fly it: reverse only if it looks like he will cross behind your tail with a little help from you — if in doubt, do not reverse. Use an unloaded roll (ease off the back-stick, roll, pull again once established) and shift your view to the other side of the canopy. Farther away, place the lift vector on the bandit; very close, place it above or below him. A correct reversal ends in a scissors, which beats being defensive.
  • Pass: the source states no pass/fail test; use the debrief.

(Source: Mike Solyom/The Ops Center, "Reversal Exercise." Every number is the source's own suggested, adjustable training parameter.)

D6Medium Range DBFM — the defensive capstone
  • Setup: the 6,000-ft perch, as in D3. It is the matched pair of D3, so one pilot can fly each side at the same time.
  • Fly it: open with the break turn — maximum afterburner, lift vector on or slightly below the bandit, pull to 5–5.5 G — to settle onto your sustained-rate turn. Against a military-power-only bandit, holding the sustained turn is often enough; against an afterburner bandit expect more attacks, but it is still the best route to survival. The close-range tools (Tighten Down, Out-of-Plane, the Jink) are in the Defensive BFM section above.
  • Pass: survive to 720° of turn after "fights on" (two full circles).

(Source: Mike Solyom/The Ops Center, "How To Survive A Close Range Dogfight." The same video recommends ending each exercise with a short debrief comparing both pilots' points of view. Every number is the source's own suggested, adjustable training parameter.)

High-Aspect BFM

  • A nose-to-nose merge resolves into one-circle or two-circle in the first couple of seconds — recognizing the choice as it happens is the skill.
  • Pick your game plan pre-merge from your aircraft's strength: wins on radius → force one-circle; wins on rate → force two-circle.
  • Lead turn: turn early into where the bandit's flight path is going — the bread and butter of a neutral-merge conversion.
  • You can't have both: the last aircraft to turn decides one-circle vs. two-circle — taking the lead turn means giving up that choice.
  • Angles or energy? Tentative bandit → go straight for angles. Aggressive bandit → let him spend energy, then go vertical. Matched angle-for-angle for 1–2 turns → switch to energy before it becomes a low, slow flat scissors.

Nose-to-nose merges — where neither side starts with an angles advantage — are their own problem, distinct from the stern-conversion case the rest of Part I mostly assumes. Whether the merge resolves into a one-circle or two-circle fight gets decided in the first couple of seconds by which way each aircraft chooses to turn — recognizing that choice as it's happening, rather than reacting a beat late, is most of the skill.

Pick your game plan from your own aircraft's strengths before the merge: if it wins on radius, you want one-circle; if it wins on rate, you want two-circle.

The lead turn carries over directly from offensive BFM here and is arguably more important: turning early into where the bandit's flight path is going, before he's even fully across your nose, is what a stern conversion off a neutral merge is actually built from — described elsewhere as "the bread and butter" of air-superiority fighters generally, not a niche technique.

You can't have bothThe last aircraft to turn decides whether the fight becomes one-circle or two-circle. A lead turn means turning first — so guaranteeing a particular fight geometry and getting a lead turn's advantage are mutually exclusive. The lead turn's payoff is large enough that it's usually still the right call, but know you're giving up the direction choice when you take it.

Exclusive turning room at the merge

Vertical turning room is often exclusive at a high-aspect merge — only one of you may actually have it. The rule for exploiting it runs both directions.

  • If you're already lower than the bandit, stay lower still and pitch up into him rather than trying to climb to his level first.
  • If you're higher, stay higher and use that altitude as an energy advantage rather than diving to meet him.

Trying to match his altitude before committing usually just surrenders whichever exclusive turning room you started with. The same idea shows up in a pure radius fight, not just vertically: whichever aircraft arrives at the second merge having covered less downrange distance effectively holds exclusive-use turning room over the other for that merge, and gets the advantage from it. (Source: Echo Victor, "The ULTIMATE BFM Guide," offensive-BFM chapter.)

Merge types

Beyond the plain neutral merge, a handful of named merge shapes each hand the advantage to a specific aircraft before either side has done anything clever.

  • Vertical merge: one aircraft descending, the other climbing. Favors the climber, who has "God's G" (gravity assisting the pull) available for a faster turn rate.
  • Slow-speed merge: both aircraft run a nose-high gameplan off the first merge and meet again atop the loop.
  • High-speed nose-low merge: the mirror case — both go nose-low after the first merge. Produces a very low turn rate for both sides, since both are now fighting God's G rather than using it.
  • Stern conversion isn't really a merge at all: being placed directly on the bandit's 6 o'clock in the rear quarter by outside cueing (radar/GCI-type "ISTAR" assets), for an immediate heat-seeker or guns opportunity with no neutral merge geometry to solve first.

(Source: Echo Victor, "The ULTIMATE BFM Guide," offensive-BFM chapter.)

The Butterfly Setup

Perch setups always start one side advantaged, so high-aspect training instead uses the Butterfly Setup, which starts both aircraft neutral. Line-abreast, then both fly a MIL-power 30° turn away from each other for 8–9 seconds, to roughly the limits of visual range. Call "turn in, fights on," then turn back toward each other.

Use the diverging leg to build turning room, vertically as well as horizontally, by climbing or descending. Pick climb vs. descend by whichever makes it easier to keep your own tally while denying the bandit's.

  • A cloud or the sun between you and him helps.
  • Staying off his altitude helps, since most people scan near the horizon out of habit.

You can only build lateral turning room by turning inside the bandit's circle on the turn-in. Floating outside costs time and shifts the merge point in his favor.

Lead-turn timing & cues

Every second of turn at your sustained rate is worth over 10° of angular advantage the bandit then has to make up. Two seconds of head start from a clean lead turn can be enough that an identical aircraft never catches up. The visual cue for exactly when to start: a rapidly increasing LOS rate from 11 to 10 o'clock (left-side pass) or 1 to 2 o'clock (right-side pass).

The most common error is a late lead turn — per the manual, "if in doubt, start early, but do not turn in front of the bandit."

  • A late turn shows the bandit drifting aft on your canopy, with little fix available once it's happened.
  • An early turn shows his LOS rate freeze and drift under your nose instead, correctable by easing off the G momentarily until it starts moving again.

In three dimensions, once turning room is built, simply place your plane of motion on the bandit — lift vector slightly above him.

An "energy item" for a bandit at ~741 km/h:

  • A purely vertical high-to-low lead turn at ~556 km/h (expect to gain ~185 km/h descending onto him).
  • A low-to-high one at ~926 km/h (expect to lose ~185 km/h climbing).
  • At his own altitude, just fly a sustained-rate turn at his airspeed.

Two-circle fights & Turn Circle Extension (TCX)

If the bandit turns toward you after your lead turn, you're in a two-circle (rate) fight. Hold your best sustained turn rather than chasing with lead or pure pursuit — chasing just produces a yo-yo of range and aspect as your turn circle, offset by the lead turn, cycles in and out of alignment with his.

Align the circles with a Turn Circle Extension (TCX): simply 2–3 seconds of easing off the G to shift your circle's post. Timing is everything — too early and the circles never converge, too late and they end up farther apart.

The cue to extend is the same 45–60° aspect assessment window used in offensive BFM (roughly one-to-two fists above the canopy bow): ease the G there. Above about 90° AA instead, go into another lead turn. Don't expect one TCX to finish the job — the manual allows for 500° to over 1,000° of accumulated turning to fully align circles.

One-circle fights: minimum radius & win/loss cues

If the bandit turns away instead, it's a one-circle (radius) fight. Turn rate alone gives no advantage here — both aircraft stay on opposite sides of their own circles. The game plan flips to minimum radius: get there by pulling more G, never by using speed brakes, which just wastes energy for nothing. A moderate buffet (or a rising tone on aircraft with a single-rate beeper/SRB) tells you you're above sustained rate and working toward minimum radius without needing to check instruments.

Read the fight as you come around:

  • Bandit moving forward on your canopy with stagnant or decreasing aspect: you're winning — lead-turn again to compound it.
  • Bandit's topside visible "like a mirror" at the halfway point: neutral — pick the next circle's direction by energy state (fast/high → two-circle, slow → stay one-circle).
  • Bandit's motion going stagnant or drifting off with his nose rotating toward pure pursuit: you're losing — transition to Defensive BFM.

Minimizing radius costs speed, so expect to end up behind the bandit but slower than him. Be ready to rebuild energy immediately after.

Scissors as an outcome

Any one-circle merge can resolve into another one-circle, a two-circle, or a scissors: both aircraft inside each other's turn circle at once, repeatedly reversing to gain on each other. Fly it the same way as a one-circle fight — minimum radius, lift vector on the bandit, max afterburner — but with the added goal of actively building turning room, not just shrinking your circle, since that's what eventually lets a weapon actually be employed. (Source for this section: Mike Solyom/The Ops Center, "Learning Nose-To-Nose Dogfights," "Mastering The Two Circle Dogfight," and "One Circle Dogfight.")

Gameplans — deciding before the merge

A gameplan is simply the merge you intend to fly, decided before you get there rather than improvised at the pass. As you approach, actively assess four things: altitude, energy, geometry, and turning room, both yours and the bandit's.

  • If you're both low, be lower than him. Exclusive-use vertical turning room lets you pitch up and over while he's forced nose-high or level — an immediate advantage.
  • If you're both high, stack yourself higher for the equivalent energy advantage.

Know each aircraft's energy state, not just your own.

  • If the bandit has more energy than you, force a 1-circle flow at a deliberately slower speed. This flushes him out in front and gets you Sensor Nose On first — don't bleed your own speed so low that you can no longer fly follow-on BFM once you get there.
  • If the bandit has less energy, force a 2-circle flow at your best-rate speed instead. You have the excess energy to trade for turn rate, which pulls him forward in the canopy.
  • If you're the one with the energy advantage right at the merge, use an energy exertion to bleed down into the rate band deliberately, buying angles and turning room rather than just carrying speed you can't use.

As a rule of thumb: a good rate-fighter wants to force 2-circle; a good radius- or low-speed-handling aircraft wants to force 1-circle. (Source: Echo Victor, "The ULTIMATE BFM Guide," offensive-BFM chapter.)

Nose-high, nose-low & level gameplans

Gameplans also come in nose-high, nose-low, and level flavors. A level gameplan is always at a disadvantage if the bandit instead chooses to go nose-high or nose-low, since he then dictates the merge geometry and you don't.

A nose-high gameplan forces the bandit into a decision: follow you up and risk his own energy, or stay level and risk being shot.

  • 1-circle nose-high merge: turn inside the bandit's own turn circle and reverse to arrive in his control zone. If he doesn't come up to meet you, ease your pull to bank energy and build exclusive-use turning room instead. If he does come up, get your nose back down below him so you arrive at the next merge already holding an energy edge.
  • 2-circle nose-high merge: fly with excess energy above the rate band, max-perform across the bandit's tail in a nose-high oblique pull, then overbank and pitch down to meet him once your airspeed decays back into the rate band.

Nose-low gameplans trade altitude for better turn rate and radius instead.
