  • 1-circle nose-low merge: flown as a lift-limit pull, with the bandit sitting above the horizon and your lift vector placed behind him as you pitch up into his control zone.
  • 2-circle nose-low merge: flown at best-rate speed, turning across the bandit's tail and overbanking nose-low for better turn performance, again pulling him forward in the canopy.

(Source: Echo Victor, "The ULTIMATE BFM Guide," offensive-BFM chapter.)

Angles or energy tactics — Shaw's comparison

The gameplans above decide the merge; this is the longer choice of how you win the fight that follows.

  • Angles tactics are quicker, more aggressive and put the bandit on the defensive early. The cost is that once you commit to a vertical move you're "betting the farm" that you can force him back down first. Rules for the guns-only angles fighter: stay within about a quarter of a turn radius (or half your gun range, whichever is less) of his altitude, never let speed drop below what you need to pull the nose straight up, and expect only 20–30° on the first turn against a similar aircraft. Greed is the main risk.
  • Angles tactics favour nose-to-nose turns, which gain the most angle per unit of speed lost, and nose-low turns, which cut the energy bleed. Attack from slightly below on each pass: it invites him nose-low too and makes an overshoot from low to high far less dangerous than one from above.
  • Energy tactics are safer and keep the exit open throughout, as long as the bandit's angular advantage stays at or under about 90° and you never go vertical without an energy edge. They take more training: you must judge his energy and fly a good rolling scissors. Let him gain angles in turns flown at about two-thirds of your maximum sustained G, using the rest to climb, then make a wings-level pull-up as he crosses behind you.
  • Reading his energy from his angles: if he gains 20–30° per pass, he's paying with a lot of speed and you have the energy edge. If he gains 10° or less, the speed difference is small and he's playing it smart, so consider a nose-to-tail extension out before he gains too much.
  • When to switch: if your angles attack is matched angle-for-angle for one or two turns, the fight is heading for a slow flat-scissors stalemate at low altitude. Switch to energy at the next pass: go nose-to-tail, relax G to the minimum that keeps sight, accelerate toward best sustained-turn speed and let him gain about 90° before you pull up. If he refuses the angles you offer, switch the other way and start angles with a low yo-yo.
  • Take the cheap shot: a short forward-quarter gun burst at a pass rarely hits, but it sets who's offensive and who's defensive in both pilots' heads. Weigh it against your ammo.

(Source: Robert Shaw, Fighter Combat, ch.3 One-versus-One Maneuvering, Similar Aircraft.)

When your gameplan doesn't match the bandit's

Four concrete cases cover what happens when a level (or mismatched) choice meets a bandit who goes vertical.

  • You go nose-high, he follows: a simple 1-circle fight in the vertical. Max-perform with just a nibble of buffet, flush him out ahead, and take a snapshot at the top of the loop.
  • You go nose-high, he goes nose-low: you risk losing sight over the top, but coming over gives you the better instantaneous turn rate and Sensor Nose On first. Attempt a snapshot, and watch for the high-to-low merge that follows, trying to flatten it back to the horizontal if you can.
  • You go nose-low, he follows: maneuver off pure nose-low so you hold the altitude advantage at the bottom going into the second merge, then work in behind him for the shot.
  • You go nose-low, he goes nose-high: a slight disadvantage, since he gains angles over the top. Maneuver off pure nose-low to minimize your own height loss and preserve turning room, and look for a snapshot as you enter the vertical merge.

(Source: Echo Victor, "The ULTIMATE BFM Guide," offensive-BFM chapter.)

Named but not yet sourced — needs a transcriptLag Reposition was reviewed via its named source ("Learning Nose-To-Nose Dogfights: Intro To High Aspect BFM," youtube.com/watch?v=k3ih3cXVy7M) but the transcript's recap section only uses that phrase as a title — no distinct technique by that name is actually explained anywhere in it. Treat as still unresolved pending a direct rewatch of that section, not a transcript-quality issue.
D7Butterfly + lead turn — stern conversion on an unaware bandit
  • Setup (Butterfly): start line abreast. On "check away" both aircraft make a military-power 30° turn away from each other at about 740 km/h. Fly the diverging leg for 8–9 s or until you reach the edge of visual range, a bit over 3.7 km apart. Call "padlocked" if you risk losing sight. Then call "turn in, fights on" and both turn back.
  • Bandit: holds the briefed altitude and speed and does not maneuver after the merge.
  • Fly it: build turning room during the check-away leg (it can be built vertically as well as horizontally; mirroring his turn gives you none). Use the energy-item rule to pick your speed: for a bandit at about 740 km/h, start a high-to-low lead turn at about 555 km/h, a low-to-high lead turn at about 925 km/h, and at his altitude fly a sustained turn at his speed. There is only 1–2 s between the turn-in and the lead-turn decision.
  • Pass: finish on the bandit's six o'clock inside about 760 m.
  • Errors it surfaces: lead-turning too early or without turning room gives him a reversal picture; lead-turning too late, too slow, or after floating to the outside leaves you outside gun range and hands him the energy.

(Source: Mike Solyom/The Ops Center, "Learning Nose-To-Nose Dogfights: Intro To High Aspect BFM." Every number is the source's own suggested, adjustable training parameter.)

D8Two-circle practice — hold the rate, then align the circles
  • Setup: the Butterfly from D7, with one change: the bandit now maneuvers, but not until you have crossed his 3-9 line. At that point he may turn toward you and make it a two-circle fight. Limit him to military power at first.
  • Fly it: use the energy item to hold a sustained-rate turn at about 705–780 km/h through the lead turn, then stay on your best sustained turn — do not pull lead or pure pursuit early or you get the aspect-and-range yo-yo. When the bandit is in the 45–60° aspect band, ease off the G for 2–3 s (a Turn Circle Extension) to align the circles. Aligning them can take 500° to over 1,000° of total turning, so one extension will often not be enough.
  • Pass (the source's training objective): reach a good weapon solution within three trips around the circle.
  • If you lose sight: keep turning and look through the slice of the weapon zone where he wants to be — never fly straight and level while you search.

(Source: Mike Solyom/The Ops Center, "Mastering The Two Circle Dogfight." Every number is the source's own suggested, adjustable training parameter.)

D9One-circle practice — min radius and repeated lead turns
  • Setup: the Butterfly from D7. You lead-turn; the bandit turns away once you cross his 3-9 line, starting a one-circle fight. At each second merge you lead-turn again and he turns away again, until you reach an offensive position.
  • If it is not working: call "knock it off" and work the problem. The most common error is not enough G — check for buffet, and if nothing is shaking you probably need to pull harder.
  • Make it harder: (1) baseline as above; (2) the bandit may choose a one-circle or a two-circle at the second and later merges, so you must pick the matching plan (min radius for one-circle, sustained rate for two-circle); (3) he may also add lead turns.
  • Pass: the source states no pass/fail test beyond reaching an offensive position.

(Source: Mike Solyom/The Ops Center, "One Circle Dogfight." Every number is the source's own suggested, adjustable training parameter.)

Dissimilar Matchups

  • Two questions set the plan: who turns better (turn time, wing loading) and who has more energy (climb, acceleration, top speed — thrust-to-weight). A gap under ~10% counts as similar.
  • You turn better → angles. Keep it flat, use nose-to-nose turns and lead turns. Only follow him up when you're at energy parity.
  • You have more energy → energy. Don't turn with him. Extend, climb, pitch back and attack from above. Leave if two turns don't show you the edge.
  • Better at both → angles, but don't overrun him: keep your speed level with or just below his.
  • Worse at both → don't take the 1v1. Hit-and-run, missiles from range, or bring a wingman.
  • Each Part V card's Fights as line says where that aircraft usually sits. It's relative to its BR, so check the bandit too.
You turn better
You turn worse
You have more energy
Double superior

Angles. Let the aircraft do the work and don't overrun him.

Energy fighter

Extension and pitch-back, high-side passes, hit-and-run. Never turn with him.

He has more energy
Angles fighter

Keep it horizontal. Nose-to-nose and lead turns. Don't chase his zoom.

Double inferior

Avoid the 1v1. Hit-and-run, missiles, teamwork. If caught, make him overshoot.

Shaw counts aircraft as dissimilar when they differ by more than about 10% in turn or energy performance. He simplifies it to two numbers: low wing loading stands for better instantaneous turn and slower minimum speed, and high thrust-to-weight (power loading for props) stands for better climb, acceleration and top speed. Neither is exact: flaps or slats, lift from the fuselage, and engine behaviour with altitude all shift the real picture, so War Thunder's own turn-time and climb figures on the Part V cards are a better guide than raw ratios. Shaw's advice is to know both aircraft well; comparison flights against captured types regularly showed pilots had overrated the enemy.

Angles fighter — you turn better, he has more energy

  • Before the merge, cruise higher than you expect him to be, so altitude offsets his acceleration and climb edge.
  • Build sideways separation for a lead turn. Fight at best sustained-turn speed rather than corner speed, and pull only as hard as you need; level sustained turns often gain small angles cheaply.
  • Keep the fight horizontal. A flat scissors should be lethal to him, since he has both a turn and a minimum-speed disadvantage. Avoid a rolling scissors if he also has the better sustained turn.
  • Once you're 60–70° ahead, continue nose-to-tail rather than reversing; his blind period costs him more than you. Take only what your turn edge allows, a few degrees at a time, and keep at least vertical-maneuvering speed.
  • When he zooms: follow only at energy parity. Otherwise level your wings and climb straight ahead to build energy while he spends his. As he nears the top, roll to put him at about 90° off your tail and turn only hard enough to hold him there. When he commits down, defend against his guns with a jink, then reverse to force a close overshoot. In any zoom, never let speed fall below level-flight control speed or the nose will drop and leave you helpless under him.
  • Against his escape: an all-aspect or rear-aspect missile lets you punish an extension that a gun alone can't.

Energy fighter — you have more energy, he turns better

  • Don't get shot while you build the energy margin; that comes first. Use lag pursuit and the vertical; nose-to-tail turns suit you better than nose-to-nose.
  • Extension and pitch-back: after the pass, climb straight ahead at best climb speed and turn only enough to keep sight. Pull up wings-level once at vertical-maneuvering speed, easing G over the top to about 1G inverted. Pass directly over him, come down in lag pursuit, then convert to lead for a high-side gun pass. Repeat as needed.
  • For an overhead attack you need about one of your minimum turn radii of altitude above him. If you have that edge at the merge, pass with roughly a quarter of his turn radius of height, enough to tempt him nose-high but not enough to give him a shot.
  • Pulling out above his altitude keeps him turning nose-high and bleeding. If he gains well under 90° in the first two turns, your energy edge is too small: disengage nose-to-tail, or reset to a neutral pass.
  • After a missed pass, quarter-roll away and dive for separation, then re-attack or leave. With a big speed edge you can engage or disengage at will.
  • The practical problems: long extensions while looking back make it easy to lose sight of the bandit, and dangerous near the ground. Climbing toward the sun helps hide you; other fighters will see you slow at the top of a pitch-back. Shaw notes these limits make full energy tactics hard even in training, so hit-and-run (stalk, one high-speed pass, leave) is often the practical answer.
  • Against a turning bandit with all-aspect missiles this matchup is very bad. Shoot first head-on before the pass, then leave whatever the result.

Double superior and double inferior

  • Better at both: you have the speed to force the fight and the turn to win it. Fly angles tactics, which are quicker and keep sight easier. The main risk is overaggression: throwing away energy lets even a weaker bandit build a temporary, lethal edge. Use the throttle to keep your speed level with or slightly below his and avoid overshooting.
  • Worse at both: you may be unable to avoid or escape the fight, so the best answer is not to start it alone. Use hit-and-run passes or fight as a pair. If caught, energy tactics give a skilled pilot the best chance: a high-G descending nose-to-tail turn to hold him off, then cut power or use speed brakes to make him close fast, and break toward him at the last moment to force an overshoot. Shaw's example is Robert Johnson's P-47 against a Spitfire IX that out-turned and out-climbed him: he never turned, used his roll rate to deny every turn, then dived and zoomed past the Spitfire.

When you're equal on one axis

SituationPlan
Similar energy, you turn betterAngles fight, but patient. Hold at least vertical-maneuvering speed at every pass as insurance against his zoom, until he has clearly bled his own speed.
Similar energy, you turn worseHe's the better dogfighter. Energy tactics without a climb edge: bleed him with sustained nose-to-tail turns at best sustained speed, let him gain about 90°, then pull up. Probe him early and disengage if he's good.
Similar turn, you have more energyAngles tactics are quicker and your energy edge is the insurance; climbing extension/pitch-back also works. If he dives away, follow from slightly above instead of diving on him from high.
Similar turn, you have less energyNo edge to exploit and little chance to escape. Fly a patient angles fight below him with nose-to-nose turns, and call for help.
Thrust-vectoring (Harrier VIFF)Against a VIFF-capable aircraft, fly angles and keep the pressure on so it spends energy. If it uses VIFF to make you overshoot, quarter-roll away and pitch up rather than following, since a VIFFing aircraft has given up its vertical. Avoid flat scissors and never follow it into a defensive spiral. If you fly the Harrier, save VIFF for defense or a final snap shot, because it costs speed very quickly.

(Source: Robert Shaw, Fighter Combat, ch.4 One-versus-One Maneuvering, Dissimilar Aircraft.)

Part II — Formation & Wingman Tactics

The Wingman Contract

  • Agree pre-merge (10 sec is enough): who calls priority when two threats look equal.
  • Support whichever fight is already committed — don't split off for your own kill.
  • A "break"/"defensive" call gets an immediate response, no need to ask why.
  • "Extending"/"bugout" means both of you disengage toward the same rally point.

Everything in Part I assumes you're alone. The moment you're squadded, worth agreeing — even a 10-second exchange before the first merge — on: who calls priority when two threats look equal; you support whichever fight is already committed rather than splitting for your own kill; a "break" or "defensive" call gets an immediate response, no need to ask why; and "extending" or "bugout" means both of you disengage toward the same rally point. Not a hierarchy — an agreement you both fall back on when there's no time to discuss it live.

Choosing a Formation

  • Default: Loose Deuce — wide separation (~1.6km), roles swap fluidly, both shoot and both cover six.
  • Fighting Wing: close (~460–610m, ~45° offset) — the escort/mentor exception only.
  • Double Attack: sequenced single-target focus fire, once you've both spotted an isolated target.
FormationHow it worksBest for
Fighting WingClose spacing (~460–610 m, ~45° offset). Lead flies fully offensive; wingman's whole job is SA and defensive cover.Escorting a committed strike run, or a newer wingman who just needs to survive and learn
Double AttackOne target, sequenced — first in commits fully, second holds altitude/spacing to exploit whatever the target does defensively.A single high-value or dangerous target you want dead fast, with a numbers edge
Loose DeuceWide separation (~1.6 km), roles ("engaged"/"free") swap fluidly, both jets shoot and both cover six.The general case — most squad play, since neither of you is locked into a pure non-scoring role

Default to Loose Deuce. Fighting Wing is the escort/mentor exception; Double Attack is the focus-fire call once you've both spotted an isolated target.

Flying Each Doctrine

  • Partner defensive = attack the bogey now. Every doctrine below agrees on this one.
  • Fighting wing: stay inside a ~60° cone either side of lead's tail, close enough to stay behind him in a max-rate turn. Your job is lookout, not kills.
  • Double attack / loose deuce free fighter: keep more energy than the engaged fighter, maneuver at right angles to his fight, keep him within ~90° of your nose.
  • Bounced: sandwich if it's clear who's targeted, defensive split if it isn't, half-split to drag the bogey into a sandwich.
  • Loose deuce kills come from the free fighter: the engaged fighter's job is to make the bogey predictable for ~360° of turn.

Choosing a Formation says which doctrine to fly; this section is how Shaw says to fly each one once you're in it. He treats all three as tools for different conditions, not a ladder from old to new.

Fighting wing (welded wing)

  • The wingman flies anywhere inside a cone reaching about 60° either side of the leader's tail. It's a working area, not a fixed slot.
  • Spacing: close enough to stay behind the leader in his hardest turn, far enough to avoid a collision. Shaw's figures are about 180 m (WWII) to 300 m (Korea), up to roughly double that at altitude.
  • Sit as far off his tail as you can hold, so you see his six and he can check yours.
  • Weak points: nobody covers the wingman's own six, a hard zoom climb by the leader leaves the wingman behind, and on offense it's effectively one shooter.
  • Best fit: a new pilot, no radio, or attacking bombers and transports.

Combat spread and height

  • Line abreast is Shaw's preferred pre-merge formation: each pilot sees the other's rear hemisphere equally.
  • Space it about 1–2 of your turn radii. Wider pushes the shared blind zone further back; too wide and you lose sight of each other.
  • Default height is slightly stepped down. On the leader's down-sun side step up, on his up-sun side stay below, so he never has to look into the sun to check you.
  • Avoid big altitude splits. The low fighter can't climb to help without bleeding its speed.

Defending the pair when bounced

CounterHowUse when
SandwichThe targeted fighter breaks away from his partner; the partner turns the same way and lands on the bogey's tail.It's clear early which fighter is being attacked
Defensive splitBoth turn away from each other. The bogey must pick one and turn its tail to the other. The defender keeps turning the same way to drag the fight back to his partner.You can't tell which fighter is the target
High/low splitOne pulls up, one goes low.Against a low-powered bogey that can't follow the zoom; not against one with an energy edge
Half-splitOne breaks, the other extends and drags the bogey out, then reverses into a sandwich.Keeps separation small enough that nobody loses sight
Thach weaveBoth turn hard toward each other so the free fighter meets the bogey nose-on with guns, then reverse and repeat.Against a better-turning guns fighter, with wide spread and good firepower

Free fighter on offense

  • Hold more energy than the engaged fighter and maneuver in a plane perpendicular to his fight: vertical loops around a level fight, level arcs around a vertical one.
  • Keep the engaged fighter within about 90° of your nose, and don't let the fight drift behind your wing line.
  • At the merge, extend and zoom rather than committing to a turn; pick a side once the fight settles.
  • Enter from the bogey's belly side, outside its turn, where it can't see you. For a missile, aim for about 90° off its tail.
  • Against a section: bracket wide, cross behind the near bogey, hit the far one. Take the trailing ("sucked") bogey first, or the higher one if they're line abreast.
  • Drag: one fighter baits the bogey just outside its weapons envelope while the other sets up. It works, but it's riskier than a bracket.

Strike-rejoin-strike

Against a pair or more, Shaw's preferred rhythm is a fast attack, a rejoin in combat spread, then another attack only if the setup is good. It keeps the section defensive except during brief attack runs and avoids the long turning fight that draws other bandits in. It's also his answer to being outnumbered (see Multi-Bogey).

Radio discipline, per ShawPersonal call signs, standard brevity, short calls, and every call from your partner acknowledged.

(Source: Robert Shaw, Fighter Combat, ch.5 Section Tactics, Two-versus-One, and ch.6 Section Tactics, Two-versus-Two.)

Lost Wingman Procedure

  • Lose sight: call it, turn slightly away from their last known position, go heads-down and reset on instruments/minimap.
  • The one rule that matters — once you commit to this, finish it. Reversing back mid-turn means you're both chasing a position that's already wrong.

The moment you lose sight of your wingman: call it, turn slightly away from their last known position, go heads-down and reset on instruments/minimap. The one rule that matters — once you commit to this, finish it. Reversing back toward where you think they are mid-turn is how you both end up chasing a position that's already wrong.

Combat Air Patrol Patterns

  • Racetrack (default): a hot leg pointed at the threat sector, a cold leg flying the reverse.
  • Solo: you're blind on the cold leg — fine with reliable outside cueing, risky without it.
  • Counter-rotating CAP (2 aircraft): trade hot/cold each pass so the sector's never unwatched.

How you fly while waiting for something to happen matters almost as much as how you fly once it does. A racetrack — two legs, a hot leg pointed at the threat sector and a cold leg flying the reverse — is the default patrol shape: predictable enough to fly precisely, and it guarantees you're periodically pointed the right way instead of just orbiting blind.

Flying it solo means accepting a real gap: you're blind on the cold leg, with no radar coverage of the threat axis, which is fine with reliable outside cueing (a minimap ping, a teammate's call) and risky without it. With a second aircraft, a counter-rotating CAP closes that gap — the two of you fly opposite legs so one is always hot while the other is cold, trading which is which each pass, so the sector never actually goes unwatched.

Also worth knowing by nameBeam CAP — oriented across rather than toward the threat axis; situational, or for a non-radar aircraft relying on outside cueing. Counter-opposing CAP — multiple pairs holding separate patrol stations with one commander deconflicting engagements across all of them, for covering more ground than one patrol can alone.

Shaw on CAP: a single fighter on a race-track only covers the threat sector less than half its station time. If you're looking out visually, a figure-8 across the threat axis with every turn made toward the threat keeps your tail away from it. Patrol near best-endurance speed unless enemy fighters are likely, then fly faster and vary the pattern so it isn't predictable. Two fighters per station is the minimum when enemy fighters are expected; small isolated CAPs are easy prey for sweeps. Choose CAP altitude for spotting the threat first, and know where friendly SAM free-fire zones are. Ground-alert interception (scrambling when a raid is detected) is usually more efficient than standing CAP if warning time allows. (Source: Robert Shaw, Fighter Combat, ch.9 Fighter Missions.)

Four-Ship & Division Tactics

Mutual support priority, post-merge
  1. Kill your assigned threat
  2. Kill other threats
  3. Help your wingman kill his threat
  4. Exit and re-establish element mutual support if lost
  5. Support the other element
  • Equal or weaker enemy: fluid four (engaged section + free section). Outnumbered: gaggle (everyone independent, support by presence).
  • In a gaggle, turn no more than ~90° without a reversal or belly-check; stay on the edge of the bogey cloud, never inside it.

A four-ship (division) is two of the pairs above stacked together, not a new unit with its own rulebook. A 1986 USAF Fighter Weapons Review article on four-ship mission planning frames it plainly: the two-ship formations are the basic fighting unit, with element integrity maintained first and inter-element support layered on top of that — not instead of it. Practically, that means the four-ship splits into two elements of two aircraft each, and each element still runs on the same lead/wingman contract described above.

Elements get their own call signs and numbering in the brief — e.g. Eagle 1/Eagle 2 as one element's lead and wingman, Raven 1/Raven 2 as the other's — so a call like "Eagle's engaged, Raven cover" is unambiguous about which pair is meant. Once the merge happens, that same source lays out mutual-support priority as a strict order, not a menu to pick from:

The ordering is the point: your own element comes before the other element, and even within your element, re-establishing lost mutual support outranks reaching over to help the far pair. A four-ship that loses element integrity chasing inter-element glory ends up worse off than one that keeps its pairs intact and only loosely coordinated.

Fluid four vs. gaggle

DoctrineHow it worksBest for
Fluid fourTwo sections replace the two fighters of double attack: an engaged section and a free (top-cover) section. Modified fluid four lets the engaged section fly loose deuce inside itself while the free section covers.Facing equal or weaker numbers and equipment: the best balance of offense and defense
GaggleLoose deuce scaled up: patrol and attack together, but once the fight starts every pilot operates on his own. Mutual support comes from presence, not formation.Facing superior numbers or better aircraft: more independent elements than the enemy has

The arithmetic behind it: three independent fighters usually beat four fighters flying as two fighting-wing pairs, because more independent elements lets the bigger force set up 2v1s locally. Shaw's general rule when committing a larger force: the engaged fighters should at least match the enemy in independent elements, with at least one element held back as cover.

Gaggle rules

  • Define the "bogey cloud" (the airspace holding most enemies) and cruise its edge picking off unaware targets. Don't fly into it; if you end up inside, get out fast with belly-checks both ways.
  • Turn no more than about 90° in one direction without a reversal or a belly-check. If you can't shoot a bogey within ~90° of turn, find another target.
  • Attack only targets that offer an easy shot. If the attack is spotted, break it off and keep hunting.
  • Use level or nose-low, sustained-G turns to keep speed. Avoid steep nose-high moves unless the bogeys are much weaker guns-only fighters.
  • Scan around any friendly you see for an attacker on him, and call it ("Break right"). Make a "bugout" call when leaving so others know the odds changed.
  • If you extend to re-assess, come back from well above or below the fight and keep it in your forward quarter rather than pointing straight at it.

Other formations worth knowing

  • Sections in trail ("battle box"): good for sequential attacks, weaker defensively than line-abreast arrangements.
  • Modified vic (3 aircraft): a section in loose trail on a lead that looks like an easy target; the stacked-high section pounces on whatever attacks it.
  • Section and stinger: one fighter trails a section, high on the sun side and slightly behind. If attacked he dives to drag the attacker down to the section. Good as an occasional variation, vulnerable as a habit.
  • Lufbery circle ("wheel"): everyone in trail around a circle, each covering the tail of the one ahead. Works in a guns-only fight; all-aspect missiles make it useless.
  • Mixed aircraft types: give each type the job it does best, and stack them so each fights in its own best altitude band. The slower type usually sets everyone's speed and bugout time.
Dicta Boelcke (1916)Shaw reprints Oswald Boelcke's rules as still valid: secure the advantage (sun behind you) before attacking; finish an attack once started; fire only at close range with the target properly in your sights; never lose sight of your opponent; attack from behind; if dived on, turn to meet it rather than run; remember your line of retreat; attack in groups of four or six, and when it breaks into single fights, don't let several of you go for one opponent. Boelcke was killed in a midair with his own wingman while both attacked the same aircraft.

(Source: Robert Shaw, Fighter Combat, ch.7 Division Tactics.)

Air Combat Maneuvering (ACM)

  • Goal: merge-to-kill in under 30 seconds — a longer fight gives every enemy within reinforcement range time to arrive and turn a 2v1 into something worse.
  • Two roles, not two ranks: Engaged fighter flies the actual BFM against the bandit; Support fighter owns deconfliction, takes shots of opportunity, and clears for more bandits.
  • Roles are set by radio, not assumed: "Engaged" declares it, "Press" accepts support, "Unable [reason]" or flight-lead "Negative" declines it.
  • Weapon deconfliction zone: a ~10° cone around the engaged fighter — never take a shot while he's inside it, factoring your weapon's time of flight.
  • Common failure mode: the support fighter drifts onto the engaged fighter's plane of motion/turn circle and accidentally re-creates old-school Fighting Wing, wasting the whole point of having a free second fighter. See Choosing a Formation for the underlying Fighting Wing / Double Attack / Loose Deuce formation choice this builds on.

ACM is the USAF's name for coordinated 2-fighter (and larger) tactics once a merge is imminent or underway — distinct from BFM, which is what one aircraft does against one bandit. The case for speed is arithmetic: a Mach-1-class fighter covers roughly 20km a minute, so a fight that takes two minutes to resolve puts every enemy aircraft within about 35–50km on notice and able to arrive before it's over (further still if they're carrying missiles with real stand-off range). Cut the same fight to 30 seconds and only aircraft already within a few km can possibly intervene. That's the entire justification for everything below — it's not about being more aggressive, it's about denying the enemy time to reinforce.

Where this came from: three generations of 2-ship doctrine

Fighting Wing (WWI-era, pre-radio): the wingman holds a tight cone behind lead, purely to watch lead's blind spot, while lead fights essentially solo. Simple to teach, but lead can't use full throttle (the wingman would never catch back up) and the formation wastes the second aircraft's firepower entirely.

Double Attack (WWII, once radios existed): the support fighter holds separation and altitude instead of glueing to lead, ready to swap in as the engaged fighter if the bandit switches targets — but stays passive until explicitly called in. This already gets real value from the second aircraft without needing much coordination discipline.

Loose Deuce (Vietnam-era): the support fighter is free to maneuver and shoot on his own initiative rather than waiting for a call — the engaged fighter's job becomes keeping the bandit's attention and flight path predictable, while the support fighter exploits that predictability for the kill. This is what the USAF's modern ACM doctrine below is built on; expect the support fighter to get the kill more often than the engaged fighter, which is normal, not a sign something went wrong.

Roles: engaged fighter vs. support fighter

The engaged fighter's job: fly the best BFM available to survive and kill the bandit (everything in Parts I and III applies directly); get a positive visual ID before shooting, since radar/IFF alone often can't clear an unknown contact as hostile; and keep tally on the wingman where possible, though the bandit is the priority.

The support fighter's job, in strict priority order: first, deconfliction — never fly through the fight or cross into the engaged fighter's weapon deconfliction zone; second, take any genuine shot of opportunity the bandit's focus on the engaged fighter presents, exactly as if the bandit were simply unaware of you; third, clear the surrounding airspace for additional bandits, since the engaged fighter is fully occupied and can't do this himself.

Establishing who's engaged

Roles aren't fixed to flight lead — they're set by a simple hierarchy, checked top to bottom:

  • Most defensive fighter is automatically engaged — if one of you is already the one under threat, surviving takes priority over deconfliction duty.
  • If neither is defensive, most offensive fighter is engaged — tie-broken first by who has tally on the bandit, then by who has the best angle-off, then by whoever reaches the merge first.
  • If it's still unclear, the flight lead becomes engaged by default.

Roles are only actually set once both calls happen: the declaration ("[callsign] engaged") and the acknowledgment ("[callsign] press"). If the support role would put you in a worse position than you're already in, respond "unable [reason]" instead of pressing; only the flight lead can respond "negative" to overrule a requested role swap.

Weapon deconfliction zone

The support fighter's clear-field-of-fire check is a roughly 10° cone around the engaged fighter — visualize it with a HUD pitch ladder (5° above and below the horizon) or, without one, the outer ring of a gunsight's combiner glass, which is normally about the same width. Never take the shot while the engaged fighter is inside that cone, and hold the check for the weapon's full time of flight, not just the instant of launch — an early rear-aspect IR missile's typical half-mile-to-one-mile shot can still be in the air for several seconds, long enough for the engaged fighter to maneuver into the cone after you've already fired.

Radio calls

Descriptive calls build shared situational awareness without asking for anything: a sighting is reported as [callsign], bogey/bandit, [clock position], [range], [high/low + degrees] — an unidentified contact is a bogey; once visually confirmed hostile it becomes a bandit for the rest of the engagement. "Tally" reports you've spotted the called contact. "Vid hostile" reports a successful visual ID as hostile — this is usually what actually clears the flight to fire, separate from just having a radar/IFF read. A kill call includes the bandit's position/altitude/direction of turn at the moment of the kill, since a fast-moving fight can leave other flight members unsure which contact just went down.

Directive calls tell a specific flight member to do something now: "break [direction]" is a maximum-performance, energy-dumping turn with flares — reserved for an imminent enemy shot, and if it's called at you, survival overrides whatever you were doing. "Hard [direction]" is a lesser, sustained-turn version used to engage a spotted threat, no flares implied. "Separate [heading]" ends the engagement and reforms the flight on a given heading, chosen to be less than 90° off the current heading so the flight spends as little time as possible banked (and therefore blind on one side).

A bracket is both a maneuver and a call: both fighters split apart and turn back in toward a bogey in the forward hemisphere, building turning room on both sides at once and immediately revealing which fighter the bogey is biased toward — called "leaning" on that fighter, readable the same way as any other unaware-bandit tell (small profile, little line-of-sight movement toward the fighter he's leaning on, lots of line-of-sight movement from the other fighter's point of view).

If the bandit swaps targets mid-fight — a real risk any time he can see both of you — whoever notices first calls "bandit switch, [callsign] engaged," and the roles flip accordingly without needing to re-run the whole establishing-roles hierarchy from scratch.

The merge: denying tally, building turning room

Approach a suspected bogey in a wide tactical formation (line abreast, meaningful vertical split) rather than tight formation — the goal is denying tally on both of you at once: if the bogey only ever sees one fighter, he can't choose to switch targets later, which makes him much easier to sandwich if it turns into a fight. The vertical split does double duty: it hides your presence and it banks altitude that becomes both energy and extra turning room for the support fighter's eventual lead turn onto the bandit's rear quarter.

Clearing for additional bandits

Once roles are set, clearing the airspace around the fight is specifically the support fighter's job — the engaged fighter is fully committed to BFM and can't do it. This is a deliberately trained scan, not something that happens automatically: check the volume of space a new bandit would have to cross to reach a good weapon shot on either fighter, including the engaged fighter's own blind spot, which he can't watch himself while fighting. Training against only ever one bandit at a time is exactly what makes this scan atrophy into a habit of not looking — worth deliberately practicing against a scenario with unannounced late-arriving bandits, not just a clean 2v1.

Common pitfalls

  • Bad spacing: too close wastes time re-aligning turn circles before anything productive happens; too far risks losing visual on your own wingman and the ability to actually support him.
  • Accidental Fighting Wing: if the support fighter ends up flying the same plane of motion/turn circle as the engaged fighter instead of using his freedom to build an independent offensive angle, the pair has quietly regressed to the old close-formation doctrine — nothing about that is faster than a solo fight, which defeats the entire point of ACM. The fix is deliberate: recognize it and actively get off the engaged fighter's turn circle to try a different angle.

Defensive ACM: bandit from the rear, and the bandit switch

If a bogey is spotted in the flight's rear hemisphere, the standard answer is to simply turn the flight toward him. That forces a choice: continuing his attack on the nearer fighter sandwiches him between both of you and hands the support fighter an easy shot; switching to the outside fighter to avoid the sandwich still leaves him at the rear of both aircraft, and gets called out immediately as a bandit switch so roles can flip. Everything else — engaged/support responsibilities, the deconfliction zone, the radio-call structure — carries over unchanged from the offensive case; only the opening geometry is different.

(Source: Mike Solyom/The Ops Center, "Air Combat Maneuvering" series, five videos covering ACM fundamentals & doctrine history, roles & the weapon deconfliction zone, a practice-scenario walkthrough, clearing for multiple bandits, and defensive ACM/the bandit switch — quoting or closely paraphrasing official USAF ACM doctrine throughout. The series' own practice method uses a free downloadable DCS World training mission with an AI bogey and optional "wildcard" bandits — a real-world/DCS-specific training tool, not something replicable in War Thunder or Ace Combat, noted here for completeness only.)

D10Two-ship ACM — merge-to-kill under 30 seconds
  • Aim: kill the bandit within about 30 s of the merge, before enemies within reinforcement range arrive.
  • Roles: the engaged fighter flies the actual BFM; the support fighter owns deconfliction (never fires while the engaged fighter is inside the ~10° weapon-deconfliction cone), takes shots of opportunity, and clears for more bandits. Roles are set by radio: "Engaged," "Press," "Unable [reason]," or a flight-lead "Negative."
  • Setup: the series' own method is a free downloadable DCS World training mission with an AI bogey and optional "wildcard" bandits — DCS-specific, not replicable in War Thunder or Ace Combat. The exercise's starting geometry is not recorded in this guide. ?
  • Watch for: the support fighter drifting onto the engaged fighter's plane of motion and recreating Fighting Wing.
