Part III — BVR & Missile Defense

The Weapons Envelope

  • A shot = range + angle-off + aspect angle together, not range alone.
  • Know your own missile's no-escape zone — a real threat, not a wasted round that gives away your position.
  • Firing outside the real envelope is the single most common way pilots burn ordnance for nothing.
  • Gun or missile first in a dogfight? The missile leads only if it meets two of three: min range under ~2 of your turn radii, no launch delay once in envelope, usable off-boresight. Otherwise fly for the gun and use the missile to stop him escaping.

A shot is defined jointly by range, angle-off, and aspect angle — not range alone. Learn your own missile's no-escape zone (where a target statistically can't evade) so a launch is a real threat, not a wasted round that gives away your position. Firing outside the real envelope is the single most common way pilots burn ordnance for nothing.

Missiles inside the dogfight

  • Which envelope to fly for: Shaw calls a missile "dogfight-compatible" if it has at least two of these: a minimum range under about two fighter turn radii against a maneuvering target, little or no launch delay once the envelope is met, and usable off-boresight capability. A compatible missile becomes the primary weapon. Otherwise the gun is primary, and the missile's job is to punish him if he tries to separate and escape.
  • Rear-aspect missiles: minimum range and the aspect limit are the hard constraints. Pure pursuit is the wrong tool, because it closes range and increases aspect. Lag pursuit opens range and reduces aspect, so energy tactics suit these missiles best. The firing envelope also swings with the target, faster the harder he turns and the further away he is, so you often reach it only briefly.
  • All-aspect missiles: take any shot before the first pass, even beyond visual range. Even a miss forces a defensive move that wrecks his game plan and usually leaves you offensive and faster. Against a similar aircraft with all-aspect missiles, energy tactics become dangerous because the big separations they create let him meet his minimum range, so stay with angles tactics.
  • Your gun vs. his missile: stay close, using angles tactics and nose-to-nose turns, to keep yourself inside his minimum range. If he reverses to open a nose-to-tail turn, decide at once whether to extend away, continue, or reverse. Extending works best with good speed and high aspect at the pass.
  • Your missile vs. his gun: keep your speed and separation (energy tactics). If you also have a gun, it's still the easier envelope to reach, and the missile stops his escape.
  • Getting away from a missile fighter: keep him in sight until you're beyond his maximum range. Dive toward low altitude and accelerate to full speed, which shrinks his missile's reach. After a missed shot, extend nose-to-tail: dive toward his six, then roll out gradually to about 180° from his heading without crossing his tail, which would invite him to reverse.

(Source: Robert Shaw, Fighter Combat, ch.3 One-versus-One Maneuvering, Similar Aircraft.)

Reading the missile "Sheet data" lines (Part V)

Each Part V card's NEZ line is player guidance — the practical range. Under it, a "Sheet data" line gives the missile's hard limits from the game's own files. Those limits bound the envelope; they are not the no-escape zone itself.

  • Lock (IR missiles) — the seeker's baseline lock range from the rear, from any aspect, and head-on against an afterburning target. No lock, no guided shot.
  • Own seeker (active-radar missiles) — the range at which the missile's own radar can lock; 16 km for every active-radar missile in this guide.
  • Motor — how long the rocket burns. After that the missile only coasts and loses speed, which is why practical ranges sit far inside the maximums.
  • Guided — how long the missile keeps guiding before it gives up. Max flight — the absolute distance cap. Neither is a usable launch range.
  • G — the missile's maximum pull. Min range — too close and it can't hit.

(Source: community "Guided weaponry data (in-game values)" Google Sheet, AAM tabs, stats last changed in game v2.57.1.91. The sheet's own "statcard" launch-range and G figures are labelled "useless" there and are deliberately not used.)

BVR Offense

  • F-pole: range to target at missile impact — bigger = more margin to disengage before he can return fire.
  • Maximize F-pole: off-angle, nose-high, throttle back, hold the target near your radar's gimbal limit (~60° off-center).
  • The no-escape zone (inside Rmax) is the only shot worth firing without a follow-up.
  • Flow: commit → meld (radars converge) → sort (assign targets) → launch → crank (open lateral separation) → decide.
  • After launch, default to skate/short skate — a banzai merge trades away every BVR advantage you just built.
  • Fire two per target ("fox twice") — a single shot isn't a guaranteed kill against a defended, maneuvering target.
  • SARH missile commits you to tracking; an IR missile is fire-and-forget — pick accordingly at the sort stage.

F-pole is the distance between you and the target at the moment your missile reaches it — the bigger it is, the more margin you have to disengage before he can return fire. Maximize it with an off-angle, nose-high approach: speed brakes and flaps out, throttle back, holding the target near your radar's gimbal limit (~60° off-center) rather than pointed straight at it. This forces the defender's choice — eat the shot, or break lock and give up his own.

F-pole is one of a small family of named ranges worth knowing together. Rough numbers for your own aircraft (even approximate) turn "should I still be pressing?" from a gut call into a line you can actually see coming.

TermMeaning
A-poleRange to target at the moment your missile goes active — its seeker takes over from your radar's guidance
E-pole (escape pole)Range from a threat at which you must already be maneuvering to defeat anything it could have fired at you — your own abort deadline
Decision RangeThe closest range at which you could still fly a full notch-and-abort sequence and actually survive it

Rmax is a volume, not a number

Rmax isn't one fixed number for a missile — it's the volume of space around a target from which a shot can be flown out successfully, and it shrinks or grows with your own altitude and speed and the target's aspect and energy state at the moment of launch. A missile fired at the edge of Rmax against a target that's already turning cold and accelerating away has a real chance of falling short.

The no-escape zone

The same missile fired inside the no-escape zone — the portion of Rmax where the target statistically cannot outrun or out-turn it regardless of what it does — is a near-guaranteed kill. That's why "he's in range" and "he's in the no-escape zone" are different claims; only the second is a shot worth committing to without a follow-up.

Source caveatSourced from FlyAndWire's Intercept Geometry series (Part II: Definitions) — written for real intercept doctrine, so treat the exact range bands as illustrative rather than directly transferable to any specific in-game missile without checking its actual performance.

Engagement flow, condensed from real intercept doctrine: commit toward the threat → meld (both your radars converge on the group) → sort (assign targets so you're not both tracking the same contact — by cardinal direction and altitude is the simplest scheme: "engaging northern bandit," "taking the one at 25 angels," or split by geometry, e.g. lead takes left/high, wingman takes right/low) → launch → crank (turn to open lateral separation, still tracking) → decide.

The decision after launch has three shapes: skate (launch and leave — abort the engagement before your Desired Out Range), short skate (leave before the harder Minimum Abort Range line, later than a full skate but still before the merge), or banzai (launch and commit to merging anyway). Default to skate or short skate — merging trades away every BVR advantage you just built.

Missile selection matters at the sort stage: a semi-active radar missile needs continuous guidance, so firing it commits you to tracking; an infrared missile is fire-and-forget, so it's the one to use if you need to stay free to maneuver immediately after the shot. Don't assume one missile is a kill — firing two at a single target ("fox twice") is standard practice, not wasteful, since a single shot isn't guaranteed against a defended, maneuvering target.

Verify before relying on thisOne source claimed missiles struggle to engage a target flying directly away (a "six o'clock" blind spot) — plausible as a specific missile-guidance quirk, but not confirmed broadly enough to trust as general doctrine. Treat as a lead to verify against current War Thunder missile behavior, not a fact to plan around yet.

Missile Defense

  • Hot = closing, cold = opening range, crank = turn to gimbal limit holding partial lock — extends missile flight without giving up track.
  • Notch: fly perpendicular to the threat's line of sight (3/9 o'clock) and descend. Against SARH notch the launching radar; against a Fox-3 notch the missile itself.
  • Notch geometry: put the missile just behind your wing line (about 90–110° off your nose, never ahead of it), keep changing altitude or speed while you hold it, and don't leave the notch until the RWR clears.
  • Fox-3 (active radar): hold the notch 10–20 s, dump chaff alongside it, and change pitch once the missile loses lock — chaff alone won't do it.
  • Fox-3 range rule: beyond ~20 km you can reliably beat it, around 15 km it's partly luck, inside ~10 km it's close to a guaranteed kill — so defend by not sitting in the shooter's envelope.
  • Terrain/low altitude: degrades the seeker and improves your own turn rate and acceleration.
  • Don't evade early — a missile burns ~10s then coasts. Hold your hardest maneuver until it's coasting on spent energy.
  • Chaff (radar) / flares (IR) buy the maneuver, they don't replace it — cut afterburner popping flares against IRCCM.
  • Common mistakes: evading too early, treating countermeasures as a substitute for maneuvering, notching without descending, flying straight and level in the notch, leaving the notch before the RWR clears, mixing up cold/crank/notch.

Hot means closing on the threat, cold means opening range. Crank is the middle option worth treating as its own move: turn the threat to your radar's gimbal limit — as far off-axis as possible while still holding a partial lock — rather than fully committing cold. It extends any missile's flight path and buys time without giving up your own track.

Notching

A threat radar tracks mainly by Doppler shift. Fly so your closure rate reads as zero — perpendicular to its line of sight — and you're indistinguishable from ground clutter. Turn until the threat sits at your 3 or 9 o'clock, ideally while descending; notching is far stronger combined with altitude loss than alone. Against a semi-active missile you notch the launching radar, since it needs that radar the whole way. Against a Fox-3 you notch the missile itself — see the Fox-3 section below.

Notching in practice

The idea is simple; the execution is where it falls apart, because the missile's bearing keeps moving while you fly. One experienced poster says there is no perfect secret trick and that you improve by recognising how these launches look on the RWR over many repetitions. These are the points that come up most often.

  • Put it just behind the wing line, not ahead of it: aim for the missile at 90–110° off your nose (3 or 9 o'clock on the RWR, or a little further back). If the missile is ahead of your beam you are no longer notching it, and the seeker tracks you far more easily. Players also report that turning past 90° sometimes works when exactly 90° doesn't.
  • Notch the missile itself, and don't count on the shooter's lock to save you: once an active-radar missile has gone live it uses its own seeker, so breaking the launcher's lock doesn't help. One poster still suggests breaking the launcher's lock too if you can, but the missile comes first.
  • Keep steering to hold the angle: the bearing changes as the missile closes, so check the RWR and re-turn into the indicated direction rather than setting a heading and hoping. Close in, the RWR stops being enough and you have to watch the missile by eye. Don't forget that a Fox-3 gives no continuous-wave warning, so the RWR can't tell you whether it still has you.
  • Never fly straight and level in the notch: keep changing altitude or speed the whole time. A missile that is angle-gating can pick out chaff that drifts the wrong way and look ahead to where you should be, so a steady target is easier for it to find again. This works like popping flares against an infrared missile.
  • Add altitude change, not just angle: descending forces the radar to look down at you through ground clutter, and more clutter makes the notch easier. Chaff adds more clutter but is not enough on its own.
  • Use the vertical when the geometry runs out: if threats are at about your altitude, going straight up or down is also perpendicular to them. Flanking high to one side sets up the same thing. The hard case is a missile coming from below or from 4–5 o'clock, where holding a clean 90° is very difficult.
  • Faster means less forgiving: the higher your speed, the more exact the notch has to be, so a loose notch at high speed is the one most likely to fail.
  • Stay in it until the RWR clears: when the warning drops, change direction in case a missile that lost you is still coming. A poster also warns that the missile can resume tracking after the notch ends, so don't relax the moment it goes quiet.
  • A radar-guided shooter can undo your notch: one poster reports F-14 pilots switching to continuous-wave mode mid-notch, which defeats it; chaff dropped after the notch helps against that.
  • Several missiles from different directions: notching one costs energy and can leave you too slow to notch the next, and I found no source with a clean answer to this. ?

(Source: War Thunder forum threads "Questions about notching," "Question about notching at high altitudes," "How to notch better? ARB," "How to evade all kind of radar missile above 12.0," "Tips against ARH/SARH missiles," "How to properly evade Fox-3?," "Notching mechanics causing balance issues," and two Steam community War Thunder discussion threads. These are community player reports, not official Gaijin data, and none of them gives the in-game Doppler gate width, the angle tolerance in degrees, or the minimum closure speed, so the 90–110° figure is the community rule of thumb, not a measured limit. Players recommend video tutorials by Defyn, Migan, Astro, llamaso12, 64Mustang and catwerfer for seeing the notch done live.) ?

Multipath / low altitude

Flying near terrain does two things: degrades the seeker through ground clutter and multipath reflection, and — genuinely underrated — denser low-altitude air improves your own turn rate and acceleration. Works best over broken or mountainous ground, not flat terrain.

Causing overshoot

Missiles burn fuel for roughly 10 seconds then coast on whatever energy remains. The instinct to evade the instant you see a launch is backwards — a missile at full energy out-turns almost anything. The real defeat window is late: hold your hardest maneuvering until its energy is already spent, forcing a correction it can't afford.

Chaff & flare discipline

Countermeasures buy the maneuver, they don't replace it. Chaff against radar missiles, flares against infrared — and cut afterburner when popping flares against a missile with counter-countermeasures, since raw heat output undercuts the flare. Against an active-radar missile: if you see it visibly fall for the chaff instead of you, you're clear — but it's angle-gating for chaff moving unnaturally, so keep varying your own altitude or speed while it tracks rather than flying straight.

Defeating a Fox-3 (active radar) in War Thunder

An active-radar missile only needs the launcher to point it. The AIM-120A, for example, switches on its own seeker about 16 km from the target, so the launcher can break away straight after firing. Your odds are set mostly by how far out the shot was taken, then by how cleanly you stack the tools below.

  • Range sets the odds: past ~20 km the techniques below work reliably, around 15 km luck plays a big part even when you do everything right, and inside ~10 km it is close to a guaranteed kill. One poster says agile top-tier jets can still notch from 4–5 km and heavier jets from 7–8 km; most others rate those distances as poor odds.
  • Notch the missile, not the launcher: put the missile near your 3 or 9 o'clock and descend while holding it. At long range use the RWR bearing to hold roughly 90°; inside ~5 km you have to watch the missile by eye. Plan to hold the notch for 10–20 seconds — a short notch doesn't clear the lock.
  • Chaff goes with the notch, not instead of it: dump chaff so it sits in the missile seeker's path while your body is hidden in the notch. Chaff alone doesn't beat a modern Fox-3, and a late last-second chaff spam only occasionally works.
  • After it falls for the chaff, keep the notch and change pitch: an Immelmann, a split-S, or just a slow pitch up or down stops the missile re-predicting where you are on inertial guidance and re-acquiring.
  • Make it correct more than once: turn the full 180° at least twice, preferably three times — a single turn gives the missile only one correction to make.
  • Several launches from 20 km or more: going cold early is the easiest answer. Past ~20 km missiles bleed energy fast, so every extra second of distance helps you.
  • Low-altitude multipath is a last resort: players report it failing even below treeline with chaff out, and most maps don't let you get low enough. Don't plan your defense around it.
  • Top-down shots are the worst case: a Fox-3 fired from above at a target near the ground is described as nearly undefendable. The answer is positional — don't be the low aircraft under a shooter's nose, and if you survive the first exchange, fire your own ARH back and go cold. As one poster puts it, if you're already defending hard you've probably made a mistake earlier.

(Source: War Thunder forum threads "How to properly evade Fox-3?", "How to Evade FOX-3 Radar Missiles," "Avoiding radar guided missiles," "Tips against ARH/SARH missiles," "Dodging multiple radar missles," "What is the recommended evasive action from top down FOX 3 attacks," and "Chaff in toptier"; AIM-120A seeker activation range per old-wiki.warthunder.com/AIM-120A. These are community player reports, not official Gaijin figures, so the distances above are estimates.) ?

Common mistakesEvading too early, while the missile still has full energy to correct. Treating chaff/flares as a substitute for maneuvering rather than what buys the maneuver. Notching without descending. Flying straight and level once in the notch. Holding the missile ahead of your beam. Leaving the notch before the RWR clears. Using cold, crank, and notch interchangeably when they trade off differently.
D11Missile defense — what the community says to practice
  • Review your matches: a forum poster recommends watching the replay of your matches in sensor mode, almost every time, saying it costs little time and helps you improve.
  • Practice partners: another poster suggests custom battles as an alternative to random battles, while noting that finding practice partners is hard, and says the main way to learn is watching instructional videos and practicing in-game.
  • Solo setup: a forum thread on test-flight customization reports air targets available for propeller aircraft but not for jets, and describes the available AI aircraft as having broken flight models. No confirmed solo setup for notching practice was found. ?
  • Pass: none sourced. There is no structured notching exercise with a pass/fail test in any source this guide holds, so none is written here.

(Source: War Thunder official forum threads "Notching fox-3 missile" (Gregghy, LostPlayer2023-psn) and "Test flight customization" (Circleati, plane_lover, RunaDacino). These are community posts, not an official syllabus. Every number is the source's own suggested, adjustable training parameter.)

Part IV — Tactics & Strategy

Fighter Mission Types

  • Fighter sweep: independent hunt ahead of a package — most offensive, but protects nothing directly.
  • Escort: stays with the protected asset — guarantees cover, ties you to its speed/route/fuel.
  • CAP: holds station/pattern, reactive — covers a fixed area or axis continuously.
  • Modern doctrine favors sweep-first over tight escort — don't let a slower asset dictate your fight.
  • GCI: a ground/airborne controller vectors you onto a target from a wider picture than your own radar.

Not every sortie has the same job, and the job you're actually flying changes what "correct" looks like before a single bandit shows up. Three shapes worth telling apart:

Show mission-type comparison table
MissionWhat it doesTrade-off
Fighter sweepFighters range out independently, ahead of or separate from any strike package, to find and destroy enemy fighters on their own terms — historically, hitting enemy airfields before defenders could even get airborne.The most offensive and flexible option, since nothing ties you to a package's track or timing — but it protects nothing directly. Miss the defenders and whatever's behind the sweep meets them unescorted.
EscortFighters stay with a protected asset (bombers, a strike package) for the duration of its exposure, positioned to engage anything that threatens it.Guarantees protection where it's actually needed, but ties your fighters to the package's speed, altitude and route — and historically, to fuel: an escort at the edge of its range can't loiter long before it has to turn for home.
Combat air patrol (CAP)Fighters hold a station or patrol pattern, ready to intercept whatever crosses it — see Part II for pattern shapes (racetrack, counter-rotating, beam, counter-opposing).Reactive rather than seeking the fight out, but covers a fixed area or axis continuously rather than committing everything to one strike package.

Modern doctrine has generally moved away from tight escort and toward a sweep-first posture — fighters ranging ahead of and to the flanks of a package to establish air superiority before it ever arrives, rather than flying glued to its wing. The underlying reasoning carries straight over from Part I: a fighter tied to a slower asset's track and speed is fighting on someone else's terms, the same problem an energy fighter has if it lets an angles fighter dictate the turn.

Escort, per Shaw

Shaw ranks the sweep as the preferred fighter mission and splits escort into four jobs, in order of value when fighters are short:

  • Remote escort: a sweep a few minutes ahead of the strike along its route, or blocking CAPs between the target and enemy airfields. Usually the most effective use of escort fighters.
  • Detached escort: elements around the strike group within visual range, each at least a pair, placed to engage attackers before they reach firing range on the bombers. Forward elements sit 2–4 turn radii apart; rear elements 1–2. Stay disciplined: chase an attacker only until it turns away, then return to position.
  • Close escort: over, under and among the strike group to catch whatever gets through. Only works if a detached escort gives warning.
  • Reception escort: meets the strike on the way home, when it is scattered and its escort is low on fuel and ammo.

Attacking bombers: deal with the escort first. If it's badly placed, hit the bombers and leave before it reacts; otherwise tie it up with some of your fighters while the rest go for the bombers. Forcing a bomber to jettison or abort is a "mission kill" and often enough. Avoid sitting behind bombers with tail guns; head-on and forward-quarter passes are usually best. A low-level penetrator may drop a retarded bomb in your face, so break hard sideways at the first sign of something falling off it.

Ground-controlled interception (GCI)

Shaw describes two kinds of control. Close control: the controller watches you and the target and gives range, bearing and suggested headings until you have your own contact, then switches to advice only. Broadcast control: the controller reports contacts relative to a reference point everyone knows, and pilots run their own intercepts. Close control gives the best offense; broadcast handles many contacts at once. Either way the controller supports the fighters, not the reverse. The geometry pilots fly from those calls is in Intercept Geometry.

Intercept Geometry

  • Collision bearing: target bearing stays constant while range drops, so you're on a collision course.
  • Forward-quarter (FQ): approach at a chosen angle off the target's nose; quick, little penetration, needs all-aspect weapons.
  • Stern conversion: build sideways displacement, then turn in behind. Rule of thumb: displacement (m) ≈ 16.5 × aspect (°) × range (km).
  • Belly-check halfway through a conversion turn: it's long, blind and close to the target.
  • Two-ship plays: single-side offset (defensive), trail, sweep, pincer, drag, lead-around, hook, option, cross-block, break-away.

Terms

TermMeaning
Target aspect (TAA)Angle between the line of sight and the target's course; how far off his nose you are
Antenna-train angle (ATA)Angle between your nose and the line of sight; also called lead angle, or lag angle if you're pointed behind
Lateral separationYour perpendicular distance from the bogey's flight path; needed to fit a conversion turn
Degrees to go (DTG)How far you still have to turn to parallel the target's course
Collision headingHeading where bearing and ATA hold steady while range drops. Turn right of it and he drifts left and crosses ahead; turn left of it and he drifts toward your nose

The two basic intercepts

Forward quarter. Turn to build the aspect you want, then turn to collision heading to hold it; you pass close in the horizontal. Good for all-aspect missiles, for coming out of the sun, and for an earlier visual ID from a side view. Weaknesses: the bogey can jink to wreck the geometry, and you may end up too close for a stern option. Simplest version: turn straight to collision heading and accept whatever aspect you have.

Stern conversion. From a head-on setup, offset to build displacement, parallel the bogey's track, then turn in at conversion range to roll out behind him in your rear-quarter envelope. Shaw's worked example: 55 km out at 2° aspect gives about 1,800 m of displacement (16.5 × 2 × 55); he wants about 6,100 m for a turn starting at 15 km. Start early if you have too much displacement, late and harder if too little. With height you can convert with zero sideways offset using an Immelmann from below or a split-S from above. It ends in the best attack position but takes the most time and fuel, is easy to beat with a small turn toward you, and the long turn exposes your belly to anyone you haven't seen, so Shaw doesn't recommend it in an unknown environment. A combined attack-reattack fires a forward-quarter shot, then converts for a stern shot.

Two-ship intercept plays

Show intercept catalog (section, two-aircraft)
PlayHowTrade-off
Single-side offsetBoth fighters on one side of the bogeys; the wingman crosses under the lead to sit in spread on the far side. Lead runs FQ or stern.Good mutual support and a known threat side, but defensive; don't stern-convert against bogeys in trail
TrailWingman drops in trail as far back as visual allows; lead makes the visual ID and passes it back so the trailer can shoot.Strong offense, poor defense for the trailer; fly very fast
SweepA stern conversion in trail: the outside wingman delays his turn to gain nose-to-tail spacing.Good offense if undetected; the wingman is exposed during the turn
PincerBoth split in opposite directions for separate FQ or stern attacks ("heart attack"). Split high and low as well.Very effective offensively but no mutual support for a while; needs training and two radars
DragShift to trail; the lead turns away at about visual range to bait the bogeys while the trailer stays hidden and takes the shot.Devastating when it works; weak defensively, poor against all-aspect missiles
Lead-aroundFrom trail, the lead breaks off to one side for displacement so the two fighters bracket the bogeys at the same moment.Simpler than the drag; one of the best against bogeys in trail
HookLead holds collision course and makes the visual ID; wingman ("hooker") takes a wide split, often low, and turns in timed by the lead's range calls to shoot at the pass.Offensive and better defensively than trail; break off within ~90° of turn if no shot
OptionSingle-side offset where the wingman chooses: cut inside to bracket, hold abeam, or drop to trail for a sweep. He tells the lead which.Very flexible; needs a well-trained wingman
Cross-blockAgainst two bogeys running a pincer, hold combat spread until they're about to lock you. Each fighter then locks the bogey on the far side, both turn in and cross, and each comes at his target from its unwatched side while the other meets it head-on.Strong counter to a pincer; needs skill, two radars and luck. If one fighter loses his target, the other continues while he regains a cover position
Break-awayFly tight enough to look like one radar contact, then split near the bogeys' lock-on range so one fighter reaches the merge unseen.A trick to confuse radar and GCI; depends on enemy radar resolution

Choosing an intercept: Shaw's three tests, in order: can you actually complete it (simple geometry beats clever geometry if your skill or sensors are marginal), how well does it keep you defended, and how much offense does it give. Pick the most offensive tactic your pair can fly that still keeps enough defense for the situation, and practise two or three until they're automatic.

War Thunder fitShaw writes for radar-equipped jets with ground controllers. In War Thunder the "controller" is your own radar, the minimap and teammates' calls, and distances are much shorter. The geometry (aspect, displacement, belly-checks during a conversion) still applies; the NM figures don't.

(Source: Robert Shaw, Fighter Combat, ch.10 Tactical Intercepts.)

Target Priority

Priority ladder
  1. Immediate threat — on your six, or about to be
  2. Team need — a bomber about to drop, an ally about to die
  3. Isolated target — alone, not buried in a furball
  4. Rearmost in a group — the historical "tail-end Charlie," killed before the rest notice
  5. Closest to your altitude — costs the least energy to reach
  6. Easy kill — hasn't seen you, damaged, or lower energy

Nearest or biggest is not automatically right — that instinct is how beginners get killed by the bandit they didn't pick. An isolated straggler beats diving into a furball where two or three others can turn on you the moment you commit.

Multi-Bogey & Section Tactics

  • Section (2+) attacks one target in spread formation (~300–1,830m apart) — one aircraft flies the perch, covering rather than joining.
  • Double Attack (shooter-cover): second aircraft waits for permission before engaging.
  • Loose Deuce (shooter-shooter): both attack independently once committed.
  • Comms: engaged fighter declares intent; cover calls tally + position; role-changes are called explicitly.
  • Outnumbered alone: defensive unless attacking; max speed; very high or very low; never more than ~90° of turn without a belly-check; one pass and leave.
  • At BVR range: shooter/cover trail — one commits forward, one holds ~37km back with weapons/radar on the threat; roles reverse when the shooter goes cold.

A section (2+ aircraft) attacking one target uses spread formation for mutual lookout — roughly 300–1,830 m apart depending on the threat — with one aircraft flying the perch: holding an offensive position above/behind, covering the engaged fighter rather than joining the attack directly.

Two doctrines structure who shoots: Double Attack (shooter-cover — the second aircraft waits for permission before engaging, a controlled "shooter-shooter-on-call" setup) and Loose Deuce (shooter-shooter — both attack independently once committed).

The comms pattern that makes either work: the engaged fighter declares intent, the covering fighter calls tally and reports position, and role-changes are called explicitly rather than assumed.

At BVR range specifically, sections often run a shooter/cover trail: one aircraft commits forward as shooter, the other holds roughly 37 km behind as cover with weapons and radar still pointed at the threat. Roles reverse the moment the shooter goes cold.

Outnumbered: Shaw's one-versus-many and few-versus-many

Shaw's starting point: about 90% of air-to-air losses in every war came from attacks the victim never saw. Alone or outnumbered, you are defensive whenever you aren't actively attacking, and offense is limited to hit-and-run.

  • Speed is your main defense. A fast target forces the attacker to use more lead, puts him further forward where you can see him, and shrinks his rear-hemisphere shot.
  • Pick very high or very low, not medium. Either extreme roughly halves the directions a threat can come from. High suits good radar/GCI coverage and guns-only enemies; low suits enemy SAMs/long-range radar and cloud cover above.
  • No turn past about 90° without a reversal and belly-check. Plan attacks so they need no more than that, and abandon targets that would.
  • Weave to clear six. Turns of 60–90° alternating side to side, timed so your blind cone is checked before an attacker can close from detection range to firing range. Shaw's WWII example: detection at ~900 m, guns at ~370 m and ~30 m/s closure gives about 18 s, so a gentle 60–90° turn every 18 s. Against missiles the timing is too short, so instead: hard sustained turn 60–90°, roll to belly-check, fly straight the same time, repeat.
  • Attack once and leave. Take the far-side rear bogey so the attack doesn't pull you into the formation, shoot at the first chance, then reverse hard to clear your belly before checking the result. Don't loiter to "sweeten" the shot.
  • If caught: turn hard into a forward-hemisphere threat for a head-on pass and extend. Outrun slower bogeys. If it becomes a fight, fight aggressively but take the first exit. Call for help early.
  • Use clouds against guns and IR: duck in, change heading about 90°, pop out. Don't stay in or near cloud against radar missiles.
  • Fuel: keep enough for a full-speed bugout, and don't go back into the fight once committed to leaving unless you're close to home or a friendly needs one high-speed pass to escape.

A pair against many: fly combat spread at high speed and use visual cross-cover instead of weaving (weaving in formation leaves your wingman's six uncovered). Turn the section in tac turns of 90° or less with straight segments between. Use a bracket on forward-hemisphere targets, attack only with an advantage and a first shot, and make one pass. If you get split, plan for it before takeoff: each pilot should be ready to fly the one-versus-many rules above, and agree a rendezvous point.

Many-versus-many: keep strike-rejoin-strike and loose deuce or gaggle. Don't pile into a fur ball your side is holding; cruise its edge in a defensive posture and catch bogeys leaving the fight or arriving late. Strict radio discipline matters most here: "a panic message is the greatest of all crimes."

(Source: Robert Shaw, Fighter Combat, ch.8 Unlimited-Aircraft Tactics.)

War Thunder Match Economy

  • Genuinely disputed — treat as community rules of thumb, not confirmed mechanics.
  • Bases/ground targets drain the enemy ticket pool — a committed strike can shorten a losing match, at the cost of survivability while loaded.
  • Base-bombing loadouts fly worse until ordnance drops — jettison if intercepted rather than trying to fight heavy.
Genuinely disputedTicket bleed and base-rushing mechanics are argued over by the playerbase itself, with no settled consensus — treat what follows as community rules of thumb, not confirmed mechanics.

Rough consensus: bases and ground targets drain the enemy team's ticket pool, so a committed strike run can shorten a losing match, but at the cost of the striker's own survivability while loaded. Base-bombing loadouts fly worse until ordnance is dropped — jettison if intercepted rather than trying to fight heavy.

Part V — Vehicle Guide

USA

28 aircraft

Props

F4U-4B Corsair Horizontal energy fighter Combat flaps to ~450 km/h · avoid the vertical vs Spitfire/Bf 109 K-4 Angles fighter — ▲ turns well · ● average speed/climb
  • Fights as: Angles fighter — turns well, average speed/climb.
  • Role: horizontal energy fighter.
  • Strength: strong horizontal energy retention and instantaneous turn.
  • Weakness: can't out-climb genuine vertical fighters (Spitfire, Bf 109 K-4).
  • Primary loadout: four 20mm AN/M3 cannon, combat flaps usable to ~450 km/h.
  • Bombing load: 2× AN-M65A1 + 2× AN-M57 (104% of a 16,000 HP base at BR 5.7). (Source: LEGION's Loadouts 2.27 Google Sheet — the smallest load from this aircraft's own drop schedule that destroys one base, using the Bomb Chart's damage values and base HP by BR. % = total bomb damage ÷ (base HP × 0.9018), the kill threshold every count in the chart works out to; 100% = one base.)
  • Use when: fighting energy-poor opponents like the Fw 190 A.

Combat Doctrine

Fight energy-poor opponents like the Fw 190 A, not genuine vertical fighters like the Spitfire or Bf 109 K-4 — you can't out-climb those. Deploy combat flaps deliberately for a turning fight, not by default at speed.

Handling

  • Combat flaps sharply improve low-speed turn performance.
  • Rudder loses effectiveness above ~550 km/h — hurts tracking on a fleeing target at high closure.
  • Plan deflection shots at lower speed where possible.
  • Climb to 3-4km at battle start and stay there — the engine is strongest low, so don't chase altitude past this band.
  • "Energy trap" opponents by entering a fight slightly slower than them — they carry the unused energy/mistake risk, not you.
  • Late in a match or outnumbered, bait an overshoot with a flaps-assisted low-speed turn, then reverse and take the stall shot rather than sustaining a turning fight.

Source: War Thunder Wiki F4U-4B review; old-wiki.warthunder.com/F4U-4B.

Flight Performance

  • Turn time: 20.0-21.9s.
  • Climb rate: 13.8-19.0 m/s.
  • Sustained turn (sea level): ? — not tested; the sheet's WWII tabs only test a handful of other props (Spitfire LF Mk IX, Ju 288, Yak-1B). (Checked against the community "Sustained turn rate tests – War Thunder" Google Sheet, v2.37.0.20 — no matching row.)

Matchup Notes

  • Favorable dogfights: Fw 190 D variants, Tempest Mk V, Sea Fury.
  • Difficult, fight with caution: Bf 109s.
  • Avoid dogfighting: Spitfires, Ki-84s, A7Ms, N1Ks — all turn/climb better.
  • In an uptier, the same energy-advantage logic that applies against the Bf 109 K-4/Spitfire Mk 24 extends to other "superprops" like the Tempest II.

Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/F4U-4B, Usage in Battles.

  • Role: boom-and-zoom energy fighter.
  • Strength: light airframe, powerful Merlin — strong speed/altitude edge.
  • Weakness: light airframe is unusually vulnerable to fire; can't match jet speeds once one appears.

  • Use when: building energy for boom-and-zoom passes, not turn-fighting.

Combat Doctrine

Boom-and-zoom is the best way to get a kill — maintain an altitude/speed advantage as the core plan. Turn-fighting is viable only at low altitude against props, and wings can fail in a zoom climb above ~550 km/h. (Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/P-51H-5-NA.)

Survivability

High-octane fuel makes this airframe unusually susceptible to fire — treat any engine hit as more serious than on a comparable prop fighter. (Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/P-51H-5-NA.)

Flight Performance

  • Turn time: 19.0-20.8s.
  • Climb rate: 12.1-18.2 m/s.
  • Sustained turn (sea level): ? — not tested; the sheet's WWII tabs only test a handful of other props (Spitfire LF Mk IX, Ju 288, Yak-1B). (Checked against the community "Sustained turn rate tests – War Thunder" Google Sheet, v2.37.0.20 — no matching row.)

Matchup Notes

  • Beats most German prop opponents — out-manoeuvres most of its German counterparts despite the Merlin's power edge.
  • Biggest threats: Me 262 (will outrun you) and Ho 229 (will out-turn you) — a specific, named two-sided danger.
  • Turn-fighting is viable at low altitude against props; don't try to out-run a jet once one appears.

Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/P-51H-5-NA, Usage in Battles.

Combat Doctrine

Dictate engagement timing with superior acceleration and climb — pick the moment rather than get drawn into someone else's fight.

Engine Management

  • R-2800 Double Wasp overheats fast at high power, unmanaged.
  • Throttle discipline during sustained climbs matters as much as the maneuver itself.
  • Climb to 5,000m+ within the first ~5 minutes to bank an altitude/energy edge before the merge.
  • Cruise at 80-85% power to avoid overheating; save full WEP for roughly a 90-second window, mainly for escaping when outnumbered rather than sustained offense.
  • Once the engine takes critical damage, disengage and return to base immediately — a damaged engine is easy prey for enemy boom-and-zoom.

Source: War Thunder Wiki "How to Play Grumman F8F-1."

Flight Performance

  • Climb rate: 35+ m/s (WEP).
  • Turn time: 19.0-19.3s.
  • Thrust-to-weight: not a published figure for prop aircraft. Engine is 2,300hp (WEP) against ~3.84-4.06t loaded weight — roughly 0.57-0.60 hp/kg at WEP (computed from those two figures, not stated directly).
  • Sustained turn (sea level): ? — not tested; the sheet's WWII tabs only test a handful of other props (Spitfire LF Mk IX, Ju 288, Yak-1B). (Checked against the community "Sustained turn rate tests – War Thunder" Google Sheet, v2.37.0.20 — no matching row.)

Matchup Notes

  • Avoid head-on passes against cannon-armed aircraft (Bf 109, P-47, P-51) — a head-on trade favors their guns.
  • Don't turn-fight Zeroes below 4,500m — below that altitude their low-speed turn advantage wins.
  • Avoid extended sustained turning against late-model Spitfires — near-equal turn rate makes it a pure energy-bleed contest.
  • Climb rate rivals the Bf 109F — a useful yardstick for "who can out-climb this."

Source: War Thunder Wiki "How to Play Grumman F8F-1: the Brilliant Bearcat" (F8F-1, same airframe family — armament differs slightly) and wiki.warthunder.com/unit/f8f1b.

F3H-2 Demon Subsonic carrier fighter — strong in downtiers, outclassed at its own BR AIM-9B > AIM-7C · avoid turning fights — no RWR or countermeasures Angles fighter — ● average turn · ▼ slow, climbs poorly
  • Fights as: Angles fighter — average turn, slow, climbs poorly.
  • Role: subsonic carrier-based fighter — strong vs. downtiers, outclassed at its own BR.
  • Strength: two hard-hitting 20mm cannons at 996rpm; decent initial turn rate.
  • Weakness: among the worst energy retention in its class; no RWR or countermeasures at all.
  • Primary loadout: AIM-9B (rear-aspect · IR) + AIM-7C (all-aspect · BVR, unreliable motor/guidance).
  • Bombing load: 1× Mk 84 + 1× Mk 82 + 4× Mk 81 + 1× AN-M64A1 (100% of a 25,900 HP base at BR 9.0). (Source: LEGION's Loadouts 2.27 Google Sheet — the smallest load from this aircraft's own drop schedule that destroys one base, using the Bomb Chart's damage values and base HP by BR. % = total bomb damage ÷ (base HP × 0.9018), the kill threshold every count in the chart works out to; 100% = one base.)
  • Use when: hunting weaker downtiered opponents; avoid turning fights and its own BR's better-equipped peers.

Combat Doctrine

Fight vertical, not level — energy retention is described by experienced players as among the worst in its class, so a turning fight bleeds speed fast against nearly anything. Use hi/lo yo-yos and the combat-flaps special input (extends the leading-edge slats) for a brief high-AoA snap rather than a sustained turn, and disengage once slow rather than pressing on. It performs far better in downtiers, where it can run down and out-turn weaker opposition (F-86A, MiG-15, Hunter F.1-class); at its own 9.0 BR it's generally outclassed by faster, better-armed, RWR-equipped peers. (Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/F3H-2; forum.warthunder.com, "F3H-2 Demon.")

Radar & EW

  • No radar model designation given by any source checked — it still carries AIM-7C Sparrow (semi-active radar homing), so a lock has to come from the aircraft's own set regardless. ?
  • No RWR and no flares/chaff of any kind — confirmed explicitly. Surprise cuts both ways: take unseen shots rather than announcing a lock, and expect zero warning of an incoming missile yourself.
  • The Sparrow's "surprise" value is highest against opponents who also lack RWR — mostly downtiered/lower-BR targets, since most aircraft at the Demon's own BR carry one.

Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/F3H-2.

Matchup Notes

  • Strong against named lower-BR/downtiered opposition: F-86A, MiG-15, Hunter F.1-class.
  • At its own BR, the field generally has "either superior armament... or vastly superior performance... or radar warning receivers that nullify any surprise" from the Sparrow — outclassed on at least one axis by most peers.

  • Ground attack (CAS) is a poor choice — vulnerable to SAM/AAA, limited value against equipped defenses; the cannons/rockets/bombs exist but this isn't where the aircraft earns its keep.

AV-8A Harrier Vertical ambush / VIFF specialist Turn time 32-34s, climb 8.4-8.76 m/s — behind the curve on both axes · AIM-9G Double inferior — ▼ turns poorly · ▼ slow, climbs poorly
  • Fights as: Double inferior — turns poorly, slow, climbs poorly (VIFF is the exception).
  • Role: vertical ambush / VIFF specialist.
  • Strength: thrust vectoring (VIFF) — no other airframe here has it.
  • Weakness: mediocre turn time and climb rate; loses any sustained fight.
  • Primary loadout: AIM-9G (rear-aspect · IR), twin 30mm ADEN cannon.
  • Bombing load: ? — not listed in LEGION's Loadouts bomb sheet. (Checked against LEGION's Loadouts 2.27 Google Sheet — no matching aircraft row.)

Combat Doctrine

Force one decisive VIFF-assisted turn or overshoot. Don't get drawn into a sustained fight — this airframe loses on both turn time and climb rate.

Flight Performance

  • Turn time: 32-34s.
  • Climb rate: 8.4-8.76 m/s.
  • G-limit: roughly -5/+14.
  • Sustained turn (sea level): best 12.2°/s at 741 km/h IAS (4.6G). Curve: 10.6 / 12.0 / 12.2 / 12.1 / 11.1°/s at 556 / 648 / 741 / 833 / 926 km/h. 100% throttle row; the WEP row differs only at 926 km/h (11.7°/s). (Source: community "Sustained turn rate tests – War Thunder" Google Sheet, Deg/S SL + G-Force SL tabs, game v2.37.0.20 — sea level, 30 min fuel, no missiles, max power; row: AV-8A/C (100%).)

VIFF Technique

  • Partial nozzle deflection (roughly 60-80%) adds thrust misalignment that tightens the turn radius beyond pure aerodynamics — this is how the Harrier compensates for otherwise poor sustained turning.
  • Nozzles angled forward for rapid deceleration force a pursuer to overshoot; the resulting stall-speed fight is claimed winnable "99.9% of the time" against most opponents.
  • Core rule: "first one to stall, loses" — VIFF turns this into a speed/stall-management duel, not a free turn-rate cheat.
  • Against a faster aircraft that climbs to convert speed into altitude (F-16, F-4 named specifically), full 100% nozzle deflection can flip the Harrier inside their turn circle while they're already slow from the climb.
  • Cannon recoil pitches the nose down hard during low-speed/hover VIFF work — compensate with manual pitch-up.
  • Avoid any fight that isn't 1v1 — prioritize isolated targets with boom-and-zoom rather than a multi-bogey furball.
  • NEZ (in-game est.): AIM-9G ~2-3km (per user in-game experience).
  • Sheet data — AIM-9G: lock 5.5 km rear / 1 km head-on vs afterburner; 18G; motor 5 s; guided 60 s; max flight 18 km; min range 30 m. (Source: community "Guided weaponry data (in-game values)" Google Sheet, AAM tabs — stats last changed in game v2.57.1.91. Hard limits from game data, not a no-escape zone — see Weapons Envelope, Part III.)

Source: Steam Community Harrier guide (community source, not the official wiki — VIFF nozzle-percentage figures are one player's characterization, not an official spec).

Matchup Notes

No named 1v1 matchups found. Community consensus rates the AV-8A as a large, sluggish target that can't out-turn or out-gun most contemporaries — survivability rests on flares and VIFF rather than raw performance, and its unusually large flare count makes it hard to kill with IR missiles specifically. (Source: Steam Community discussion.)

Matchup Notes

  • Fights as: Energy fighter — turns poorly, fast, climbs well.
  • Role: high-altitude interceptor, precursor to the F-4S.
  • Strength: strong afterburning speed; heavy guided A2G payload (Bullpup).
  • Weakness: zero countermeasures — no flares or chaff at all.
  • Primary loadout: 4× AIM-7D (all-aspect · BVR), 4× AIM-9B/E (rear-aspect · IR).

  • Use when: picking off distant or unaware targets from altitude only.

Combat Doctrine

Fly as a high-altitude interceptor: use the speed advantage to engage distant targets and prioritize AIM-7D against them, staying out of close dogfights entirely. Pair AGM-12 Bullpups with AAMs for long-range guided strikes. Carrying zero flares or chaff means every missile threat has to be avoided before it's fired, not defeated after. (Source: wiki.warthunder.com, "F-4C Phantom II: Multirole Master.")

Radar & EW

  • Advanced-for-era radar with IFF, but cannot detect Soviet J-band emissions.
  • RWR confirmed: AN/APR-25 (E/G/I band) — cannot detect tracking-mode or pulse-Doppler radar emissions, but can detect S-125 ("Volna") SAM launches specifically. Notably weaker than the F-4E's AN/ALR-46. (Source: official Gaijin dev blog, "Updated RWR — More realism and features!")

  • AIM-7D Sparrow is the primary weapon — SARH, unreliable at close range.
  • AGM-12B/C Bullpup (command-guided) and AGM-45 Shrike for guided ground strikes.

Survivability

  • Countermeasures access plus a naturally low heat signature give real defensive value against early IR missiles.
  • This is important for its battle rating.

Matchup Notes

  • No named 1v1 matchups sourced — best used as a mid-range "support fighter": bait enemies into wasting missiles on its large flare/chaff count, or pick off anyone chasing a friendly.

  • Below ~850 km/h (Mach 0.85) it loses speed rapidly in a sharp turn — the hard floor for when the energy-fighter plan stops working.

F-5E Tiger II Sustained-turn angles fighter Turn time 26.0-27.2s · out-turns most, but loses to MiG-21/Kfir/JA37 Viggen Angles fighter — ▲ turns well · ● average speed/climb
  • Fights as: Angles fighter — turns well, average speed/climb.
  • Role: sustained-turn angles fighter.
  • Strength: holds a turning advantage against most fighters at its BR.
  • Weakness: loses the turn-fight to MiG-21, Kfir, and JA37 Viggen specifically.
  • Primary loadout: AAMs, bombs, gun pods, rockets, AGM-65B Maverick.

(Source: LEGION's Loadouts 2.27 Google Sheet — the smallest load from this aircraft's own drop schedule that destroys one base, using the Bomb Chart's damage values and base HP by BR. % = total bomb damage ÷ (base HP × 0.9018), the kill threshold every count in the chart works out to; 100% = one base.)
  • Use when: fighting in the 550-700 mph cornering band, approaching from the flanks.

Combat Doctrine

Hold the turn-fight against most opponents by working in the 550-700 mph (~885-1,127 km/h) cornering band, staying below ~3,000m, and approaching from the sides. MiG-21, Kfir, and JA37 Viggen are the exceptions — beat these by forcing sustained turning to bleed their speed rather than trying to out-turn them directly. Prioritize MiG-23, F-4J, and other F-5Es as the most dangerous targets to deal with first. (Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/F-5E, Usage in Battles — the current wiki has no tactical section for this aircraft, but old-wiki does.)

  • Sheet data — AN/APQ-159: transceiver range 30 km (max 75 km); tracks out to 20 km; scans ±45° azimuth, −40/+45° elevation; no PD mode listed; I-band. The radar is listed as "AN/APQ-153 and AN/APQ-159(V)3"; the sheet's column is plain "AN/APQ-159" and has no APQ-153. (Source: community "Radar data" Google Sheet, stats last changed in game v2.37.0.86; radar identified via old-wiki.warthunder.com/F-5E.)

(Source: community "Sustained turn rate tests – War Thunder" Google Sheet, Deg/S SL + G-Force SL tabs, game v2.37.0.20 — sea level, 30 min fuel, no missiles, max power; row: F-5E.)

  • Priority threats (dangerous, not just weak): MiG-23, F-4J, other F-5Es.
  • AIM-9J is most effective against a target that's lost speed or is distracted by a friendly.
  • Vulnerable and "an easy target" without ally support — not a lone-wolf aircraft.

Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/F-5E, Usage in Battles.

  • Fights as: Energy fighter — turns poorly, fast, climbs well.
  • Role: energy fighter, first USA Phantom with an internal gun.
  • Strength: high acceleration and top speed; internal M61A1 cannon.
  • Weakness: inferior sustained-turn performance versus contemporaries.

  • Use when: opening with Sparrow at range, closing to gun/Sidewinder at the merge.

Combat Doctrine

Lead with acceleration and top speed rather than sustained turning — energy and speed retention "drive effective employment in combat." Pair Sidewinders with Sparrows for layered engagement ranges: a BVR Sparrow opener, then the Sidewinder for the merge. General Phantom-family forum advice applies: terrain-mask at low altitude to delay radar detection, and avoid getting pulled into a turning fight at all. (Source: wiki.warthunder.com/unit/f-4e; forum.warthunder.com, "How to Play on Phantoms.")

F-4S Phantom II Missile-sniper / 2nd-line support AIM-7F primary · avoid turning fights with F-16/MiG-29 · see Part I energy-fighter doctrine Energy fighter — ▼ turns poorly · ● average speed/climb

(Source: LEGION's Loadouts 2.27 Google Sheet — the smallest load from this aircraft's own drop schedule that destroys one base, using the Bomb Chart's damage values and base HP by BR. % = total bomb damage ÷ (base HP × 0.9018), the kill threshold every count in the chart works out to; 100% = one base.)

Radar & EW

  • PDV head-on is the primary mode, not standard search.
  • Better against clutter and chaff.
  • HMD/ACM gives fast lock once the furball starts.

Weapon Systems & Engagement

  • AIM-7F (all-aspect · BVR) is the primary weapon.
  • Check for friendlies before every shot, especially head-on.
  • AIM-9H (rear-aspect · IR) is for close shots the Sparrow can't take.
  • Gunpod is last resort only.
  • NEZ (in-game est.): AIM-7F ~under 5km head-on for a near-sure hit, per general AIM-7 Sparrow-family player guidance (not F-4S-specific) · AIM-9H ?.
  • Sheet data — AIM-7F: 25G; motor 15.5 s (two-stage 4.5+11); guided 75 s; max flight 70 km; min range 400 m.
  • Sheet data — AIM-9H: lock 5.5 km rear / 1 km head-on vs afterburner; 18G; motor 5 s; guided 60 s; max flight 18 km; min range 30 m. (Source: community "Guided weaponry data (in-game values)" Google Sheet, AAM tabs — stats last changed in game v2.57.1.91. Hard limits from game data, not a no-escape zone — see Weapons Envelope, Part III.)

Combat Doctrine

Break off the moment the fight turns unfavorable. Disengage, extend, and reset — repeatable resets beat one all-in fight.

Flight Performance

  • Turn time: 26.0-27.4s.
  • Climb rate: 145.2-185.0 m/s.
  • Thrust-to-weight: roughly 0.60 (max gross weight) to 1.15 (empty) at 0m on full afterburner — computed from published thrust/mass specs, not stated directly.
  • Sustained turn (sea level): best 13.5°/s at 926 km/h IAS (6.3G). Curve: 10.8 / 12.1 / 12.9 / 13.0 / 13.3 / 13.5°/s at 463 / 556 / 648 / 741 / 833 / 926 km/h. Tested with gunpod; the sheet notes ~+0.8°/s without it. (Source: community "Sustained turn rate tests – War Thunder" Google Sheet, Deg/S SL + G-Force SL tabs, game v2.37.0.20 — sea level, 30 min fuel, no missiles, max power; row: F-4S (w/ gunpod | + ~0.8 deg/s w/o).)

Matchup Notes

  • Outclassed in flight performance by F-14, F-15A, F-16A, and MiG-29 — avoid turning or extended fights with any of them.
  • AV-8B+ Harrier is a specific threat despite its lower BR — its AIM-120A outranges the F-4S's defensive options. Don't try to notch it; go cold (fly a full 180° away) or descend to exploit radar multipathing instead.
  • Below ~970-1,000 km/h, leading-edge slats let you pull more AoA and turn tighter at the cost of energy bleed; above that speed they retract, trading turn radius for energy retention.

Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/F-4S, Usage in Battles.

Matchup Notes

  • Vs. MiG-29: at high speed the MiG-29 keeps a slight maneuverability edge, but the F-16A's superior low-speed handling wins if you slow the fight down — at low speed it can easily gain position on a MiG-29.
  • Vs. R-27ER: stay low to exploit radar multipathing, or notch while dropping chaff.
  • Vs. MiG-29SMT's R-73 specifically: treat it as exceptionally flare-resistant — use constant awareness and burst (not single) countermeasure drops.
  • Recommended countermeasure loadout: 1 flare/1 chaff mixed, for 30 total drops against either missile type.
  • Can pull up to 13G in most cases — real pilot-blackout risk from over-pulling, on top of the G-limit above.

Combat Doctrine

No dedicated tactics writeup was found for this aircraft. F-14A Early Swing-wing fleet defender — AIM-54A Phoenix and AN/AWG-9, a rate fighter with wings forward AIM-54A + AIM-7F + AIM-9L/H · M61A1 (676 rds) · AN/AWG-9 radar, TWS soft lock Even — pick by opponent — ▲ strong rate turn (wings forward) · ▼ slow to accelerate and climb
  • Fights as: Even — pick by opponent — rate fighter with the wings forward, but accelerates and climbs poorly.
  • Role: rank VIII two-seat carrier fighter at BR 12.7 in Air RB — the first fourth-generation fighter and the first with an active radar-homing missile (AIM-54 Phoenix) in the game.
  • Strength: large weapon load, good flight characteristics, a strong radar and suitability for air superiority; excellent manoeuvrability and energy retention with the wings swept forward — one of the best rate fighters in the game.
  • Weakness: low survivability; powerful engines make flares less effective even without afterburner; underpowered early TF30 engines give below-average acceleration and climb, so faster-accelerating jets outpace it.
  • Primary loadout: 2× AIM-54A Phoenix (ARH) or AIM-7F Sparrow (SARH) with AIM-9L/H (IR); M61A1 20mm (676 rounds).
  • Bombing load: ? — this aircraft was not in the LEGION Loadouts sheet when it was mined (v49), so no base-bombing figure is available. Bombs available: Mk 81 (6× or 8×), Mk 82 (6× or 8×), Mk 83 (2×) and Mk 84 (2×), plain or ballute-retarded; 8× Zuni rockets; maximum suspended load 6,580 kg.
  • Use when: climbing above 5 km, searching with the AN/AWG-9 and firing Sparrows or Phoenixes, then diving on lower targets; dogfight only on the terms in the doctrine.

Combat Doctrine

Climb above 5 km, search for targets and fire long-range Sparrows or Phoenixes; once the high ground is clear, dive on lower enemies and use the energy advantage for missile kills from unexpected angles; engage what remains in a dogfight. For dogfighting switch from auto to manual wing sweep and hold the wings fully forward (0%): it gives high energy retention and strong instantaneous and sustained turn rate, and is used at low speed and for takeoff and landing. Against poor-energy deltas (F-4s, MiG-21s, J35s, JA37s) force a prolonged two-circle fight with turn rate — best rate speed is about 750 km/h, and 600 km/h still out-rates them. Against better-energy jets (F-8s, MiG-23s) use instantaneous turn rate to force a one-circle fight. Avoid extended turn-fighting unless necessary: the aircraft bleeds speed and becomes an easy target. Keep speed up; MiG-23s, Mirage 2000s, F-16s and MiG-29s accelerate faster, and even F-4s do at low speed, so avoid vertical fights with them. Against IR missiles, throttle down to 80–85% as well as dropping flares — afterburner off and flares alone may not defeat an AIM-9L, AIM-9M, Magic 2 or R-73. (Source: wiki.warthunder.com, "Using the F-14A (Early) in Realistic Battles" — published 26 Dec 2022.)

Radar & EW

  • Radar: AN/AWG-9 — tracks to 185 km and detects to 370 km. Display ranges of 37 km suit most Air RB maps. A hard lock is needed for Sparrow guidance; Phoenix launches can use a hard lock or a soft lock.
  • SRC PD HDN (pulse-Doppler): good for very low targets and head-on shots; can be notched (target flying perpendicular is hidden); poor against receding targets. SRC (standard): cannot be notched and tracks receding targets more easily, but suffers ground clutter and cannot see targets very close to the ground. TWS HDN (track-while-scan): tracks several targets; hovering the cursor makes a soft lock that does not trigger the enemy RWR, from which Phoenix launches are possible and AIM-9G/H can be slaved; Sparrows need a hard lock; it is the preferred mode, with SRC used to overcome pulse-Doppler limits. SRC PDV HDN: shows velocity in place of range; the only AWG-9 mode that does not use IFF, so take care in Simulator battles.
  • The radar can switch between pulse-Doppler and SRC tracking without breaking an existing lock, which lets the pilot answer notching or low-altitude targets quickly. Enemy pulse-Doppler radar at low altitude suggests they may notch you — break lock by notching.
  • Countermeasures and RWR: listed as features; the counts are not shown. ? IR missiles: throttle to 80–85% and deploy flares. Engine heat is about 1,150 °C (2,100 °F) at high throttle and afterburner, roughly 66% hotter than the F-4J.

Source: wiki.warthunder.com/unit/f_14a_early; wiki.warthunder.com, "Using the F-14A (Early) in Realistic Battles".

  • Wing sweep: forward (0%) gives high energy retention and strong instantaneous and sustained turn rate but limits top speed; backward sweep allows top speed but reduces lift and manoeuvrability at low speed; AUTO is fine for general flight.
  • Sustained turn (sea level): ? — the community sheet has F-14A and F-14B rows, but the row was not retrieved for this card, so no figure is given.

Source: wiki.warthunder.com/unit/f_14a_early; wiki.warthunder.com, "Using the F-14A (Early) in Realistic Battles"; four unlabeled values per figure, split into Air RB / AB / SB the same way as the F/A-18 cards (pattern-matched, not labeled on the page).

Matchup Notes

Rank VIII; BR 12.7 in Air RB, read from the first of three unlabeled BR groups (a second group lists RB 11.7 — not mapped to a mode). Added in Update 2.17 "Danger Zone"; research order F/A-18A, then F-14A Early, then F-14B and F/A-18E. Historically the TF30 engines failed often and handling problems caused regular accidents. Named matchups from the usage guide: poor-energy deltas (F-4, MiG-21, J35, JA37) are beaten in a two-circle fight; better-energy jets (F-8, MiG-23) need a one-circle fight; MiG-23s, Mirage 2000s, F-16s and MiG-29s out-accelerate it. The F-14D card in this guide applies this card's sweep guidance by analogy. (Source: wiki.warthunder.com/unit/f_14a_early; wiki.warthunder.com, "Using the F-14A (Early) in Realistic Battles".)

No usage guidance specific to this aircraft has been gathered. ? F-15C MSIP II Eagle with eight AMRAAMs — a slightly heavier, slightly slower F-15A with HMD AIM-120A ×8 + AIM-7M + AIM-9L/M · M61A1 (940 rds) · HMD slaves IR missiles and radar Energy fighter — ● average turn · ▲ fast, climbs well

  • Role: rank VIII fighter at BR 13.7 in Air RB — the F-15C after the mid-1980s MSIP II refit, with the AN/APG-63 PSP radar and a helmet-mounted display.

Matchup Notes

Rank VIII; BR 14.0 in Air RB, read from the first of three unlabeled BR groups (a second group lists RB 12.7 — not mapped to a mode). Added in Update 2.41 "Firebirds"; no research-tree position is listed (the F-15C supplied its conformal tanks). The F-15E was designed to replace the F-111 as the USAF's frontline heavy attacker, entered service in the late 1980s and remains in use through upgrades. Same family as the F-15C MSIP II (BR 13.7).   • Strength: long-range APG-71 radar feeding a 3-tier missile loadout.
  • Weakness: large IR/radar signature — seen earlier than most opponents.
  • Primary loadout: AIM-54C+ (all-aspect · BVR), AIM-7M (all-aspect · BVR), AIM-9M (all-aspect · IR).

(Source: LEGION's Loadouts 2.27 Google Sheet — the smallest load from this aircraft's own drop schedule that destroys one base, using the Bomb Chart's damage values and base HP by BR. % = total bomb damage ÷ (base HP × 0.9018), the kill threshold every count in the chart works out to; 100% = one base.)
  • Use when: engaging BVR; turn-fight only as an inferred last resort.

Combat Doctrine

Engage BVR and let the radar/missile tier do the work. Treat any turning fight as a last resort, not the plan.

Radar & Engine

  • APG-71 radar feeds a 3-tier missile loadout (AIM-54C+/AIM-7M/AIM-9M).
  • F110 engines give strong acceleration to build or rebuild energy after a shot.
  • Manage the variable-sweep wing like the MiG-23MLD's: swept for speed/acceleration, unswept for sustained turning — concretely (F-14A analogy), switch to manual sweep and hold fully forward (0%) for dogfighting, automatic only while cruising.
  • Against a modern heat-seeker, cutting afterburner and popping flares may not be enough — reducing throttle to ~80-85% to actually cool the engine signature is often necessary (F-14A analogy).
  • NEZ (in-game est.): AIM-9M ~1.5-3km, best inside 2km · AIM-7M ~5km at low altitude, 12km+ achievable at high altitude (read the radar's own launch-window cursor rather than a fixed number) · AIM-54C+ ~40km as a practical/energetic baseline, ~50km "pushing it," opportunistic kills reported out to ~75km in ideal conditions — per player discussion, not a hard rule.
  • Sheet data — AIM-9M: lock 11 km rear / 3 km all-aspect / 6 km head-on vs afterburner; 30G; motor 5.3 s; guided 60 s; max flight 18 km; min range 30 m.
  • Sheet data — AIM-7M: 25G; motor 15.5 s (two-stage 4.5+11); guided 75 s; max flight 70 km; min range 400 m.
  • Sheet data — AIM-54C+: own seeker locks at 16 km; 25G; motor 27.8 s; guided 160 s; max flight 185 km; min range 30 m. (Source: community "Guided weaponry data (in-game values)" Google Sheet, AAM tabs — stats last changed in game v2.57.1.91. Hard limits from game data, not a no-escape zone — see Weapons Envelope, Part III.)
F-14A analogy, not F-14D-specificNo F-14D-specific dogfight or wing-sweep writeup exists; the detail above is sourced from the F-14A (Early) guide and applied by analogy given the shared swing-wing airframe. Treat any turning engagement as a last resort consistent with Part III's "the missile is the plan" framing.

Flight Performance

  • Sustained turn (sea level): ? — not tested — the sheet has F-14A and F-14B rows only. (Checked against the community "Sustained turn rate tests – War Thunder" Google Sheet, v2.37.0.20 — no matching row.)

Matchup Notes

  • Favorable two-circle fights vs. poor energy-retainers: F-4s, MiG-21s, delta-winged fighters (e.g. J35 Draken) — sustain a turn near 750 km/h and let your superior energy retention bleed theirs down.
  • Favorable one-circle fights vs. better energy-retainers: F-8s, MiG-23s — use instantaneous turn rate to force a one-circle fight instead of a prolonged two-circle one.
  • Avoid extended engagements or the vertical against MiG-23s, Mirage 2000s, F-16s, MiG-29s — these out-accelerate the Tomcat, so you may not be able to out-run them if you need to disengage.

Source: War Thunder Wiki "Using the F-14A (Early) in Realistic Battles," applied by analogy — no F-14D-specific matchup writeup exists; the D has a better radar/missiles/engine than the A, so treat this as directionally correct, not exact.

Combat Doctrine

Play as a BVR poke platform, engaging with AIM-120D from range rather than committing to extended fights. Community consensus rates the airframe as roughly comparable to the F/A-18E Super Hornet — a slightly better sea-level top speed, but sharing the Hornet's weakness of bleeding energy in turns. It's viewed as under-armed and under-defended relative to peers at its BR, so the viable playstyle is disciplined BVR poking and disengaging, not a turning fight. (Source: forum.warthunder.com, "F/A-18E, F-15C Golden Eagle, or F-16CM PoBIT?"; forum.warthunder.com, "F-16CM PoBIT should be 13.7-14.0.")

F/A-18E Super Hornet — AMRAAM carrier and strike jet, slow in the fight AIM-120B/C-5/D + AIM-9M · fire from low altitude, bomb in mixed battles Double inferior — ▼ turns poorly · ▼ slow, climbs poorly
  • Fights as: Double inferior — turns poorly, slow, climbs poorly (missile count and strike load are the answer).
  • Role: Rank IX Super Hornet at the top of the USA tree — a missile carrier with stronger ground-attack ability than the F/A-18C Late.
  • Strength: a large missile count (AIM-120 and AIM-9M) and a wide strike load: laser-guided and JDAM bombs, JSOW, Maverick, HARM and rockets.
  • Weakness: maneuverability and flight performance are underwhelming, and the Typhoon and Rafale F3 outclass it in close-range dogfights; forum players add that it is slow, climbs poorly at altitude and has weaker countermeasures than the F-15C.
  • Primary loadout: AIM-120C-5/D (all-aspect · BVR) mixed with AIM-9M (all-aspect · IR); AIM-120B and AIM-7P (all-aspect · BVR) also available.
  • Bombing load: ? — this card wasn't in the guide when the LEGION Loadouts sheet was mined (v49). Carries GBU-10/12/16/24/32/38/31/54/62/64 bombs, GBU-53 SDB II, AGM-154A1 JSOW and Mk 82/83/84 bombs.
  • Use when: firing AMRAAMs from low altitude at targets above you inside about 20 km, with teammates covering; or striking ground targets in a mixed battle.

Combat Doctrine

Forum players advise staying with teammates rather than flying it alone, firing AIM-120s from low altitude, and launching at targets above you from under about 20 km. Lead the target instead of relying on a hard pull, because the AIM-120's high-off-boresight ability is limited. The jet is slow, so AIM-120 range falls off unless it is fast and high, and chaff on side aspect can defeat the missile; it struggles to get value from the AIM-120D unless it is fast and high. It works best in mixed battles, using AGM-65 and Paveway bombs, and one forum thread recommends GBU bombing as the more effective role. (Source: wiki.warthunder.com/unit/fa_18e_block_2; forum.warthunder.com, "Super hornet starter help"; forum.warthunder.com, "F/A-18E at 14.3?" — community opinion, not official.)

The East German Air Force took 24 in the 1980s, all passed to the Luftwaffe, and 22 were sold to Poland in 2003 for €1 each. F/A-18C Hornet Angles fighter — trades speed for turn performance AIM-7P/AIM-9L · maneuverable but speed-limited — avoid prolonged chases Angles fighter — ▲ turns well · ▼ slow, climbs poorly
  • Fights as: Angles fighter — turns well, slow, climbs poorly.
  • Role: angles fighter — trades speed for turn performance.
  • Strength: excellent maneuverability and handling — strong turn-fighter.
  • Weakness: "a lack of speed" — struggles in extended pursuits.
  • Primary loadout: AIM-9L (all-aspect · IR), AIM-7P Sparrow (all-aspect · BVR), AGM-65 Maverick (CAS only).
  • Bombing load: 3× Mk 77 (139% of a 25,900 HP base at BR 12.7). Mk 77 counted as mod 2/4 (10,860 damage) — the only variant consistent with the sheet's 3-per-base schedule at 25,900 HP. The sheet's Germany tab lists "F/A-18C" (12.7) and "F/A-18C Late" (14.0) with the same bomb schedule; % uses the 12.7 row's base. (Source: LEGION's Loadouts 2.27 Google Sheet — the smallest load from this aircraft's own drop schedule that destroys one base, using the Bomb Chart's damage values and base HP by BR. % = total bomb damage ÷ (base HP × 0.9018), the kill threshold every count in the chart works out to; 100% = one base.)
  • Use when: gaining an angular advantage; avoid prolonged chases or head-on sprints.

Combat Doctrine

Play from stand-off: hang back around 5km or just below contrail altitude and snipe distracted targets with AIM-7P rather than closing to merge. Gain an angular advantage and take it once merged — the "combat flaps" special-maneuver input is the concrete way to exploit the turn-fight advantage. Avoid prolonged chases or head-on sprints, which play to its lack of speed. In a downtier, play more aggressively; in an uptier, stay passive. (Source: forum.warthunder.com thread on the closely-related F/A-18C Early — same airframe/missiles, applied by analogy.)

Weapon Systems & Engagement

  • Don't fire AIM-9L above 3-4km, and only at a target that's paying little attention — the same "pick off distracted targets" principle as the MiG-21F-13 entry, now sourced for the Hornet specifically.
  • AIM-7P is semi-active radar homing (needs a lock) — take shots on high-flying targets or head-ons; avoid targets flying directly away, since the pulse-Doppler track struggles with pure tail-aspect returns.
  • NEZ (in-game est.): AIM-9L ~2km both front and rear aspect, per a dedicated forum Q&A thread — under ~3km against unaware/lower-BR targets, under ~2.4km (preferably under 2km) against a fleeing target, head-on shots around 700-800m for tracking time · AIM-7P ? — no AIM-7P-specific figure found, but general AIM-7 Sparrow-family guidance (near-sure hit under ~5km head-on) is a reasonable proxy given it's a late-model Sparrow.
  • Sheet data — AIM-9L: lock 11 km rear / 3 km all-aspect / 6 km head-on vs afterburner; 30G; motor 5.3 s; guided 60 s; max flight 18 km; min range 30 m.
  • Sheet data — AIM-7P: 25G; motor 15.5 s (two-stage 4.5+11); guided 75 s; max flight 70 km; min range 400 m. (Source: community "Guided weaponry data (in-game values)" Google Sheet, AAM tabs — stats last changed in game v2.57.1.91. Hard limits from game data, not a no-escape zone — see Weapons Envelope, Part III.)

Flight Performance

  • Turn time: 22.3-24.7s (range — the table columns couldn't be confidently split).
  • Climb rate: 178.2-275.5 m/s (range — the table columns couldn't be confidently split).
  • Sustained turn (sea level): ? — not tested — no Hornet of any variant in the sheet. (Checked against the community "Sustained turn rate tests – War Thunder" Google Sheet, v2.37.0.20 — no matching row.)

Matchup Notes

Fly low: many missiles can't effectively engage at low altitude until already close, while flying high exposes this Early Hornet (AIM-7P/SARH only, no active-radar Fox-3) to advanced long-range ARH threats. Defensive multipathing — diving toward the ground/sea to force enemy radar missiles to fight ground clutter — is rated by an experienced forum player as "a free win 90% of the time," though it sacrifices offensive position and is less effective against a missile already coming from above. Because this Hornet has no Fox-3, the forum consensus favors using it as a head-on joust weapon or in a defensive/support role — a "missile bus of SARH," similar in function to Su-27s/F-15s at higher BRs — rather than trying to win pure high-altitude BVR duels. Named matchups: roughly even against F-14A, Kfir C10, and JA37DI (Viggen); considered outclassed against Su-30MKK, Su-30MKV, and Su-27SM, which forum players describe as under-tiered relative to this Hornet's loadout. (Source: forum.warthunder.com, "F/A-18C Early Hornet is not fun anymore"; forum.warthunder.com, "When will they move F/A-18C Early and SU-30MK2 to a higher BR?")

Combat Doctrine

Fight low and stay there — never climb to engage. Performance collapses above roughly 4km.

Flight Performance

  • Turn time: 18-19.4s.
  • Climb rate: 21.8-26.5 m/s.
  • Sustained turn (sea level): ? — not tested; the sheet's WWII tabs only test a handful of other props (Spitfire LF Mk IX, Ju 288, Yak-1B). (Checked against the community "Sustained turn rate tests – War Thunder" Google Sheet, v2.37.0.20 — no matching row.)

Matchup Notes

  • Turn-fights well against less maneuverable opponents, including the P-51 line.
  • Entice opponents — mainly Germans and Americans — down to low altitude, since engine performance degrades above roughly 2-3.5km.
  • Low dive-speed limit (~700 km/h) — don't try to out-dive P-51/Tempest-type opponents.
  • A skilled Bf 109 can win a close 2-circle turn fight — treat it as a live threat, not a free kill.
  • P-51 pilots are taught to fight you very fast with vertical maneuvers, or boom-and-zoom from altitude — both require you to be slow or low-energy first, so stay fast and low to deny both.
  • Dragging the fight above ~6km negates the Yak-3U's advantage — reinforces staying low.

Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/Yak-3U; forum.warthunder.com thread on countering the Yak-3 family (reverse-matchup intel).

  • Fights as: Energy fighter — turns poorly, fast, climbs well.
  • Role: energy fighter — speed over agility.

Combat Doctrine

Run an energy-fighter plan — use the acceleration and speed edge, don't turn with anyone.

Flight Performance

  • Speed at sea level: 940 km/h.
  • Turn time: 24.0-25.7s.
  • Climb rate: 25.3-33.0 m/s. (Corrected — previously listed as 3.3 m/s, an order of magnitude too low.)
  • Sustained turn (sea level): best 17.2°/s at 463 km/h IAS (4.1G). Curve: 17.2 / 16.2 / 13.9 / 13.3 / 10.3°/s at 463 / 556 / 648 / 741 / 833 km/h. (Source: community "Sustained turn rate tests – War Thunder" Google Sheet, Deg/S SL + G-Force SL tabs, game v2.37.0.20 — sea level, 30 min fuel, no missiles, max power; row: Su-11.)

Combat Tactics

  • Build speed to roughly 725-805 km/h, then execute a 20-30 degree zoom climb to gain altitude quickly — excellent energy retention lets you regain lost altitude after diving on a target.
  • If someone gets on your tail, you can typically out-accelerate them and force a disengage rather than maneuvering defensively.
  • Against a similarly maneuverable aircraft, drain their energy with long sweeping turns rather than trying to out-turn them tightly.
  • Only 40 rounds of 37mm and 200 of 23mm — the 37mm can drop heavy bombers in a couple of hits but has low velocity, so lead carefully.

Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/Su-11.

Matchup Notes

Against slower aircraft (e.g. F2G Corsair, Meteor Mk 3): avoid aggressive turning and trade energy instead — pull upward in a spiral, or lure them into a six, exploiting this jet's energy-retention advantage. Against faster/more agile jets (e.g. Meteor Mk 8, which has higher top speed, better acceleration, and better maneuverability): don't try to out-turn or out-accelerate directly — exploit the opponent's energy loss over a prolonged fight instead. Named threat: F-89B interceptors can generate strong lead angles from behind, but lose speed quickly in sustained maneuvering — survive the first pass and extend, and the fight can turn back in your favor. (Source: wiki.warthunder.com/8007-su-11-the-soviet-swallow.)

La-200 High-altitude boom-and-zoom Top speed 1,000+ km/h · never slow down — low-speed handling is "terrible" Energy fighter — ▼ turns poorly · ▲ fast, climbs well
