Combat Doctrine

Dive to attack and climb away — never slow down to fight. Speed is this airframe's greatest advantage: it can outrun every jet at its BR and even some above it. Accelerate to roughly 1,000 km/h early to bank an escape advantage over pursuers, even in a dive, and use zoom-climbs to gain altitude and surprise unprepared targets. Any turning fight that bleeds speed below its comfortable band is a losing proposition; disengage rather than grind it out. (Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/La-200, Usage in Battles.)

(Source: community "Sustained turn rate tests – War Thunder" Google Sheet, Deg/S SL + G-Force SL tabs, game v2.37.0.20 — sea level, 30 min fuel, no missiles, max power; row: La-200.)

Matchup Notes

The G.91 is called out by name as a dangerous matchup thanks to its superior maneuverability — treat it as a real threat despite its BR. (Source: Steam Community guide — community source, not official wiki.)

MiG-21F-13 Speed-focused hit-and-run Climb 143.8 m/s, 2,240 km/h top speed · R-3S is IR-only, rear-aspect, short range Energy fighter — ▼ turns poorly · ▲ fast, climbs well
  • Fights as: Energy fighter — turns poorly, fast, climbs well.
  • Role: speed-focused hit-and-run.
  • Strength: strong instantaneous turn and AoA authority at speed.
  • Weakness: abysmal energy retention once that speed is spent.
  • Primary loadout: R-3S (IR-only, rear-aspect), 30mm cannon (60 rounds total).
  • Bombing load: 2× ZB-360 (111% of a 25,900 HP base at BR 9.3). (Source: LEGION's Loadouts 2.27 Google Sheet — the smallest load from this aircraft's own drop schedule that destroys one base, using the Bomb Chart's damage values and base HP by BR. % = total bomb damage ÷ (base HP × 0.9018), the kill threshold every count in the chart works out to; 100% = one base.)
  • Use when: picking off distracted targets, then disengaging immediately.

Combat Doctrine

Pick off distracted targets, then disengage immediately — energy retention is too poor to press further once speed is spent.

Weapon Systems & Engagement

  • R-3S needs a tail shot, unlike the radar-assisted R-3R on later MiG-21 variants.
  • Don't expect a head-on or beam shot to work.
  • Climb 143.8 m/s, top speed 2,240 km/h.
  • Limited cannon rounds demand precise, short bursts rather than sustained fire.
  • NEZ (in-game est.): R-3S ~3-4km rear-aspect for a reliable guided hit — official specs list a 3.5km rear-aspect lock range and 9km theoretical max launch range, but the 9km figure needs high altitude and a non-maneuvering/unaware target to matter. (Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/R-3S.)
  • Sheet data — R-3S: lock 3.5 km rear / 0.5 km head-on vs afterburner; 11G; motor 2.2 s; guided 21 s; max flight 11 km; min range 30 m. (Source: community "Guided weaponry data (in-game values)" Google Sheet, AAM tabs — stats last changed in game v2.57.1.91. Hard limits from game data, not a no-escape zone — see Weapons Envelope, Part III.)

Flight Performance

  • Sustained turn (sea level): best 12.7°/s at 556 km/h IAS (3.7G). Curve: 11.9 / 12.5 / 12.7 / 12.6 / 12.6 / 12.4 / 12.0°/s at 370 / 463 / 556 / 648 / 741 / 833 / 926 km/h. (Source: community "Sustained turn rate tests – War Thunder" Google Sheet, Deg/S SL + G-Force SL tabs, game v2.37.0.20 — sea level, 30 min fuel, no missiles, max power; row: MiG-21F-13.)

Matchup Notes

Beware the F-4C specifically — it can match or outrun the MiG-21F-13, so the standard hit-and-disengage plan doesn't reliably create separation against it. No specific matchup detail was found for the Sabre, Hunter, or F-100. (Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/MiG-21F-13, Usage in Battles.)

MiG-17 Low-speed angles fighter, missile-vulnerable Turn time 20.3-23.2s · extremely dangerous vs all-aspect IR missiles (AIM-9L/R-60M) Angles fighter — ▲ turns well · ▼ slow, climbs poorly
  • Fights as: Angles fighter — turns well, slow, climbs poorly.
  • Role: low-speed angles fighter, missile-vulnerable.
  • Strength: excellent low-speed agility, small hard-to-hit airframe.
  • Weakness: no countermeasures or RWR vs all-aspect IR missiles.
  • Primary loadout: internal cannon armament (an edge over early cannon-less F-4s).
  • Bombing load: ? — not listed in LEGION's Loadouts bomb sheet. (Checked against LEGION's Loadouts 2.27 Google Sheet — no matching aircraft row.)
  • Use when: close-range turning fights, kept strictly horizontal.

Combat Doctrine

Facing all-aspect missiles like the AIM-9L or R-60M is "an almost guaranteed death sentence" for this airframe — avoid presenting any aspect to an opponent known to carry them, ahead of any performance consideration. Otherwise fight close-range and strictly horizontal, turn time 20.3-23.2s.

Handling

  • Transonic handling is improved over the MiG-15.
  • Compression at high speed is still a real limit.
  • Climb rate: 39.1-50.0 m/s.
  • Safely reaches 1,150 km/h in a dive, approaching Mach 1.10 — a useful ceiling for boom-and-zoom passes or extending out of a bad fight.

Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/MiG-17.

Flight Performance

  • Sustained turn (sea level): best 17.6°/s at 463 km/h IAS (4.2G). Curve: 15.8 / 17.6 / 16.6 / 16.1 / 14.9 / 13.3 / 12.0°/s at 370 / 463 / 556 / 648 / 741 / 833 / 926 km/h. (Source: community "Sustained turn rate tests – War Thunder" Google Sheet, Deg/S SL + G-Force SL tabs, game v2.37.0.20 — sea level, 30 min fuel, no missiles, max power; row: MiG-17 / J-4 / MiG-17AS.)

Matchup Notes

Outmaneuvers the F-86 Sabre and Hawker Hunter, particularly in vertical engagements — when it's a guns-only fight rather than an all-aspect-missile threat, these are winnable. Play it like the MiG-15: strong 1v1 via superior maneuverability, but prolonged multi-aircraft fights become a liability due to weight/energy-retention penalties; can also be flown as a boom-and-zoom energy fighter. (Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/MiG-17, Usage in Battles.)

Combat Doctrine

Fly hit-and-run passes and disengage rather than press a bad merge. Manage the swing wing like the MiG-23MLD: unswept for turning, swept for speed.

Weapon Notes

  • NEZ (in-game est.): R-60M ~1-2km, best under 1.5km, per player guidance — a post-nerf complaint thread describes it as unable to "reach someone over a mile and a half away," notably worse range than AIM-9L. (Source: forum.warthunder.com, "How to play mig 23ml?")

Matchup Notes

This is honestly an attacker pressed into an A2A support role: "will suffer against most targets it comes across." Play a support role and avoid direct dogfights rather than trying to win 1v1s against dedicated fighters — fire R-60M opportunistically at distracted targets, not head-on, and use the RWR to react before a BVR shot lands. No named enemy-aircraft matchup ("beats X / loses to Y") was found. (Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/Su-17M4, Usage in Battles.)

MiG-23M First true production MiG-23 — swing wing, R-23 missiles and look-down radar, but a flimsy airframe R-23R/T + R-13M1 + R-60M · GSh-23L 23mm (200 rds) · 12 countermeasures Energy fighter — ▼ turns poorly · ▲ fast

MiG-23MLDSweep wings 0% for the merge, 100% to escape Energy fighter — turns poorly · fast, climbs well
  • Fights as: Energy fighter — turns poorly, fast, climbs well.
  • Role: variable-sweep energy fighter.
  • Strength: R-24R/T missiles under 10km; passive IRST avoids tripping RWR.
  • Weakness: large turn radius, sluggish low-speed handling, weak 4-sector RWR.
  • Primary loadout: R-24R/T, low-velocity cannon.
  • Bombing load: 2× ZB-500 (111% of a 25,900 HP base at BR 11.7). (Source: LEGION's Loadouts 2.27 Google Sheet — the smallest load from this aircraft's own drop schedule that destroys one base, using the Bomb Chart's damage values and base HP by BR. % = total bomb damage ÷ (base HP × 0.9018), the kill threshold every count in the chart works out to; 100% = one base.)
  • Use when: unswept (0%) to turn; swept (100%) to accelerate and escape.

Combat Doctrine

Sweep wings 0% for the merge, 100% to escape. Hit-and-run below ~5,500m to avoid contrails; never exceed ~1,470 km/h at sea level (wing rip speed).

  • NEZ (in-game est.): R-24R ~7-10km (forum consensus; degrades past ~10-12km) · R-24T ?.

  • Turn time: 33.0-33.9s.
  • Climb rate: 186.0-220.0 m/s.
  • Sustained turn (sea level): best 18.1°/s at 741 km/h IAS (6.8G); up to 18.7°/s at 833 km/h, but at 7.8G — above the sheet's own 7.5G sustainability line. Curve: 10.8 / 14.4 / 16.3 / 17.5 / 18.1 / 18.7 / 17.5°/s at 370 / 463 / 556 / 648 / 741 / 833 / 926 km/h. (Source: community "Sustained turn rate tests – War Thunder" Google Sheet, Deg/S SL + G-Force SL tabs, game v2.37.0.20 — sea level, 30 min fuel, no missiles, max power; row: MiG-23MLD (min % sweep) (outdated).)

Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/MiG-23MLD (turn/climb table).

Matchup Notes

  • Vs. F-14: approach using IRST rather than radar to avoid tripping its RWR, then fire an R-24T from medium range. Close-range dogfighting with an F-14 is a losing plan, especially against more than one.
  • Can pull harder than the base MiG-23M thanks to aerodynamic improvements, but only above ~600 km/h — below that, turning performance drops off.
  • Fully sweep wings (100%) only when repositioning or escaping; always unsweep fully before committing to sustained combat, where it should win prolonged dogfights if flown well.
  • R-24R is most effective under 10km, keeping the target below your altitude to hold radar in MTI mode; R-60M is best "shotgunned" head-on under 1km or fired at distracted targets within 2km.
  • No specific matchup advice found against F-16, F-15, or Mirage variants.

Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/MiG-23MLD, Usage in Battles; War Thunder Wiki "MiG-23ML/MLA: A Comprehensive Guide" (adjacent variant, same airframe family).

MiG-29 HMS "kill-on-sight" close-range fighter Shchel-3UM helmet sight + R-73/R-60M off-boresight · R-27ER for BVR Double superior — ▲ turns well · ▲ fast, climbs well
  • Fights as: Double superior — turns well, fast, climbs well.
  • Role: HMS "kill-on-sight" close-range fighter.
  • Strength: helmet-sight cueing for high off-boresight R-73/R-60M shots.
  • Weakness: no confirmed turn-time or climb-rate figures for this variant.
  • Primary loadout: R-27ER, R-73, R-60M.
  • Bombing load: 4× FAB-500M-62 (108% of a 25,900 HP base at BR 12.7). The sheet's 9-12 (12.7) and 9-13 (13.0) rows carry the identical schedule, so this holds whichever variant the card is. (Source: LEGION's Loadouts 2.27 Google Sheet — the smallest load from this aircraft's own drop schedule that destroys one base, using the Bomb Chart's damage values and base HP by BR. % = total bomb damage ÷ (base HP × 0.9018), the kill threshold every count in the chart works out to; 100% = one base.)
  • Use when: close-range "kill on sight" engagements; R-27ER opens the BVR phase.

Combat Doctrine

Open with R-27ER at BVR range, then close for a "kill on sight" engagement — Shchel-3UM helmet sight plus R-73/R-60M off-boresight lets you take shots a locked-radar aircraft can't.

Radar & Weapon Systems

  • R-27ER is called "one of the strongest SARH missiles in-game."
  • Backed by a proper pulse-Doppler radar — a real upgrade over the pseudo-PD sets on the MiG-21/23.
  • SPO-15 RWR is marketed as all-aspect but is actually divided into 8 sectors — don't over-trust a single RWR tone as "this exact aircraft is locking me" when multiple enemies have you lit up.
  • Functions best as a solo interceptor rather than in group formations — carry the external tank at match start and drop it before engaging for better agility.
  • NEZ (in-game est.): R-27ER launch envelope up to ~50km at high altitude per official specs, but practical guidance is "best used in a range of 20-50km" — treat the top of that band as an opportunistic outer shot, not a guaranteed hit · R-73 ~1-2.5km best, up to 3.5km "if everything is in your favor," per player guidance — under ~1.5km for a reliable rear-aspect shot on a defensive/afterburning target · R-60M ~1-2km, best under 1.5km.
  • Sheet data — R-27ER: 35G; motor 8 s (two-stage 3.2+4.8); guided 60 s; max flight 67.5 km; min range 30 m.
  • Sheet data — R-73: lock 11 km rear / 3.4 km all-aspect / 6 km head-on vs afterburner; 40G; motor 5.5 s; guided 20 s; max flight 25 km; min range 30 m.
  • Sheet data — R-60M: lock 7.4 km rear / 2 km all-aspect / 3 km head-on vs afterburner; 30G; motor 3 s; guided 25 s; max flight 15 km; min range 30 m. (Source: community "Guided weaponry data (in-game values)" Google Sheet, AAM tabs — stats last changed in game v2.57.1.91. Hard limits from game data, not a no-escape zone — see Weapons Envelope, Part III.)

Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/MiG-29, Usage in Battles.

Flight Performance

  • Turn time: 19.7-20.5s.
  • Climb rate: 258.6-318.0 m/s.
  • Sustained turn (sea level): ? — the sheet tests the "MiG-29 9.13" only (best 17.7°/s at 741 km/h, 6.6G), and this card doesn't pin down which MiG-29 variant it covers — not applied until confirmed. (Checked against the community "Sustained turn rate tests – War Thunder" Google Sheet, v2.37.0.20 — no matching row.)

Matchup Notes

The F-16 is the MiG-29's most dangerous opponent. A 1v1 can favor the MiG-29 on missiles, but the moment an F-16 teams up with another, they become a formidable and dangerous pair — engage F-16s individually, at distance, with R-27, and avoid letting a pair gang up on you. (Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/MiG-29, Usage in Battles.)

Su-27 Aggressive generalist — missiles + post-stall agility 10 A2A missiles incl. 4× R-27ER · Cobra maneuver at low speed · large IR signature Even — pick by opponent — ● average turn · ● average speed/climb
  • Fights as: Even — pick by opponent — average turn, average speed/climb.
  • Role: aggressive generalist — missiles + post-stall agility.
  • Strength: deep 10-missile loadout plus post-stall agility (Pugachev's Cobra).
  • Weakness: large thermal signature — vulnerable to IRCCM missiles.

(Source: LEGION's Loadouts 2.27 Google Sheet — the smallest load from this aircraft's own drop schedule that destroys one base, using the Bomb Chart's damage values and base HP by BR. % = total bomb damage ÷ (base HP × 0.9018), the kill threshold every count in the chart works out to; 100% = one base.)
  • Use when: versatile engagements; avoid a straight-line speed duel with F-15s.

Combat Doctrine

"A jack of all trades yet a master of almost none" — win through versatility, not specialization, across a deep 10-missile loadout.

Matchup Notes

  • Against F-15 variants specifically, expect to lose a sustained high-speed duel — the Eagle has superior thrust-to-weight and high-speed handling. Favor low-speed maneuvering and missile range instead.
  • Vs. F-16: kill it as fast as possible, ideally in the first turn — don't let the fight drag out, or its superior energy retention in sustained turns compounds.
  • Vs. Gripen: avoid direct close-range confrontation entirely — its superior maneuverability wins that fight. Use missile range instead.

Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/Su-27, Usage in Battles.

  • Sheet data — N001: transceiver range 40 km PD / 80 km head-on PD (max 50 / 100 km); tracks out to 100 km; scans ±70° azimuth, −45/+60° elevation; TWS, 12 targets; I-band. Opening & Weapon Employment

  • Push afterburner to ~1,200 km/h IAS and hold it until contact; stay low and follow terrain to induce radar clutter on enemy scopes before the merge.
  • R-27ER's inertial/datalink update (IOG/DL) keeps missile tracking persistence even if the target briefly breaks radar lock.
  • Dogfighting sweet spot is 500-700 km/h, where it can pull very high AoA for a short burst — sustained low-speed turning is a real weakness, consistent with the Gripen/F-15/F-16 notes above.
  • NEZ (in-game est.): R-27ER launch envelope up to ~50km at high altitude per official specs, but practical guidance is "best used in a range of 20-50km" — treat the top of that band as an opportunistic outer shot, not a guaranteed hit.
  • Sheet data — R-27ER: 35G; motor 8 s (two-stage 3.2+4.8); guided 60 s; max flight 67.5 km; min range 30 m.   • Strength: effective medium/short-range missile assortment compensates for agility.
  • Weakness: low thrust-to-weight — poorly suited for prolonged close-range maneuvering.
  • Primary loadout: R-27ER1/ET1, RVV-AE, R-73E.
  • Bombing load: 2× KAB-1500Kr (107% of a 25,900 HP base at BR 13.3). (Source: LEGION's Loadouts 2.27 Google Sheet — the smallest load from this aircraft's own drop schedule that destroys one base, using the Bomb Chart's damage values and base HP by BR. % = total bomb damage ÷ (base HP × 0.9018), the kill threshold every count in the chart works out to; 100% = one base.)
  • Use when: fighting BVR on missile range, not trying to out-turn opponents.

Combat Doctrine

Fight on missile range, not by trying to out-turn opponents — low thrust-to-weight makes prolonged close-range maneuvering a losing plan.

Weapon Notes

  • NEZ (in-game est.): R-27ER1 launch envelope up to ~50km at high altitude, effectively bounded by the need to keep radar-illuminating the target throughout the flight (semi-active homing) — a dedicated AMV "Usage in Battles" writeup independently cites the same ~50km high-altitude figure · R-27ET1 shares R-27ER1's motor/kinematics but is IR-guided instead of radar-guided — no separate practical-range figure found · RVV-AE ~2-5km is where it out-turns the China-tree PL-12/R-77-family missile, per a forum comparison thread; beyond ~20km a shot is generally considered unreliable · R-73E under ~2km ideally rear-aspect, per player guidance — a useful combined-missile tactic reported by forum players: fire an R-73E and R-27ER1 together, "if the target doesn't notch, the R-27 will get them; if they do, you'll have a clean side shot where the R-73 will excel." (Source: wiki.warthunder.com/6315-su-30mk2-amv-the-venezuelan-flanker; old-wiki.warthunder.com/R-27ER; forum.warthunder.com, "R73s Being flared instantly from inside 1.5-3km"; forum.warthunder.com, "How big of a gap is there between PL12 and RVV-AE/R-77?")
  • Sheet data — R-27ER1: 35G; motor 8 s (two-stage 3.2+4.8); guided 60 s; max flight 67.5 km; min range 30 m.
  • Sheet data — R-27ET1: lock 18 km rear / 4.8 km all-aspect / 9 km head-on vs afterburner; 35G; motor 8 s (two-stage 3.2+4.8); guided 60 s; max flight 67.5 km; min range 30 m.
  • Sheet data — RVV-AE: own seeker locks at 16 km; 50G; motor 6 s; guided 90 s; max flight 80 km; min range 30 m.
  • Sheet data — R-73E: lock 11 km rear / 3.4 km all-aspect / 6 km head-on vs afterburner; 40G; motor 5.5 s; guided 20 s; max flight 25 km; min range 30 m. (Source: community "Guided weaponry data (in-game values)" Google Sheet, AAM tabs — stats last changed in game v2.57.1.91. Hard limits from game data, not a no-escape zone — see Weapons Envelope, Part III.)

Airframe Notes

This Su-30MK2 (AMV/Venezuelan variant) has no thrust vectoring — don't expect Cobra-type post-stall tricks. It's an AL-31F-powered Su-27 airframe carrying extra weight, so its agility is strictly worse than the base Su-27's, not compensated by TVC. This is a settled fact, not "unconfirmed" — Gaijin's own devblog and the official pre-order forum post both explicitly state no thrust-vectoring/canards on this variant (that feature belongs to the separate Su-30SM line). (Source: wiki.warthunder.com/6315-su-30mk2-amv-the-venezuelan-flanker; forum.warthunder.com pre-order thread.)

Flight Performance

  • Turn time: 25.0-25.7s (medium-high confidence — pattern-matched from an unlabeled 4-value table; the fully unseparated fallback is 23-25.7s).
  • Climb rate: 157.6-169.2 m/s (same caveat; unseparated fallback is 157.6-243.8 m/s).
  • Sustained turn (sea level): ? — not tested — no Su-30 variant in the sheet. (Checked against the community "Sustained turn rate tests – War Thunder" Google Sheet, v2.37.0.20 — no matching row.)

Matchup Notes

A dedicated "Usage in Battles" writeup (distinct from the plain unit encyclopedia page, which has none) advises climbing early to leverage radar/TWS for long-range engagement and "airspace control," reducing the risk of being bounced from above, before dropping to engage lower targets. Explicitly advises against prolonged dogfights — weak sustained maneuverability means missile engagements and separation should be prioritized over turning fights; treat the R-73E's high off-boresight capability as a last-resort defensive tool in an unavoidable merge, not the primary plan. For CAS/strike work, benefits from terrain masking and fast attack runs — release ordnance from a safe distance, then reposition behind cover immediately, since the airframe can't out-maneuver SACLOS-guided SAMs/AA. (Source: wiki.warthunder.com/6315-su-30mk2-amv-the-venezuelan-flanker.)

Combat Doctrine

Attack from a dive, then climb out to reset. Keep the fight below 4,000m, where its speed and acceleration edge (including over the Tempest Mk V) actually holds up — engine performance drops sharply above it.

Flight Performance

  • Turn time: 21.0-23.2s.
  • Climb rate: 17.2-23.9 m/s.
  • Max speed at 3,657m: ~723 km/h. Max altitude: 11,800m.
  • Sustained turn (sea level): ? — not tested; the sheet's WWII tabs only test a handful of other props (Spitfire LF Mk IX, Ju 288, Yak-1B). (Checked against the community "Sustained turn rate tests – War Thunder" Google Sheet, v2.37.0.20 — no matching row.)

Matchup Notes

  • Vs. Ho 229: it out-turns the Tempest, but the Tempest can spiral up at speed to bleed its energy and corner it — out-climb/out-energy it, don't try to out-turn it.
  • Vs. Meteor F Mk.3: treat with caution — it matches or beats the Tempest in most metrics except sea-level top speed.
  • Vs. Yak-15/17: these early jets out-turn the Tempest, but their dive performance is much lower — beat them on the dive/energy axis, not by turning.
  • General rule vs. jets: avoid shallow-angle fights; use steep-angle energy exchanges instead, since jets generally have superior raw speed/weight.
  • Most aircraft at this tier can turn circles around it if caught mid-turn or unaware — losing the position/energy advantage first is what gets it trapped.

Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/Tempest_Mk_II, Usage in Battles.

Combat Doctrine

The default Air RB approach is narrower than pure "flexible": gain an altitude advantage, then boom-and-zoom or hit-and-run. Hunter F.6Energy retention over supersonics; SRAAM inside 1km Angles fighter — turns well · slow, climbs poorly
  • Fights as: Angles fighter — turns well, slow, climbs poorly.
  • Role: energy retention over supersonics.
  • Strength: energy retention far better than true supersonic contemporaries.
  • Weakness: no countermeasures, RWR, or drogue chute.
  • Primary loadout: SRAAMs (inside ~1.2km), quad 30mm ADEN cannon.
  • Bombing load: ? — not listed in LEGION's Loadouts bomb sheet. (Checked against LEGION's Loadouts 2.27 Google Sheet — no matching aircraft row.)
  • Use when: extending after a turning engagement, rather than out-turning from a stop.

Combat Doctrine

Transonic in level flight, supersonic in a dive. Against subsonics: use speed superiority, avoid prolonged turning. Against supersonics (F-100D, MiG-19PT): hold 800-1,000 km/h to deny them a good closure rate — dropping below that band is what gets the Hunter caught. If you force a supersonic opponent to overshoot, a SRAAM inside 1km is described as "nearly impossible to evade" — that overshoot-then-SRAAM combo is the actual win condition against supersonics, not turning. Against subsonic aircraft that do get on your tail, don't try to out-extend indefinitely alone — lean on teammate support. (Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/Hunter_F.6, Usage in Battles.)

Weapon Notes

  • NEZ (in-game est.): SRAAM ~1km or closer for a reliable hit — official specs list a 4km lock range and 2km launch range, but guidance flags it as "generally unreliable beyond 1km," consistent with this card's existing "inside ~1.2km" framing. (Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/SRAAM.)
  • Sheet data — SRAAM: lock 4 km rear / 0.5 km head-on vs afterburner; 45G; motor 5.75 s; guided 6 s; max flight 6 km; min range 30 m. (Source: community "Guided weaponry data (in-game values)" Google Sheet, AAM tabs — stats last changed in game v2.57.1.91. Hard limits from game data, not a no-escape zone — see Weapons Envelope, Part III.)

Flight Performance

  • Climb rate: 50.0-70.0 m/s.
  • Max altitude: 15,500m.
  • Sustained turn (sea level): best 16.7°/s at 833 km/h IAS (7.0G). Curve: 15.1 / 16.4 / 16.0 / 16.7 / 16.4°/s at 556 / 648 / 741 / 833 / 926 km/h. (Source: community "Sustained turn rate tests – War Thunder" Google Sheet, Deg/S SL + G-Force SL tabs, game v2.37.0.20 — sea level, 30 min fuel, no missiles, max power; row: Hunter F.6.)

Matchup Notes

Loses a straight-line speed race to true supersonics (F-100D, MiG-19PT), but can separate from them in extended turning fights via superior energy retention. Against subsonic contemporaries, it has a clear speed advantage — extend and disengage rather than turn-fight, especially below ~800 km/h where the Hunter itself gets weak. (Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/Hunter_F.6.)

JAS39C Gripen Lightweight, missile-armed, heavily defended Turn time 24.0-24.1s, climb 202.8-245.0 m/s · close to 6-7km to win · 700+ countermeasures Double superior — ▲ turns well · ▲ fast, climbs well
  • Fights as: Double superior — turns well, fast, climbs well.
  • Role: lightweight, missile-armed, heavily defended.
  • Strength: small profile, light airframe, "incredible flight performance".
  • Weakness: effective missile range (~20km) is shorter than many opponents' (~30km) — closing that gap without being picked off first is the real challenge.
  • Primary loadout: RB 99 (AIM-120A-equivalent), RB 74(M), helmet-cued boresight.
  • Bombing load: 2× GBU-64 + 1× GBU-62 (105% of a 25,900 HP base at BR 13.7). (Source: LEGION's Loadouts 2.27 Google Sheet — the smallest load from this aircraft's own drop schedule that destroys one base, using the Bomb Chart's damage values and base HP by BR. % = total bomb damage ÷ (base HP × 0.9018), the kill threshold every count in the chart works out to; 100% = one base.)
  • Use when: flying agile hit-and-disengage passes, not a slow attritional fight.

Combat Doctrine

Fly low and deflected off enemy flight paths to avoid being detected first, using wide TWS radar (roughly 74km detection) to build the picture. Switch from TWS to ACM at ~19km as targets close — the Gripen's radar scan rate and accuracy are weak once things get close and fast-moving. The real doctrine is closing to inside 6-7km, where opponents' escape attempts become "futile" against the Gripen's turn performance — don't try to win at range against BVR-superior jets (F-16C, Su-27, F-15C); survive to the merge instead. Over 700 rounds of countermeasures via the BOL dispenser lets this airframe defend against missiles far more liberally than most in this guide before running dry. (Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/JAS39C_(Great_Britain), Usage in Battles.)

Weapon Systems & Engagement

  • Loadout: 6 missiles total — 2× AIM-9L/M fixed at the wingtips, plus 4 more on center hardpoints (mixed IR/radar). Pair IR missiles with countermeasure pods rather than flying bare.
  • Fuel: minimum fuel (9 min) plus external drop tank is the efficient baseline; performance visibly suffers past 25 minutes of total fuel. Never let fuel drop under 2 minutes remaining — that's your margin to disengage home.
  • "Furball fighter" playstyle: drop the external tank on entering the fight, dispense flares periodically, snipe non-flaring targets with AIM-9M (near-guaranteed after 2-3s unopposed flight), keep RB 99 in reserve for aggressive opponents.
  • "Interceptor" playstyle: use RB 99 via TWS lock or low-altitude surprise shots from ~10km — it's highly maneuverable while the booster burns but lofts hard and barely turns afterward, making it weak at extreme range against AIM-120A-equipped opponents specifically.
  • In a forced long-range 1v1, lock and shoot down the enemy's incoming missile with your own RB 99 before pressing the attack.
  • HMD enables off-boresight shots without a sustained lock, but switching HMD↔ACM costs time — stay in ACM while targets are still beyond visual range to avoid losing track during the mode swap.
  • Abundant flares plus a comparatively cold single-engine signature make it "almost invulnerable" to IR missiles when flaring at low throttle.
  • NEZ (in-game est.): RB 99 ? · RB 74(M) no direct figure found, but it's functionally an AIM-9M-equivalent, so this guide's AIM-9M figure elsewhere (~1.5-3km, best inside 2km) is a reasonable proxy — not confirmed RB 74(M)-specific.
  • Sheet data — RB 99: own seeker locks at 16 km; 35G; motor 6.7 s (two-stage 1.4+5.3); guided 80 s; max flight 80 km; min range 30 m.
  • Sheet data — RB 74(M): ? — the sheet lists plain RB 74 only, not the (M). (Source: community "Guided weaponry data (in-game values)" Google Sheet, AAM tabs — stats last changed in game v2.57.1.91. Hard limits from game data, not a no-escape zone — see Weapons Envelope, Part III.)

Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/JAS39C_(Great_Britain), Usage in Battles.

Flight Performance

  • Turn time: 24.0-24.1s.
  • Climb rate: 202.8-245.0 m/s.
  • Max altitude: 14,500m.
  • Sustained turn (sea level): best 18.4°/s at 741 km/h IAS (6.9G). Curve: 16.9 / 17.3 / 18.0 / 18.3 / 18.4 / 18.0 / 17.9°/s at 370 / 463 / 556 / 648 / 741 / 833 / 926 km/h. (Source: community "Sustained turn rate tests – War Thunder" Google Sheet, Deg/S SL + G-Force SL tabs, game v2.37.0.20 — sea level, 30 min fuel, no missiles, max power; row: JAS39C Gripen (30 min).)

Matchup Notes

  • Vs. F-16C: inferior in a straight missile duel (its AIM-120 outranges RB 99), but the Gripen's agility dominates at the merge — the F-16C loses if it ever lets the fight get close.
  • Vs. F-16AM: similar story, though the F-16AM's flight performance is closer to the Gripen's than the base F-16C's.
  • Vs. Su-27: dangerous at stand-off range (10 missiles, R-73 threat) but "much inferior" to the Gripen in a dogfight — survive the opening high-AoA R-73 launch with countermeasures, then win the merge.
  • Vs. F-15C MSIP II: "deadly across all ranges" (4×AIM-120 + 4×AIM-9M) — no easy edge here; treat as genuinely dangerous at both BVR and close range.
  • Vs. Mirage 2000-5F: dangerous close-range (MICA/Magic 2), but the Gripen is noticeably superior in flight performance, especially at low speed — win by staying slow and turning, not by out-running it.

Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/JAS39C_(Great_Britain), Usage in Battles.

Combat Doctrine

Play aggressively — the full RWR/MAWS/laser-warning suite covers both close and BVR ranges. Don't expect to out-turn everything at this bracket on reputation alone (turn time 20.8s, climb 251.8 m/s).

Economy & Confidence Caveat

Note: this guide's earlier working name "Typhoon FGR.3" doesn't match a unit entry — Tranche 1 Block 5 aircraft with the PIRATE IRST system are designated FGR.4 (the in-game unit specifically represents a Tranche 2 Eurofighter), so this entry covers that variant.

RB repair cost: 7,503 → 12,943 Silver Lions (stock → fully researched) — genuinely high relative to most rank VII-VIII jets, confirming rather than just inferring the "high repair cost" claim. (Source: wiki.warthunder.com/unit/ef_2000_fgr4, Economy section.)

Verify before relying on thisNo "Usage in Battles" section exists for this aircraft, and it postdates the older reference content — the "steep learning curve" claim remains unsourced (BR-inferred only), despite a real search attempt. Matchup/tactics content below comes from forum threads instead — see Matchup Notes.

Flight Performance

  • Sustained turn (sea level): ? — not tested — no Typhoon/EF-2000 in the sheet. (Checked against the community "Sustained turn rate tests – War Thunder" Google Sheet, v2.37.0.20 — no matching row.)

Matchup Notes

Strong at altitude (20,000-30,000ft is the optimal band) — can out-turn/out-dogfight Su-27s and F-16s once in "fighter mode" (low-speed/high-AoA regime), and AIM-120s against unaware targets are described by players as "stupidly overpowered" in that role; the 25mm BK27 cannon is a strong close-range fallback. The radar is the major weakness — players call it "one of the worst radars in game right now," reportedly reusing Blue Vixen-derived data (shared with the Sea Harrier FA2 line) rather than a proper CAPTOR-M model, needing multiple scans to hold detections; lock is reported to fail above ~600 km/h closure in some configurations, and several players report losing missile trades to incoming AIM-120s as a result. Given the weak radar, forum tactical advice favors launching missiles off the Helmet-Mounted Display rather than relying purely on radar-guided BVR, and using "snake" (weave) maneuvers to bleed enemy missile energy when targeted. Stock-grind advice: carry 4-6 AIM-120s alongside a bomb loadout (6x 1,000lb, later 2x 1,000lb + 2x 2,000lb) for reward income, play conservatively while stock, and use terrain/mountains as defensive cover. (Source: forum.warthunder.com, "Typhoon FGR.4 is one of the worse jets in top tier"; forum.warthunder.com, "Skill issue thread: how do I stock grind Typhoon FGR.4?")

MiG-21 Bison Helmet-cued WVR ambusher, scarce missiles R-73E for unaware/fast targets · only 4 missiles total — avoid BVR duels Energy fighter — ▼ turns poorly · ▲ fast, climbs well
  • Fights as: Energy fighter — turns poorly, fast, climbs well.
  • Role: helmet-cued WVR ambusher (premium, Indian Air Force livery).
  • Strength: R-73E all-aspect helmet-cued IR missile; strong maneuverability/acceleration.
  • Weakness: only 4 total missiles; weak energy retention; wings rip if oversped too long.

(Source: LEGION's Loadouts 2.27 Google Sheet — the smallest load from this aircraft's own drop schedule that destroys one base, using the Bomb Chart's damage values and base HP by BR. % = total bomb damage ÷ (base HP × 0.9018), the kill threshold every count in the chart works out to; 100% = one base.)
  • Use when: medium/low altitude, terrain-masked from BVR; hunting unaware or fast targets.

Combat Doctrine

"The best way to use the Bison is to fly at medium to low altitude and use map terrain as cover from BVR missiles, notching and deploying chaff when necessary." The R-73E is the main weapon of choice — go for bombers or unaware fast targets above you. Reserve R-27 missiles for less maneuverable targets like bombers, watch the RWR continuously, and compensate for the airframe's age with turn radius and positioning rather than a straight fight. The cannon is a last resort given very limited ammo. (Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/MiG-21_Bison_(Great_Britain), Usage in Battles.)

Radar & EW

  • Pulse-Doppler radar with an air-to-ground tracking (GTM) mode; forum-cited A2A range is only around 10km.
  • Improved RWR (TARANG-type) plus an integrated jamming/countermeasures suite.
  • Can go supersonic, but "after a while, the wings rip" — manage speed rather than pushing past Mach 1 continuously.

Source: wiki.warthunder.com/unit/mig-21_bison; forum.warthunder.com/t/mig-21-bison.

(Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/R-73; old-wiki.warthunder.com/R-27R.)

Phantom FG.1 The ultimate high-altitude energy fighter Side-climb to 8-9km · never join the early furball Energy fighter — ▼ turns poorly · ▲ fast, climbs well
  • Fights as: Energy fighter — turns poorly, fast, climbs well.
  • Role: the ultimate energy fighter — stand-off missile-hauler.
  • Strength: excellent climb/roll/thrust-to-weight at low altitude; internal M61 cannon.
  • Weakness: energy bleeds hard in sustained turns; poor control above ~7,500m.
  • Primary loadout: 2× AIM-9G (rear-aspect · IR) + AIM-7E/Skyflash (all-aspect · BVR).
  • Bombing load: 5× H.E.1000 (113% of a 25,900 HP base at BR 12.0). (Source: LEGION's Loadouts 2.27 Google Sheet — the smallest load from this aircraft's own drop schedule that destroys one base, using the Bomb Chart's damage values and base HP by BR. % = total bomb damage ÷ (base HP × 0.9018), the kill threshold every count in the chart works out to; 100% = one base.)
  • Use when: side-climbing to 8,000-9,000m and attacking from above/below on energy.

Combat Doctrine

Billed as "the ultimate energy fighter" — advantages are sheer power, roll rate, and the ability to climb to high altitude, plus good speed and thrust-to-weight at lower altitudes. Side-climb to 8,000-9,000m and attack opponents from above or below on energy; it has an excellent climb advantage over almost any opposition up to ~5,000m. "Any British Phantom should not be taken close to the beginning furball" — instead act as a long-range missile-hauler, picking off tail-sitting targets and supporting teammates from range and altitude. It can dogfight acceptably with the M61 via hit-and-run passes, or (high-risk, spaded aircraft only, below 5,000m) a takeoff-flaps-plus-afterburner trick at 700-950 km/h to out-turn non-Spey-engine Phantoms. (Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/Phantom_FG.1, Usage in Battles.)

Radar & EW

  • Westinghouse AN/APG-59, pulse-Doppler, 370km scan in a 120° arc; "Air Combat Mode" gives an 11×11° search pattern out to 9.25km.
  • RWR can differentiate a simple radar ping from an actual lock.
  • Defeat pulse-Doppler locks by notching — turning 90° off the threat's nose/tail to zero relative velocity.
  • Sheet data — AN/APG-59: transceiver range 70 km pulse / 90 km head-on PD (max 150 km); tracks out to 70 km pulse / 90 km PD; scans ±60° azimuth, −60/+60° elevation; no TWS; I-band. (Source: community "Radar data" Google Sheet, stats last changed in game v2.37.0.86; radar identified via old-wiki.warthunder.com/Phantom_FG.1.)

Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/Phantom_FG.1.

Weapon Systems & Engagement

  • Gun: internal M61 Vulcan 20mm, 1,200 rounds — no gunpod needed, unlike the FGR.2's external mount.
  • AIM-9D/G optimal launch range 1-4km; can maintain lock at much longer distances, occasionally scoring 5-6km kills. Skyflash covers high-altitude BVR.
  • Against IR missiles: pop flares and break-turn with afterburner. Against SARH at 6km+: notch and chaff. Against close-range (~2km) SARH: an elevator-aileron roll.
  • NEZ: AIM-9D/G optimal 1-4km (occasionally 5-6km) · Skyflash for high-altitude BVR.
  • Sheet data — AIM-9D / AIM-9G (identical rows): lock 5.5 km rear / 1 km head-on vs afterburner; 18G; motor 5 s; guided 60 s; max flight 18 km; min range 30 m.
  • Sheet data — Skyflash: 25G; motor 2.8 s; guided 40 s; max flight 50 km; min range 30 m. (Source: community "Guided weaponry data (in-game values)" Google Sheet, AAM tabs — stats last changed in game v2.57.1.91. Hard limits from game data, not a no-escape zone — see Weapons Envelope, Part III.)

Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/Phantom_FG.1.

Flight Performance

  • Top speed: 2,268-2,355 km/h at 10,667m (stock-upgraded).
  • Turn time: 25.5-28s.
  • Climb rate: 165.5-246.6 m/s.
  • Thrust-to-weight (0m, WEP): 0.81 at MTOW, up to 1.33 at 10-minute fuel.
  • Sustained turn (sea level): best 14.6°/s at 926 km/h IAS (6.8G). Curve: 12.8 / 13.9 / 14.4 / 14.5 / 14.6°/s at 556 / 648 / 741 / 833 / 926 km/h. Tested with gunpod; the sheet notes ~+1.1°/s without it. FG.1 and FGR.2 share identical rows. (Source: community "Sustained turn rate tests – War Thunder" Google Sheet, Deg/S SL + G-Force SL tabs, game v2.37.0.20 — sea level, 30 min fuel, no missiles, max power; row: FG.1 / FGR.2 (w/ gunpod | + ~1.1 deg/s w/o).)

Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/Phantom_FG.1, cross-checked against wiki.warthunder.com/Phantom_FG.1.

Matchup Notes

Dominant in high-altitude energy fights against sustained-turn fighters it can out-climb and out-run. Struggles in low-altitude turning fights and above ~7,500m, where handling degrades badly (control authority "suffers drastically" and the aircraft "flies like a brick" past that altitude). Best used as a stand-off missile platform, not a turn-fighter. (Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/Phantom_FG.1.)

Combat Doctrine

No FGR.2-specific "Usage in Battles" text was found — the aircraft has no such section, and its older reference page was inaccessible on every attempt despite sibling pages loading normally. Treat this as the same airframe/weapons family as the FG.1 above, flown by the same nation: energy-fight at altitude, avoid the early furball, and use the Sparrow/Skyflash as a stand-off weapon rather than closing to guns.

FG.1 analogy, not FGR.2-specificNo dedicated FGR.2 doctrine paragraph exists; the framing above is carried over from the FG.1 (same Rolls-Royce Spey-engine airframe, same nation) by analogy, not sourced to the FGR.2 directly. Genuine FGR.2-specific tactical color (BVR weaknesses, stock-loadout advice) is now sourced separately — see Matchup Notes below.

Radar & EW

Only generic "Radar" and "RWR" characteristics are listed, with no model name or mode detail for this specific aircraft — confirmed still genuinely unsourced after a repeat search attempt; the FGR.2's own older reference page returned a persistent access error across five separate attempts (WebFetch, a MediaWiki diff URL, and a direct proxy bypass all failed), and no substitute source names the aircraft's actual in-game radar model. (Historically the RAF-spec FGR.2 used the AN/AWG-11/AN/AWG-12 fire control radar, distinct from the USN-spec FG.1's AN/APG-59 — but no War Thunder-specific source confirms which is modeled in-game.) ?

Matchup Notes

Struggles badly in BVR — Skyflash reportedly "cannot hit past 13km" and loses engagements against opposing standard AIM-7Es. Outclassed at its BR by aircraft like the Tornado ADV/F.3 and other contemporaries with superior missiles. Strengths are a pulse-Doppler radar, AIM-9G, and a Skyflash with proper countermeasure support — an improvement over earlier Phantom variants in the tree — but it still faces "much more modern aircraft such as F-16s, F/A-18 Hornets, MiG-29s" at its BR that outclass it in maneuverability/missile tech; its Skyflash is "basically the AIM-7E-2," not the superior AIM-7F found on rivals. Players describe it as a "support fighter with limited use" rather than a solo BVR combatant — lean on team coordination rather than lone engagements — and its radar reportedly struggles to track low-altitude targets (e.g. MiG-23s). The stock loadout (2x AIM-9D + gunpod) is very weak; many players recommend bypassing this BR/vehicle if possible (e.g. via the MiG-21 Bison) rather than stock-grinding it. Once upgraded it has real strengths: strong bomb capacity, a viable 10.7 ground-battle option, and a decent thrust advantage over the F-4J/F-4S variants in the same tree. (Source: forum.warthunder.com, "Phantom FGR.2 at 12.0 makes no sense"; forum.warthunder.com, "Balance Concern – FGR.2 Battle Rating Placement"; forum.warthunder.com, "Stock Phantom FGR.2... Just why?")

Sea Harrier FRS.1 VTOL missile-truck / VIFF specialist Climb to overwatch and snipe · avoid dogfighting almost entirely Double inferior — ▼ turns poorly · ▼ slow, climbs poorly
  • Fights as: Double inferior — turns poorly, slow, climbs poorly (VIFF is the exception).
  • Role: radar-equipped Harrier — missile-truck / VIFF specialist.
  • Strength: one of few radar-equipped Harriers, enabling AIM-9L missile-slaving.
  • Weakness: subsonic in a mostly-supersonic bracket; sluggish turn radius despite high thrust.

(Source: LEGION's Loadouts 2.27 Google Sheet — the smallest load from this aircraft's own drop schedule that destroys one base, using the Bomb Chart's damage values and base HP by BR. % = total bomb damage ÷ (base HP × 0.9018), the kill threshold every count in the chart works out to; 100% = one base.)
  • Use when: climbing to 5,000-8,000m to overwatch and snipe unaware targets.

Combat Doctrine

"Bricks Fly When Thrust is Enough" — despite the Pegasus engine's high power-to-weight ratio, the heavy airframe still flies like "a flying brick." Climb to 5,000-8,000m and act as overwatch, picking off unsuspecting enemies with missiles rather than dogfighting, which it handles poorly. The thrust-vectoring nozzles can pull tighter turns and make split-second adjustments at the cost of speed and energy — a viable but risky move, since a jet slowed to propeller-like speed becomes easy prey even for subsonic attackers with guns. Avoid dogfighting outright unless in a dire situation. (Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/Sea_Harrier_FRS.1, Usage in Battles; wiki.warthunder.com/Sea_Harrier_FRS.1.)

Radar & EW

  • Search radar capable of missile slaving — cues the AIM-9L onto target.
  • Modern RWR able to detect track, launch, and TWS-mode emissions being used against it.
  • Engines overheat under sustained 100% throttle — requires active management.

Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/Sea_Harrier_FRS.1.

Matchup Notes

No RAAF-specific matchup thread exists yet. As a reasonable proxy — same flight model, US-tree variant of the same airframe — forum discussion of the F/A-18C describes "crazy nose authority even at very low speeds" (favors dogfighting/turn-fighting) and a bigger missile loadout than rivals like the J-10A, though it's slower, giving BVR-missile-range opponents an edge; against a Eurofighter Typhoon, forum consensus is the Typhoon "should win" a BVR fight (better AMRAAM tempo, height/energy advantage), so the Hornet's edge is only in a close, energy-neutral turn-fight — force that engagement rather than an extended BVR or vertical fight. (Source: forum.warthunder.com, "J-10A vs F/A-18C: overall performance in-game for air-to-air"; forum.warthunder.com, "F-18 vs EF2K" — both describe the plain F/A-18C, applied here by analogy, not RAAF-confirmed.)

France

16 aircraft
F8F-1B (France) Prop-era Boom & Zoom fighter-bomber — same airframe as the guide's existing USA F8F-1B 4x 20mm cannon · up to 3,000lb bombs/HVAR/Tiny Tim · overheats hard on WEP · avoid turning Energy fighter — ● average turn · ▲ fast, climbs well
  • Fights as: Energy fighter — average turn, fast, climbs well.
  • Role: multirole prop fighter — a "very competent multirole fighter" capable of both air combat and ground attack; historically, 200 of these were surplus-sold to France in 1951 and flown in close-air-support operations during the First Indochina War.
  • Strength: excellent dive speed and fast acceleration, powerful and high-ammo-capacity cannon armament, great roll rate, respectable climb up to about 5km, and substantial bomb capacity for a fighter of its era.
  • Weakness: severe engine overheating on WEP unless the radiator modification is unlocked; performance drops badly above 5km; the 20mm cannons jam quickly under sustained fire; sluggish controls below 300 km/h; loses velocity fast in high-G turns.
  • Primary loadout: no missiles (pre-missile era) — 4x 20mm M3 cannon (826 rounds total, 750 rds/min) is the primary air-to-air weapon, with 2x 12.7mm M2 Browning as a secondary gun option.
  • Bombing load: ? — this card wasn't in the guide when the LEGION Loadouts sheet was mined (v49). Carries 250/500/1,000/1,600lb bombs and HVAR/Tiny Tim rockets, up to roughly 3,000lb total.
  • Use when: playing as a Boom & Zoom fighter-bomber — specific guidance: side-climb at the start of a match to bank energy, avoid WEP until the radiator mod is unlocked, stay below 6,500m where the airframe actually performs, and don't try to turn-fight — dive on targets, use short cannon bursts to avoid jamming, and disengage back to altitude rather than sustaining a turning engagement.

Combat Doctrine

Realistic Battles play with the F8F-1B is built entirely around managing two things: energy and heat. "Side-climb at the beginning of a match as the 1B needs all the energy it can get," building the altitude advantage that its Boom & Zoom game plan depends on — this works best "below 6,500 meters," above which the airframe's performance drops off. The engine overheating problem is treated as a real tactical constraint, not a minor footnote: WEP should be avoided entirely until the radiator modification is unlocked, since sustained full power will cook the engine. Turning is explicitly discouraged — "turning is not recommended due to mediocre turn rates" — reinforcing that every engagement should be a diving pass followed by a climb back to altitude, not a sustained circle. On the cannons, short bursts are recommended specifically to avoid jamming, with Air Targets belts selected for air-to-air work. The aircraft's substantial bomb capacity also makes it a credible fighter-bomber on the side, consistent with its historical close-air-support role in French service.

Weapon Systems & Engagement

  • Cannon: 4x 20mm M3 — 826 rounds total, 750 rds/min; short bursts recommended to avoid jamming.
  • Secondary guns: 2x 12.7mm M2 Browning (optional loadout).
  • Air-to-air missiles: none — pre-missile era airframe. ?
  • Air-to-ground: 250lb, 500lb, 1,000lb, or 1,600lb bombs; HVAR or Tiny Tim rockets; incendiary bombs; magnetic mines — up to roughly 3,000lb total ordnance.

F-84G-26-RE (France) Early jet strike fighter — no air-to-air missiles, boom-and-zoom only 6x .50cal MG · HVAR/Tiny Tim rockets + up to 2,710kg bombs · no AAMs · bleeds energy fast Double inferior — ▼ turns poorly · ▼ slow, climbs poorly
  • Fights as: Double inferior — turns poorly, slow, climbs poorly.
  • Role: early-generation jet strike fighter — the Thunderjet family's French-operated gun-armed variant, built before air-to-air missiles existed on this airframe.
  • Strength: respectable sea-level speed for its era, six centrally-mounted .50cal guns give a tight, consistent bullet stream, an uncommon-for-its-time airbrake useful in a fight, and a heavy ground-attack payload (up to 2,710kg suspended).
  • Weakness: no air-to-air missiles at all — guns only; bleeds speed severely when maneuvering and struggles to reaccelerate; less agile than contemporary rivals; engine efficiency drops noticeably above sea level; .50cal rounds are individually weak, needing multiple hits to down a target.
  • Primary loadout: no missiles — 6x 12.7mm M3 Browning (1,800 rounds total) is the only air-to-air weapon; ordnance is HVAR or Tiny Tim rockets plus 100lb-1,000lb bombs (AN-M30A1, AN-M57, AN-M64A1, AN-M65A1) for ground targets.
  • Bombing load: ? — this card wasn't in the guide when the LEGION Loadouts sheet was mined (v49).
  • Use when: playing as a boom-and-zoom striker — general F-84G-family guidance (not France-specific, but applicable to this variant) says to never let speed bleed off excessively, especially against piston-engine opponents where recovery is hard; fire short bursts rather than sustained fire to conserve the limited ammunition, and attack ground targets with a vertical zigzag pattern to compensate for the lack of a ballistic computer.

Combat Doctrine

With no air-to-air missiles at all, the F-84G-26-RE's entire air-combat plan is boom-and-zoom on guns. The operational profile is summed up plainly: "flying slowly makes for an easy target," so the aircraft is best flown fast, using energy to dictate engagements rather than sustaining a turn fight it will lose. A general F-84G-family tactical writeup (Gaijin's own "Isaac's Vision" guide, not France-specific but covering the shared airframe/handling) reinforces this: the aircraft "bleeds speed severely when maneuvering" and is "less agile than its rivals," so prolonged dogfights should be avoided in favor of opportunistic energy-advantage passes against lower-BR opponents. Ground-attack ordnance is substantial for the rank, so a common pattern is to expend bombs/rockets first, then transition to boom-and-zoom once light. In-flight refuelling capability and Mark 7 nuclear-bomb compatibility are real-world historical notes, not confirmed as gameplay-relevant in-game features.

Super Mystère B2 France's first level-flight-supersonic jet — face-puncher, weak vertical energy retention 2x 30mm DEFA 552 · AIM-9B + AA-20 Nord · strong ground-attack variety · can't sustain a dogfight Energy fighter — ▼ turns poorly · ▲ fast, climbs well

Combat Doctrine

The Super Mystère B2 excels in head-to-head engagements — a "face-puncher" that wins the merge with short cannon bursts and its guided AA-20 missile, then uses Boom & Zoom to keep finding targets of opportunity rather than settling into a sustained turn fight, which the aircraft explicitly "cannot survive." The weapon-selection discipline named is specific: AA-20 goes at incoming fighters, AIM-9B is reserved for slower aircraft like bombers where its more limited performance still suffices. When pursued rather than pursuing, the defensive answer isn't more turning — it's reduced throttle combined with air brakes and combat flaps together, forcing the faster pursuer to overshoot. The aircraft's poor vertical energy retention means none of this works if the fight is allowed to go vertical or prolonged; every piece of guidance here is about ending engagements quickly on the Super Mystère's own terms.

F-8E(FN) Naval "harasser" — no countermeasures at all, only 2 missiles carried at once 4x 20mm cannon · AIM-9B/Matra R530/R550 Magic 1 · zero RWR/flares · exploit chaos, don't linger Energy fighter — ● average turn · ▲ fast, climbs well
  • Fights as: Energy fighter — average turn, fast, climbs well.
  • Role: carrier-based naval fighter — France's "first entry of the supersonic era" for carrier aviation.
  • Strength: excellent flight performance for its BR, powerful 20mm cannon battery, and — with the Matra R550 Magic 1 fitted — a genuinely dangerous 30G-overload, Mach-3 dogfight missile; excellent sustained turning and strong acceleration/climb.
  • Weakness: a complete absence of flare/chaff countermeasures and no RWR — it is "vulnerable to all-aspect infrared missiles" as a result; only two missiles can be carried at once regardless of type; fragile wings and prone to fire; no low-altitude supersonic capability; no ground-attack ordnance options at all.
  • Primary loadout: Matra R550 Magic 1 (all-aspect · IR, 30G) is the strongest weapon carried, followed by Matra R530/R530E (all-aspect · SARH) for a radar-guided option; AIM-9B (rear-aspect · IR) is the oldest and weakest of the three.
  • Bombing load: not applicable — this airframe "lacks ground-attack options" entirely.
  • Use when: playing the "harasser" role — arrive at an already-engaged furball to exploit the chaos with superior maneuverability rather than opening a fight cold, stay near-supersonic continuously since that speed is your main defense against older IR missiles (though it won't save you from a modern AIM-9L-class shot), and re-engage repeatedly rather than lingering in one exchange where the total lack of countermeasures will eventually catch up with you.

Combat Doctrine

Every piece of guidance for the F-8E(FN) flows from one fact: it carries zero flares or chaff and no RWR, in an environment with all-aspect IR and radar-guided missiles. The recommended role is explicitly named a "harasser" — arrive at enemy groups already engaged with each other and use superior maneuverability to pick off a distracted target, rather than initiating a fresh 1v1 where a countermeasure-less airframe is at a structural disadvantage. Staying near-supersonic continuously is presented as the aircraft's actual defensive system in place of flares: its speed helps it out-run and out-maneuver earlier-generation IR missiles, though this stops working against later missiles like the AIM-9L. High altitude is avoided specifically because that's where radar-guided threats dominate and the F-8E(FN) has the least room to hide. With only two missiles available at any time, each shot needs to count — there's no reserve to fall back on if a first attempt misses.

Mirage F1C High-altitude energy support fighter Magic 2 (IRCCM) is the reliable weapon · radar weak at low altitude Energy fighter — ▼ turns poorly · ▲ fast, climbs well
  • Fights as: Energy fighter — turns poorly, fast, climbs well.
  • Role: high-altitude energy support fighter.
  • Strength: excels at high-speed, high-G energy maneuvers.
  • Weakness: not suited to high-AoA maneuvers; radar weak at low altitude.
  • Primary loadout: Magic 2 (IRCCM, primary weapon), R530-series (longer range, unreliable low).
  • Bombing load: 2× SAMP 84 + 1× SAMP 83 (104% of a 25,900 HP base at BR 12.0). (Source: LEGION's Loadouts 2.27 Google Sheet — the smallest load from this aircraft's own drop schedule that destroys one base, using the Bomb Chart's damage values and base HP by BR. % = total bomb damage ÷ (base HP × 0.9018), the kill threshold every count in the chart works out to; 100% = one base.)
  • Use when: climbing to altitude, acting as an energy-advantage support fighter.

Combat Doctrine

Climb to altitude and work as an energy-advantage support fighter — excels at high-speed, high-G energy maneuvers, not high-AoA turning. Radar is weak at low altitude, so Magic 2 is the reliable weapon there; R530-series covers the longer-range shot when it isn't. Carrying Super 530F missiles measurably degrades flight performance, so expect worse energy retention while still loaded, and the DEFA cannons are weak against high-speed targets — don't rely on the gun against a fast boom-and-zoom pass. (Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/Mirage_F1C.)

Combat Doctrine

Stay close to the ground, where maneuverability and acceleration edge matter most, and rebuild energy after each turn rather than grinding one continuous fight — the delta wing bleeds energy fast at low speed and the missile payload is smaller than many competitors'. The guiding line: "get in, and out as quickly as possible." (Source: old-wiki.warthunder.com/Mirage_2000C-S5.)

Mirage 2000-5F High-tier multirole — RDY multi-target radar, 8 missiles, extensive precision-guided A2G kit 2x 30mm DEFA 554 · Magic 2/MICA-EM/Super 530F-D · Thales RDY radar · DAMOCLES pod + AS-30L, GBU series Angles fighter — ▲ turns well · ● average speed/climb
  • Fights as: Angles fighter — turns well, average speed/climb.
  • Role: high-tier multirole fighter combining air-to-air and precision air-to-ground capability in a single airframe, adaptable to "varied operational scenarios."
  • Strength: Thales RDY (Radar Doppler, multi-target) radar for rapid multi-target acquisition; up to 8 air-to-air missiles across three types; low stall speed and great maneuverability; heavy-hitting DEFA 554 cannons; a DAMOCLES targeting pod with third-generation thermal imagery enabling precision laser-guided strikes and the AS-30L missile; genuine anti-ship capability via PGM-2000.
  • Weakness: poor energy retention; the Matra R550 Magic 2's range is limited relative to other short-range options at this BR; the DEFA 554's muzzle velocity (820 m/s) is slow, hurting gunnery at range.
  • Primary loadout: MICA-EM (all-aspect · active-radar BVR) and Matra Super 530F/530D (all-aspect · SARH) for medium/long range, Matra R550 Magic 2 (all-aspect · IR) for the merge — both Magic 2 and MICA-EM are available from stock, unusual generosity for a top-tier fighter.
  • Bombing load: ? — this card wasn't in the guide when the LEGION Loadouts sheet was mined (v49). Strike options: GBU-12/16/24 Paveway laser-guided bombs, BGL-1000, PGM-500/2000, and conventional bombs up to 1,000+kg.
  • Use when: playing as a true multirole fighter — use the RDY radar and Magic 2 for close-in air combat exploiting the airframe's agility and low stall speed, and switch to the DAMOCLES pod with GBU-series or AS-30L for precision ground strikes, or PGM-2000 against armored ships, when the air picture allows; manage energy carefully given the airframe's noted weak retention.

Combat Doctrine

The description doubles as the doctrine: the Mirage 2000-5F's real strength is "combining air-to-air and air-to-ground roles within single missions" rather than excelling narrowly at either. In the air-to-air role, it leans on "exceptional agility and advanced avionics" — the RDY radar for target acquisition and the Magic 2 for close-range finishing, both available stock. On strike missions, the DAMOCLES pod's third-generation thermal imagery is called out as enabling genuinely precise laser-guided bombing and AS-30L missile employment, extending to anti-ship work against armored vessels with the PGM-2000. The tradeoff for this breadth is energy: "poor energy retention" is a real weakness, so the aircraft's maneuverability advantage needs to be spent deliberately in a fight rather than assumed to regenerate quickly, and the Magic 2's comparatively short range means closing distance carefully rather than firing early and hoping.

Radar & EW

  • Thales RDY (Radar Doppler, multi-target) — enabling "rapid target acquisition" and multi-target engagement.
  • HMD (helmet-mounted sight), thermal imaging, and MAW (missile approach warning).

Source: wiki.warthunder.com/unit/mirage_2000_5f; old-wiki.warthunder.com/Mirage_2000-5F.

  • Short-range / merge: Matra R550 Magic 2 (all-aspect · IR) — available stock; range is limited relative to competing short-range missiles at this BR.
  • Medium-range: Matra Super 530F, Super 530D (all-aspect · SARH).
  • BVR: MICA-EM (all-aspect · active-radar) — available stock alongside Magic 2.
  • Total missile capacity: up to 8, combining the above types.
  • Air-to-ground: GBU-12, GBU-16, GBU-24 Paveway-series laser-guided bombs; BGL-1000; PGM-500, PGM-2000 (anti-ship capable); AS-30L laser-guided missile; SNEB rockets; conventional bombs up to 1,000+kg. DAMOCLES targeting pod (3rd-gen thermal imagery) enables the guided ordnance.

Source: wiki.warthunder.com/unit/mirage_2000_5f; old-wiki.warthunder.com/Mirage_2000-5F.

Play as a true all-rounder — capable at both turn-fighting and energy-fighting, canards making it "highly responsive during tight maneuvers." Verify before relying on thisNo explicit energy-vs-turn doctrine or matchup notes exist for this specific variant — the dual-threat framing above is inferred from its stated armament and flight characteristics, not a sourced tactical writeup.

Matchup Notes

  • Countermeasure count is a real limitation — 45 total (30 normal + 15 large) versus the JAS39D's roughly 640; community consensus rates the F-16AM "simply inferior" to the JAS39D at the same BR mainly for this reason.
  • Tune the countermeasure loadout to your altitude habits: mostly-low flyers (using terrain/water multipath cover) should carry more flares than chaff; mostly-high flyers should carry more chaff than flares.
  • AIM-120A (active radar homing) generally outperforms the R-27ER (semi-active) in this matchup — abuse multipathing (fly low over terrain or water) as the defensive counter to enemy radar-guided missiles.

J29A Early Swedish jet fighter — no missiles, inadequate acceleration, needs teamwork 4x 20mm cannon only · no missiles · poor energy retention · hit-and-run/support role Angles fighter — ● average turn · ▼ slow, climbs poorly
  • Fights as: Angles fighter — average turn, slow, climbs poorly.
  • Role: Sweden's first operational jet fighter — swept-wing design informed by captured German wartime research, powered by a licensed de Havilland Ghost engine.
  • Strength: four cannons (an upgrade over its piston predecessors) give real firepower, adequate turning capability once at speed, and a large ammunition count that forgives less-precise shooting.
  • Weakness: "inadequate at accelerating" — reaching high speed takes a while; poor energy retention in sustained turns; no missiles of any kind.
  • Primary loadout: no missiles — 4x 20mm Akan m/47C cannon (720 rounds total, 750 rds/min) is the only weapon, with selectable belts (default HEF-T/AP-T mix, air-targets HEFI-T focus, ground-targets AP-T focus).
  • Bombing load: ? — this card wasn't in the guide when the LEGION Loadouts sheet was mined (v49); the loadout shows no bombs/rockets for this variant.
  • Use when: playing as a support fighter rather than a lone hunter — the framing is explicit: this airframe "requires teamwork and hit-and-run tactics rather than prolonged dogfighting," so pick fights alongside teammates and disengage on the cannon-only firepower advantage rather than trying to out-turn or out-run anything solo.

Combat Doctrine

The J29A's doctrine is dictated by what it lacks: no missiles, sluggish acceleration, and energy that bleeds away in a sustained turn. The guidance is to lean entirely on the four-cannon battery and to fight as part of a team rather than solo — hit-and-run passes where the cannons can do damage, then disengage before a turning fight develops, since the airframe can't out-turn or out-run its way clear once committed. This is an aircraft to fly patiently: its adequate turning ability "at speed" means energy has to be husbanded and spent deliberately, not assumed to regenerate.

  • Strength: strong energy retention under afterburner giving a good rate of climb and acceleration; excellent turning at high speed for both dogfighting and hit-and-run tactics; tough airframe; superior roll rate; high ammo count.
  • Weakness: mediocre top speed compared to contemporaries; sluggish tail controls; underwhelming firepower per-hit despite the ammo count; short landing gear; tiny, inefficient air brakes.

Comparable in practice to the MiG-15bis.

Combat Doctrine

The J29F plays similarly to the MiG-15bis, with the RB24 missile as its real differentiator from the rest of the Tunnan family. "A J29F keeps energy very well when the afterburner is used, giving it a strong rate of climb and acceleration" — so the doctrine is to use that afterburner deliberately rather than conserving fuel, since energy retention is the aircraft's core advantage. The RB24 is not a long-range weapon: the optimal launch distance is 1-3km, and side-rushing — approaching from an angle to get behind an enemy formation before firing — is named as the preferred delivery method, forcing faster opponents to disengage rather than trying to out-fly them directly. The aircraft can intercept unprepared opponents on a rush, but this requires teammate support, since getting caught in a defensive position exposes its mediocre top speed and sluggish tail controls.

J32B All-weather interceptor — devastating quad-30mm cannons, notoriously hard to land 4x 30mm cannon · up to 4x RB24 · radar equipped · excellent top speed, mediocre turning Energy fighter — ▼ turns poorly · ▲ fast, climbs well
  • Fights as: Energy fighter — turns poorly, fast, climbs well.
  • Role: all-weather interceptor built around vertical performance and cannon firepower — consistently named the top pick for its rank across multiple community "best per rank" threads.
  • Strength: excellent top speed that outruns most subsonic opponents; "incredible burst mass and damage" from the quad 30mm cannon battery; a powerful afterburning engine with exceptional energy retention; integrated radar and above-average roll rate; Fowler flaps give excellent low-speed lift.
  • Weakness: mediocre maneuverability — outmaneuvered by most opponents in a turn; a genuinely difficult landing procedure with restrictive flap-speed limits; a very inefficient airbrake design requiring aggressive deployment angles; wings rip easily without the wing-reinforcement modification; no countermeasures against modern missiles.
  • Primary loadout: up to 4x RB24 (rear-aspect · IR) for the merge, with the 4x 30mm Akan m/55 cannon (360 rounds total) as the primary damage dealer — the cannon burst is "incredible" for one-pass kills.
  • Bombing load: ? — this card wasn't in the guide when the LEGION Loadouts sheet was mined (v49). Main ground-attack option is 19x srak m/57B rockets rather than bombs.
  • Use when: playing as a boom-and-zoom interceptor — keep altitude and avoid strong aerial maneuvers, engage from above and dive through, deploy afterburner to escape when needed (fuel consumption rises sharply), and against missile-equipped BR 9.0-9.7 opponents specifically, keep turning continuously when attacked from behind rather than flying straight, since continuous turning complicates an enemy's missile lock. Against supersonic aircraft, stay low at max speed and exploit a tighter turning radius than heavy fighters like the F-4E.

Combat Doctrine

The J32B's doctrine follows directly from its numbers: excellent speed and climb, devastating but ammunition-hungry cannons, and mediocre turning. It is a boom-and-zoom interceptor that should "avoid strong aerial manoeuvres by keeping altitude," engaging from above rather than getting drawn into a turning fight it will lose. Against the missile-equipped opponents that start appearing around its own BR bracket (9.0-9.7), the specific defensive guidance is to keep turning continuously when attacked from behind — a straight flight path is what lets an IR missile track cleanly, while continuous turning complicates the shot. For aggressive play, a reduced fuel load (around 20 minutes) is even suggested purely to improve energy retention and escape performance, accepting the shorter sortie length as a tradeoff. Landing is treated as its own hazard: the airframe holds speed even unpowered, so air brakes and Fowler flaps need to be deployed below 500 km/h with an approach around 300 km/h to avoid flap damage — the guidance treats this at the same level of detail as air-combat tactics, which says something about how real a problem it is.

AJ37 Viggen strike variant — TV-guided RB 75 Maverick-equivalent, no radar-guided A2A missile 30mm cannon · RB24J self-defense · RB75/RB75T (TV-guided A2G) · RB05A · no radar-guided AAM Energy fighter — ▼ turns poorly · ▲ fast, climbs well
  • Fights as: Energy fighter — turns poorly, fast, climbs well.
  • Role: strike aircraft — the attack-optimized branch of the Viggen family, described as "a relatively capable fighter for air battles" that nonetheless "excels at ground attack."
  • Strength: powerful 30mm cannon with excellent range performance; outstanding speed, especially at low altitude; access to the TV-guided RB 75 (a Maverick equivalent) for precision stand-off ground attack; remarkable maneuverability across speed ranges; a capable radar system.
  • Weakness: limited armament variety — only two air-to-air weapon types across four pylons; poor energy retention when flying slow; small bomb capacity; countermeasure pods eat into already-limited hardpoints; no radar-guided air-to-air missile at all.
  • Primary loadout: RB24J (rear-aspect · IR) is the only self-defense missile — "always carry RB24Js, flares, and guns," treating the 30mm cannon as equally central to air-to-air survivability rather than a backup.
  • Bombing load: ? — this card wasn't in the guide when the LEGION Loadouts sheet was mined (v49). Conventional bomb option is 4x 120kg m/71 bombs (standard or high-drag retarded), alongside the guided RB75/RB75T and RB05A missiles.
  • Use when: playing as a strike aircraft with self-defense capability rather than a dedicated fighter — ground-attack guidance: gain altitude quickly when firing the RB 75 to stay outside typical SAM engagement ranges (the missile allows stand-off attack beyond 12km), deploy chaff against SAM threats, and either avoid detection entirely or destroy the SAM first if playing aggressively to free up ordnance slots. In air combat, take maximum fuel, stay fast, and avoid high altitude where poor energy retention becomes a liability.

Combat Doctrine

Community "best per rank" threads named the AJ37 as "about the best you get" for its rank, with a specific loadout recommendation of "one flare pod and one gun pod, and 2x RB-24J's" — prioritizing self-defense tools over a larger missile count given the airframe's limited pylon count. The guidance for air combat is simple: "Always carry RB24Js, flares, and guns," take maximum fuel, and keep speed up while avoiding altitude, since poor energy retention at low speed is the aircraft's defining air-to-air weakness. Where the AJ37 genuinely excels is stand-off ground attack: the TV-guided RB 75 (functionally a Maverick equivalent) allows engaging from beyond 12km, well outside most SAM engagement envelopes, and the recommendation is to gain altitude quickly right after firing it to stay clear of any residual threat. For a more aggressive ground-attack approach, destroying the SAM system before it can react is presented as an alternative that frees up ordnance slots that would otherwise go to defensive countermeasure pods.

  • Radar-equipped (model not specified by either source), plus RWR and a ballistic computer for weapons delivery.
  • Countermeasure (chaff) pods available but occupy hardpoints that would otherwise carry weapons.

  • Use when: playing as a radar-led BVR interceptor — the core summary is "get fast, and stay fast": perform best below 3,000m where maneuvering and speed advantages are strongest, keep velocity above 700 km/h for acceleration, and use the PS-46/A radar to set up RB71 shots early rather than closing to a turning fight the airframe can't sustain. Take a full fuel load despite the afterburner's thirst, since running out of energy mid-fight is the aircraft's defining failure mode.

Combat Doctrine

The summary doubles as the whole doctrine: "get fast, and stay fast." The JA37C's PS-46/A radar and RB71 (Skyflash-equivalent) missile give it a genuine BVR tool — the RB71 is "very effective and hard to dodge" when launched head-on around 3km — but everything about the airframe punishes trying to sustain a fight once engaged, since energy retention in sustained turns is described as "extremely poor." The practical answer is to fight at low altitude (below 3,000m, where the aircraft's maneuvering and speed advantages actually show up), keep speed above 700 km/h at all times for acceleration, and treat any drop below that threshold as a reason to disengage rather than push through it. The framing as a "jack of all trades" that can "effectively dogfight heavier opponents like the F-4 Phantom while maintaining solid armament options" is consistent with this: it isn't the best at any one thing, but the radar and RB71 combination lets it punch above its raw flight-performance numbers if the pilot never lets the fight slow down.

  • Weakness: the airframe is "no longer fast or agile enough" against its BR bracket's competition, and its sensors are described as "outdated," which "limits its combat effectiveness despite modern missile armament" — the RB 99 upgrade doesn't fix the underlying airframe's age.

Combat Doctrine

The summary is the clearest doctrine available for this card: the JA37DI F21 "gains modern RB 99 SARH missiles over the baseline JA37D" (RB 99 is the Swedish AIM-120 AMRAAM equivalent — this guide's own existing JAS39D card already establishes RB 99 as active-radar, "AMRAAM-equiv," so the missile itself is a genuine fire-and-forget BVR weapon whatever the exact guidance-type wording used elsewhere), yet the aircraft "remains hampered by 'no longer fast or agile enough' performance and obsolete sensors," making it "difficult to use effectively in combat." Read together, that's a doctrine in itself: this card's entire value proposition is the RB 99 shot taken early and from range, not a airframe that can out-turn, out-run, or out-sense its BR bracket the way the guide's China F-16A MLU or France Mirage 2000-5F can. The older reference article for this specific card is an unfilled template with no tactics content, so the summary above is the only sourced doctrine available — a genuine gap rather than an omission, flagged here plainly.

J-6A Pure vertical-energy day fighter — no radar or RWR, huge acceleration once fast 2x 30mm cannon · 2x PL-2 (rear-aspect IR) · no radar/RWR · exceptional climb & acceleration Energy fighter — ▼ turns poorly · ▲ fast, climbs well
  • Fights as: Energy fighter — turns poorly, fast, climbs well.
  • Role: light day fighter — a MiG-19 derivative built around raw acceleration and vertical energy retention rather than sensors or missile range.
  • Strength: immense acceleration once above roughly 600-900 km/h — it "will out-accelerate almost all other aircraft" at that point, making a sustained pursuit hard to escape; superior climb rate; two 30mm cannons hit very hard when they land.
  • Weakness: no radar or RWR at all — only basic 1960s-era instrumentation; heavy high-speed compression and poor low-speed maneuverability; wing fragility; the PL-2 (a licensed R-3S copy) is rear-aspect only and short-ranged, useless in a turning fight.
  • Primary loadout: PL-2 (rear-aspect · IR) is the only missile — a close-range finishing shot on an already-committed target, not an opener; the 2x 30mm Type 30-1 cannon (140 rounds total, 850 rds/min) is the real weapon.
  • Bombing load: ? — this card wasn't in the guide when the LEGION Loadouts sheet was mined (v49). Ground-attack fit: 100kg/250kg bomb options and 8x S-5KP rockets.
  • Use when: playing as a boom-and-zoom energy fighter — take opponents vertical rather than turning with them, keep the throttle up at all times (the engine has a long spool time, so backing off lets a target escape during your next acceleration), use the air brake to avoid overshooting, and finish with the cannons once you have an energy advantage.

Combat Doctrine

The J-6A's whole game plan is written into its numbers: enormous acceleration and climb, no radar, no RWR, and a rear-aspect-only missile with almost no engagement envelope. The tactics guidance is blunt about it — "take the enemies vertical," since opponents bleed energy fast while the J-6A holds onto its own, and once it's built up speed it "will out-accelerate almost all other aircraft," making it difficult for a target to disengage from. The air brake is called out as a real tactical tool for preventing overshoots on a diving or extending target, and rolling scissors are viable given the aircraft's roll rate. The single biggest piloting discipline named across sources: never reduce throttle to "save" energy mid-fight, since the long engine spool time means a target can accelerate away during the lag before power comes back up.

Radar & EW

  • No radar and no radar warning receiver — "basic instrumentation typical of 1960s-era fighters" only. An older community pros/cons list separately mentions "radar system" as a strength, which conflicts with the avionics description; the explicit no-radar description is treated as authoritative here. ?

Combat Doctrine

The Q-5A has no air-to-air missiles of any kind — the only way it can respond to a fighter is with its twin 23mm cannon. That single fact should drive the whole plan: this is not an aircraft to go looking for a dogfight in. Sources describe it as excelling in vertical energy fighting, inheriting MiG-19-derived climb characteristics — the recommended defensive answer to an intercepting fighter is to "pull them into a climbing spiral or other vertical manoeuvres" rather than turn-fight on the horizontal, where the lack of missiles and the weaker 23mm cannons leave it outgunned. Control compression at high speed is a documented limitation, so speed needs active management in a dive rather than assuming the airframe will hold together at redline. On the ground-attack side it's built for multiple passes rather than one big strike — 130mm rockets for armor (overpressure-based, so precision matters less), 90mm HEAT rockets and 250kg bombs for other targets, aimed with the ballistic computer.

Radar & EW

  • No onboard radar — target acquisition is visual-only.
  • Defensive suite: 18 flares (the first Chinese aircraft in-game to carry them) plus a radar warning receiver (RWR) for situational awareness against IR-guided threats.
