Combat Doctrine

The J-8B's identity is "big, fast, and armed with China's first SARH missile" — it leans on "excellent climb rate, top speed, and acceleration" rather than turn performance, which degrades badly ("severe speed loss during turns"). The two-missile loadout has a clear division of labor: PL-5B is an IR heat-seeker best flown patient and close (over 1.5km, once its acceleration has time to work), while the Aspide-1A trades that for stand-off range at the cost of needing altitude and a roughly 10km engagement bubble for the radar to hold a reliable lock. Because the airframe is unusually large and visually easy to spot, and because the radar itself is called out as unreliable rather than a strength, the recommended approach is patient and stand-off rather than aggressive — rushing into combat zones is explicitly warned against.

Radar & EW

  • Type 208A fire-control radar — 120° sweep angle, roughly twice the maximum range of the MiG-21's radar, but lacks boresight targeting and is "notoriously unreliable, no PD capability" (no pulse-Doppler, so no reliable look-down/shoot-down against ground clutter).
  • Large-caliber countermeasures load (flare/chaff count not confirmed from either source). ?

J-7E MiG-21/F-5 hybrid dogfighter — double-delta wings, strong energy retention, no radar 1x 30mm cannon (offset) · PL-5B/PL-2 (IR) · no radar · 72 countermeasures · double-delta agility Double superior — ▲ turns well · ▲ fast, climbs well
  • Fights as: Double superior — turns well, fast, climbs well.
  • Role: dogfighter — "a hybrid between MiG-21 and F-5 platforms," using a distinctive double-delta wing to trade some of the MiG-21 lineage's rough handling for much better low-speed manoeuvrability and energy retention.
  • Strength: lighter than the Soviet MiG-21 variants with correspondingly better acceleration; the double-delta wing gives "impressive manoeuvrability and energy retention"; strong RWR paired with a generous 72 countermeasures; PL-5B rated at 30G overload; comprehensive ground-attack loadout options for a dedicated fighter.
  • Weakness: a single 30mm cannon with only 60 rounds, and it's mounted off-center to starboard — aim slightly left at close range to compensate; no fire-control radar or radar-guided missile at all; missile capacity below average at 4 total; engine prone to overheating under sustained use.
  • Primary loadout: PL-5B (IR, 30G overload) as the main air-to-air weapon, PL-2 (rear-aspect · IR) as an older alternative; it "lacks all-aspect IR capability," so shot angle discipline still matters even with the newer missile.
  • Bombing load: ? — this card wasn't in the guide when the LEGION Loadouts sheet was mined (v49). Ordnance options: 250kg/500kg bombs and Type 90-1/130-2 rockets.
  • Use when: playing as an energy-retention dogfighter — a high-altitude supersonic approach against distracted targets and a lower-altitude patrol picking off tunnel-visioned opponents both work; launch PL-5B while the target is still inattentive, use the airframe's superior T/W and energy retention to control the fight, and disengage rather than press a disadvantaged fight — "one small wrong move can mean your quick demise" against a well-flown F-5.

Combat Doctrine

The clearest summary available: the J-7E plays as a hybrid of the MiG-21 lineage and the F-5 line, using its double-delta wing for markedly better low-speed handling and energy retention than a standard MiG-21. Two openings are named specifically — a high-altitude supersonic pass against a target that hasn't noticed you, or a lower-altitude patrol against someone tunnel-visioned on their own target — both built around using PL-5B while you still have surprise, since the aircraft has no radar to build a firing solution the hard way. Because the single cannon is both low on ammunition (60 rounds) and mounted off-center, the guidance is explicit: compensate by aiming slightly left at close range. The recommended overall posture is aggressive early and cautious once committed — disengage from a losing exchange rather than pressing it, since the missile count (4 total) and ammunition don't support a long fight.

Radar & EW

  • No fire-control radar and no radar-guided missile capability.
  • Advanced RWR paired with 72 countermeasures — a notably large flare/chaff count for this BR bracket.

J-11 Lighter single-Flanker interceptor — huge missile count, IRST, Pugachev's Cobra capable up to 10x R-73E/R-27 combo · radar/IRST · FBW, 110° AoA · large target profile Energy fighter — ● average turn · ▲ fast, climbs well
  • Fights as: Energy fighter — average turn, fast, climbs well.
  • Role: interceptor — a China-operated single-Flanker, lighter and more agile than the guide's existing Su-30MKK, which is the same Flanker family built as a heavier two-seat missile truck.
  • Strength: up to 10 total air-to-air missiles combining short- and medium/long-range types, radar plus IRST for a secondary lock-on path, fly-by-wire controls enabling extreme-AoA maneuvers ("Pugachev's Cobra" up to 110° AoA), powerful twin AL-31F engines giving a 1.18 thrust-to-weight ratio at full fuel/combat power, and a large internal fuel capacity.
  • Weakness: a large target profile (21m length, large wing area) that's easy to visually spot and hit; avionics and RWR described as inferior to Western counterparts at the same BR; only 150 rounds for the single cannon; lacks precision-guided air-to-ground weapons.
  • Primary loadout: R-73E (all-aspect · IR, 40G, thrust-vectoring) for the merge — best used inside roughly 4km before a target can deploy countermeasures; R-27ER1 (all-aspect · SARH) as the BVR opener thanks to superior speed/range; R-27T1/ET1 (all-aspect · IR) as a mid-range alternative pair.
  • Bombing load: ? — this card wasn't in the guide when the LEGION Loadouts sheet was mined (v49). Ordnance options: OFAB/FAB bombs (100-500kg) and S-8KO/S-13OF/S-25 rockets.
  • Use when: playing as a missile-rich interceptor that leans on its 10-missile capacity rather than the cannon — open with R-27ER1 at range, use R-27T1/ET1 as a mid-range follow-up, and hold R-73E's thrust-vectoring for a committed close-range shot; on mixed air/ground maps, the guide's community source recommends prioritizing "careless players" focused on ground attack over contesting well-flown fighters directly.

Combat Doctrine

The J-11 is built to fight primarily as an interceptor rather than a turn-fighter, even though its fly-by-wire controls and Flanker-family aerodynamics give it genuinely impressive maneuverability — including the "Pugachev's Cobra" extreme-AoA maneuver up to 110°. The community source frames early engagements around the R-27T1/R-73E pairing: R-73E is the close-range finisher, with 40G of overload and thrust vectoring making it dangerous inside about 4km, ideally before the target has a chance to deploy countermeasures. R-27ER1 is called out specifically for its superior speed and range as the preferred BVR opener among the R-27 family carried. On mixed-objective maps the guide's source suggests a secondary role: with substantial air-to-ground ordnance still on board despite being flown as an interceptor, watching for and punishing "careless players" absorbed in a ground-attack run is presented as a live tactical option, not just a side note.

Su-30MKK Heavy missile-truck multirole — huge BVR loadout, low T/W hurts in the merge up to 6x PL-12/RVV-AE + 4x PL-8B · N001VE radar · massive strike arsenal · low thrust-to-weight Double inferior — ▼ turns poorly · ▼ slow, climbs poorly
  • Fights as: Double inferior — turns poorly, slow, climbs poorly (missiles are the answer).
  • Role: heavy multirole strike-fighter built to fight as a BVR missile-truck, with a secondary role as an all-aspect precision-strike platform.
  • Strength: enormous air-to-air missile capacity (up to 6x PL-12/RVV-AE + 4x PL-8B simultaneously), N001VE radar with multi-target tracking, one of the widest stand-off strike arsenals of any Part V entry.
  • Weakness: low thrust-to-weight ratio — a heavy airframe that bleeds energy fast and is poorly suited to sustained turning fights.
  • Primary loadout: RVV-AE / PL-12 (all-aspect · active-radar BVR) as the primary punch; PL-8B / R-73E (all-aspect · IR) for the merge; R-27ER1 (all-aspect · SARH) / R-27ET1 (all-aspect · IR) as a mid-range alternative pair.
  • Bombing load: 2× FAB-1500 (104% of a 25,900 HP base at BR 13.3). (Source: LEGION's Loadouts 2.27 Google Sheet — the smallest load from this aircraft's own drop schedule that destroys one base, using the Bomb Chart's damage values and base HP by BR. % = total bomb damage ÷ (base HP × 0.9018), the kill threshold every count in the chart works out to; 100% = one base.)
  • Use when: playing as a stand-off radar-missile platform — open at range with PL-12s using the multi-target radar, hold PL-8B/cannon in reserve for a forced merge, and avoid extended turning fights.

Combat Doctrine

The Su-30MKK is a heavy, missile-truck-style multirole fighter. It is "a heavy aircraft with a low thrust-to-weight ratio that is poorly suited for close-range dogfights" but "performs well in combat at medium and long ranges" thanks to its payload capacity. Forum discussion describes it carrying up to six PL-12 (Fox-3) plus four PL-8B (Fox-2) missiles simultaneously — one player likened this to feeling "like two MiG-29SMT or 2 F-16C in one plane" — backed by an N001VE radar described as comparable to the Su-27SM's, giving "better detection range and enhanced capabilities for tracking multiple targets." The doctrine follows from that loadout: engage at range, launch PL-12s early using the radar's multi-target tracking, hold PL-8B and the cannon in reserve for a merge forced on you, and avoid extended turning fights where the low T/W ratio will bleed energy against lighter opponents.

Radar & EW

  • N001VE pulse-Doppler radar — per forum discussion, multi-target tracking comparable to the Su-27SM's, giving "better detection range and enhanced capabilities for tracking multiple targets."
  • Standard defensive suite: flares/chaff, radar warning receiver (RWR), ballistic computer (for A/G aiming), helmet-mounted sight (HMD), and night vision.

Source: wiki.warthunder.com/unit/su_30mkk; forum.warthunder.com discussion threads on the Su-30MKK/MK2.

F-16A MLU (China) Multirole hybrid — F-16A Block 15 MLU airframe/avionics feel with F-16C-derived hardware M61A1 cannon · AIM-9L/9P + AIM-7M + AIM-120A AMRAAM · APG-66 radar · LANTIRN, guided bombs Double superior — ▲ turns well · ▲ fast, climbs well
  • Fights as: Double superior — turns well, fast, climbs well.
  • Role: multirole fighter — "a hybrid version between the F-16A Block 15 MLU and the airframe of the F-16C," offering "a reliable multirole fighter" for both interception and ground attack.
  • Strength: AIM-120A AMRAAM gives it active-radar BVR capability the guide's older research pass didn't expect at this slot; strong maneuverability across speed ranges; a genuinely flexible air-to-ground kit including AGM-65 Maverick, AGM-84D Harpoon, and GBU-10/12 Paveway II laser-guided bombs paired with a LANTIRN targeting pod.
  • Weakness: no IRST sensor, so all air-to-air targeting outside visual range depends on the APG-66 radar alone; heavy fuel consumption under sustained afterburner use.
  • Primary loadout: AIM-120A (all-aspect · active-radar BVR) as the primary stand-off weapon, AIM-7M (all-aspect · SARH) as a radar-guided backup, AIM-9L/AIM-9P (all-aspect/rear-aspect · IR) for the merge.
  • Bombing load: ? — this card wasn't in the guide when the LEGION Loadouts sheet was mined (v49). Strike options: Mk82 (up to 12x) or Mk84 (up to 4x) plus GBU-10/12 guided bombs.
  • Use when: playing as a balanced multirole fighter that leans on radar-guided BVR — open with AIM-120A/AIM-7M using the APG-66's tracking, fall back on the AIM-9 pair and the M61A1 cannon for a forced merge, and use the LANTIRN pod and guided bombs for precision strikes when the air picture is clear.

Combat Doctrine

The framing — "a hybrid version between the F-16A Block 15 MLU and the airframe of the F-16C" — captures the doctrine directly: fly it as a balanced multirole F-16, not a specialist. The guidance is to "leverage radar superiority while managing fuel consumption during afterburner use," which matters more here than on a lighter airframe given the fuel-hungry sustained-AB weakness noted above.

Radar & EW

  • AN/APG-66 pulse-Doppler radar with track-while-scan (TWS) capability — no IRST fitted.
  • Thermal imager and night vision (LANTIRN-associated), ballistic computer, radar warning receiver (RWR).

Matchup Notes

Rank VII; BR 11.0 in Air RB, read from the first of three unlabeled BR groups (AB 11.3, SB 10.7; a second group lists RB 10.3 — not mapped to a mode). Added in Update 1.97 "Viking Fury"; research order F-104J, then F-4EJ, then F-4EJ Kai. Japan bought 140 F-4EJs in 1968, based on the USAF F-4E but without aerial refuelling and ground-attack capability; Mitsubishi built 138 more under licence. It was Japan's main air-defence fighter for many years; the RF-4EJ retired in March 2020 and the last F-4EJ in December 2020. Its speed, turn and climb figures equal the F-4EJ Kai card's. (Source: wiki.warthunder.com/unit/f-4ej.)

Matchup Notes

Rank VIII; BR 12.7 in Air RB, read from the first of three unlabeled BR groups (SB 13.0; a second group lists RB 12.0 — not mapped to a mode). Added in Update 2.25 "Sky Guardians"; listed between the AV-8S Late (Thailand) and the F-2A in the research tree. It represents a proposed Japanese F-16A promoted by General Dynamics in the 1980s: the JASDF evaluated 13 candidates to replace its F-104J fleet, narrowed them to the F-14, F-15 and F-16, and chose the F-15, which became the F-15J. The F-16 concept later evolved into the Mitsubishi F-2. Its speed, turn and climb figures equal the Israeli Netz card's. (Source: wiki.warthunder.com/unit/f_16aj.)

Added in Update 2.37 "Seek & Destroy"; research order F-15J, then F-15J(M). Japan's fleet modernisation began in 1987 based on the F-15C MSIP II upgrades; a December 2004 mid-term programme added ejection seats, engines and avionics for the domestic AAM-4. The programme was delayed and all 102 planned aircraft were upgraded by August 2014. See the F-15J and F-15C (MSIP II) cards. (Source: wiki.warthunder.com/unit/f_15j_kai.)

Rank VIII; BR 13.0 in Air RB, read from the first of three unlabeled BR groups (AB 13.3; a second group lists RB 12.0 — not mapped to a mode). Added in Update 2.29 "Sons of Attila"; research order Tornado IDS (1995), then AV-8B Plus. Italy lifted its ban on fixed-wing naval aviation in 1989 and in 1990 contracted 14 AV-8B+ and 2 TAV-8B; three were built in the US and delivered before a 1995 peacekeeping deployment to Somalia, and later orders were assembled by Alenia Aeronautica. Part VI — Weaponry & Tools

Radar & RWR

  • Radar mode is a deliberate choice — default TWS for the group, STT only for the shot itself.
  • RWS: wide sweep, no track file — least warning given to the target.
  • TWS: tracks multiple contacts, standard for multi-bogey BVR — some cost to update rate per contact.
  • STT: best firing solution, but blind to everyone else and the loudest signal on their RWR.
  • Common mistake: locking STT early out of habit — it wins nothing over TWS until you're actually about to shoot.

Your radar mode changes what you can see and what the other guy's RWR sees of you — pick it deliberately, not by default. Default to TWS for the group, reserve STT for the shot itself or a target that's maneuvered outside what TWS can hold.

ModeWhat it doesTrade-off
RWS (range-while-search)Sweeps a wide area, no track file — see contacts, not shoot themGives the target the least warning
TWS (track-while-scan)Builds track files on multiple contacts while still scanning around them — the standard mode for a multi-bogey BVR engagement, since a fired missile can still get guidance updates without giving up the wider pictureSome cost to update rate per contact
STT (single-target track)Locks one contact continuously for the best possible firing solutionFully blind to everyone else; the loudest, most obvious signal the target's RWR can receive
Common mistakeLocking STT early out of habit. It wins you nothing over TWS until you're actually about to shoot, and it both blinds you to the rest of the group and hands the target maximum warning the whole time you hold it.

Gimbal limits

Every radar has a gimbal limit — roughly 60° off the nose on a typical fighter radar — past which it physically can't keep pointing at a target. Losing a contact off the gimbal edge mid-turn is one of the most common ways a TWS or STT lock breaks; managing your own heading to keep the target inside that cone matters as much as which mode you're in.

Reading an RWR display, generally

An RWR display generally separates threats by distance from center (closer to center = stronger signal = a closer or more directly-aimed threat) and by symbol/tone escalation as a radar's behavior changes: a search radar sweeping past you reads very differently from the same radar locked and tracking, which reads differently again from the distinct mode-change tone a radar makes switching to missile guidance.

War Thunder's SPO-15-style display specifically

The SPO-15-style RWR shows this as rings of square lights (signal strength/proximity) with several front sectors but only left/right resolution to the rear — both rear lights together means directly behind you — plus threat-type letter codes (AI air-intercept radar, PD pulse-Doppler, and several ground-based codes). Treat any front-sector spike as "watch it," a steady strong signal as "he's tracking you, consider notch/crank," and the distinct launch tone as "defend now" — per the missile-defense timing in Part III.

Named but not yet sourced — needs a transcriptThe War Thunder Wiki's own video guide, "War Thunder RWRs: The Ultimate Guide" (wiki.warthunder.com/video/162), almost certainly has the current, patch-accurate symbology for both classic SPO-15-style and newer digital RWRs — but it's video-only content this environment can't pull a transcript from. Worth a watch-and-note pass the same way the Part I BFM videos were handled.

Reading the radar "Sheet data" lines (Part V)

Nine Part V cards carry a line of radar figures from a community sheet of in-game radar values. The sheet lists radars, not aircraft, so a line only appears where a source names the aircraft's radar.

  • Modes: P = pulse, PD = pulse-Doppler, head-on PD = PD that only sees closing targets, MTI = moving-target indication.
  • Transceiver range — the sheet's baseline range figure per mode; "max" is its hard cap. Treat these as relative comparisons between radars, not a promise you'll see a given target that far out.
  • Tracks out to — the furthest distance the radar can hold a lock.
  • Azimuth/elevation — how far off the nose it can look (compare the gimbal limit above).

(Source: community "Radar data" Google Sheet — Home Page notations and air-based radar tabs, stats last changed in game v2.37.0.86. The sheet predates later radar additions: Hornet, F-14D, PoBIT, Typhoon, Rafale, Gripen and Su-30 radars aren't in it.)

Base Bombing

  • 4-base maps (most mid/high-tier maps): bases respawn after a while, so a big payload can keep killing them. All loadout numbers in this guide assume these maps.
  • 3-base maps (mostly low tier): bases don't respawn and take about half the payload. Once all three fall, the airfield becomes the last target.
  • Arcade: non-respawning bases have twice the health — drop double the payload.
  • Many small bombs beat a few big ones: base damage isn't simply total explosive mass.
  • Use the weapon selector to pick which bombs drop first, and secondary weapon ripple quantity to set how many drop per release.

The chart's top bracket is labelled 8.0–13.7. Aircraft above 13.7 (F-16CM PoBIT, F/A-18E, Typhoon, F/A-18A late, F/A-18F, Rafale) are treated as 25,900 HP here; their own schedules in the sheet fit that figure.

What counts as a kill

Every bombs-per-base count in the sheet's chart equals base HP × 0.9018 ÷ the bomb's damage value, rounded up. So about 90% of a base's HP in bomb damage counts as destroyed. The guide's "% of a base" figures use the same threshold: 100% = one base.

The sheet's own example of why size isn't everything: one FAB-3000 (1,400 kg TNT equivalent) barely dents a 4-base-map base, while four FAB-500s (4 × 325 kg) take about 95% off it, with base bleed finishing the rest. The sheet's author suspects the game models blast falling off with distance, so spreading many smaller bombs pays.

Part V aircraft: one-base bombing load

For each aircraft, the smallest load from its own drop schedule in the sheet that destroys one base — 100%, or the nearest figure above it — rather than everything it can carry. Each card shows the same line directly under its primary loadout, in Full mode only. Not listed in the sheet: AV-8A, F-16A ADF, Yak-3U, Su-11, La-200, MiG-17, Tempest, Spitfire F24, Sea Fury, Hunter F.6, Mirage 2000C-S5.

Training

Learning Path & Drills

Reading gets you to comprehension; only repetition gets you to application. This part turns the guide into something you can practice. Every drill here comes from a training source already in the guide — mainly Mike Solyom/The Ops Center's BFM and ACM series, plus Echo Victor for the briefing format and one DCS forum poster for a range ladder. Where no real exercise has been found for a topic, the coverage table says so instead of filling it in. The order follows Solyom's own video order, then Shaw's chapter order for what comes after BFM.

Track your deathsAfter each match, log how you died and which skill failed in the Debrief Log, a separate private page. It keeps every entry, counts which skills you fail most, and names your next practice target and its drills from this part. Its skill and drill lists match the cards here.
Running any repBrief it with PADS first — position (usually combat spread, also called abeam), altitude, distance, speed — and agree the tolerances up front: ±30 m altitude, ±185 m distance, ±10° bearing, ±19 km/h speed. Start with "fights on." End with the flight call sign plus "knock it off" (a safety-of-flight factor or real doubt) or "terminate" (a routine end); each member then acknowledges with their position number. Pick a floor — a minimum altitude that stands in for the ground (Solyom suggests a floor about 3,050 m with a start about 4,570 m). Limit a beginner's bandit to military power. Every number in every drill is a suggested, adjustable parameter, not a rule. Finish with a short debrief comparing both pilots' views, then log it in the debrief form below. (Source: Echo Victor, "The ULTIMATE BFM Guide," PADS setup; Mike Solyom/The Ops Center, Quarter Plane, Defensive Ranging and Medium Range DBFM exercises.)

The path

  1. Extended Trail (two-ship). The USAF fighter-fundamentals course flies this before the BFM block, and Solyom says much of the section-level instinct is built there. The exercise itself is not yet reviewed. ?
  2. Terminology and the EM diagram. Read Energy & turn performance and Turn circles. No dedicated exercise is recorded for these.
  3. Heat-To-Guns. Offensive BFM and Pursuit geometry. D1
  4. Quarter Plane, then Medium Range OBFM. Offensive BFM. D2 D3
  5. Defensive Ranging. Defensive BFM. D4
  6. Reversal. Defensive BFM. D5
  7. Close-range survival and Medium Range DBFM. Defensive BFM. D6
  8. High-aspect BFM: Butterfly + lead turn, then two-circle, then one-circle. High-Aspect BFM. D7 D8 D9
  9. Missiles (Shaw ch.3 comes next in the book). Weapons envelope, BVR offense, Missile defense. No sourced exercise structure yet; the community practice habits are in D11. ?
  10. Two-ship work: wingman contract, formations, section maneuvers, ACM. D10
  11. Strategy and the rest: division tactics, missions, target priority, multi-bogey, radar, base bombing. No sourced drills yet.

A separate community ladder for range and 1v1/2v1 progression is in D12.

Flying these in War ThunderSolyom's series is flown in DCS (an F-5 standing in for a T-38), so the perch distances and speeds are DCS-based and meant to be adjusted. For War Thunder, a forum thread reports that test flight offers air targets for propeller aircraft but not jets, and a poster says custom battles work but practice partners are hard to find. No confirmed solo setup for jets was found. ? A custom CDK mission can script a bandit's route, but per the CDK documentation it has no AI G-limit or distance-trigger conditions, so it can only approximate the perch and power limits. (Source: War Thunder forum thread "Test flight customization"; Mike Solyom/The Ops Center, Defensive Ranging and Medium Range DBFM; CDK documentation.)

D12Community range ladder (one DCS forum poster)
  • Offense: start directly behind the bandit at the same altitude, at about 915 m, then 1,830 m, then 2,745 m, using IR missiles and guns only. Learn to recognize and enter the turn circle; repeat each stage until mastered.
  • Defense: the bandit starts directly behind you at the same three ranges; learn to survive until you reach the floor or can go offensive.
  • 1v1: bandit on your nose at the same altitude from about 8 km ("something like 5 miles"); practice one-turn and two-turn fights to learn how your own aircraft performs. With a helmet-mounted sight and AIM-9X, try shots across the circle.
  • 2v1: once 1v1 is comfortable, add a wingman for cooperative ACM. The post does not say who starts behind whom.
  • Pass: "master it" — no numeric test is given.

(Source: DCS World forum thread "Suggestions for improving ACM skills" (poster Notso). A single community poster for DCS, not an official syllabus. Every number is the source's own suggested, adjustable training parameter.)

Reference

Glossary

Show glossary (A–Z)
TermMeaningSee
Angles fighterWins by spending energy for a tighter turnPart I
AA / HCA / ATA / AOTAspect angle (0° astern–180° head-on) / heading crossing angle / antenna train angle (angle-off-nose) / angle-off-tail — ATA and AOT read the same when the bandit is on your tailPart I
Angle off nose (AON) / Target aspectAON: angle away from your own nose the target sits (low AON = ahead of you, high AON = behind you). Target aspect: angle the bandit's nose points relative to you — 0° facing straight at you; distinct from aspect angle, which is measured from his tailPart I
A-pole / E-pole / Decision RangeRange at missile go-active / range you must already be defending by / closest range a full notch-abort sequence can still workPart III
Attack window / Attack Window EntryThe point in space from which an offensive break turn delivers range, angles and closure all under control at once — the third element of a turn circle alongside the bubble and control zonePart I
Bandit / BogeyBandit: a visually-confirmed-hostile contact. Bogey: unidentified — becomes a bandit once ID'd, a bandit for the rest of the engagementPart II
Bandit switchBandit swaps which fighter he's attacking mid-fight; whoever notices first calls "bandit switch, [callsign] engaged" and roles flip without re-running the establishing-roles hierarchyPart II
Boresight / off-boresightBoresight: dead along the aircraft's nose axis — a boresight lock/shot needs the target straight ahead. Off-boresight: helmet-sight cueing lets the seeker lock a target away from the nose insteadPart V
Bug-outDeliberate escape: max thrust, unloaded dive, ≤2 check turns of 30°; succeeds past ~1.85 km separation with >90° left on the bandit's turnPart I
Butterfly SetupLine-abreast, mutual check-away setup for training a high-aspect merge from a neutral startPart I
CAP (Racetrack / Counter-rotating)Hot-leg/cold-leg patrol pattern; two aircraft trading hot/cold so the threat axis is never unwatchedPart II
Control zone~760–1,370 m slant range within a 25–45° aspect-angle cone — close enough to a bandit's turn circle to assess and commit to a shotPart I
Corner velocitySpeed at which instantaneous max turn rate is achievedPart I
Cold / Hot / CrankOpening range / closing / turning to radar gimbal limit while holding partial lockPart III
The DeckReal life: the ground. Training: a set altitude known to both pilots (often ~3,050 m / 10,000 ft) standing in for it — same role as "the floor" elsewhere in this guidePart I
The Ditch / Ditch FollowDefender's pure nose-low idle-throttle escape to force an overshoot / the climbing counter that preserves energy and re-attacks with a Split-SPart I
Double AttackTwo aircraft, sequenced strike on one targetPart II
Element / Division (four-ship)A four-ship split into two two-aircraft elements, each still run on the lead/wingman contractPart II
Energy fighterWins by preserving speed/altitude, using the verticalPart I
Engaged fighter / Support fighterThe two ACM roles: engaged fighter flies the actual BFM against the bandit; support fighter owns deconfliction, takes shots of opportunity, and clears for additional banditsPart II
Exclusive use turning roomTurning room available to only one aircraft — e.g. one low/one high, or whichever aircraft covers less downrange distance into a second mergePart I
Fighter sweep / EscortIndependent hunt for enemy fighters ahead of a package / staying with a protected asset to defend it directlyPart IV
Fighting WingClose formation, lead offensive / wingman defensive-onlyPart II
The floorChosen minimum altitude standing in for the ground in training; past it, altitude can no longer be traded for turn performancePart I
F-poleDistance between you and the target when your missile arrives — bigger is saferPart III
GCI (ground-controlled interception)A controller with sensor coverage vectors an interceptor onto a targetPart IV
Gimbal limitOff-nose angle (~60°) past which a radar physically can't keep tracking a targetPart VI
Loose DeuceWide-separation formation, roles swap fluidlyPart II, IV
Lost Sight GameplanIf sighting is lost defensively: max-perform toward the bandit's last known direction; reorient the lift vector regularly near the deck; dive to the deck from altitude to silhouette him against the skyPart I
Meld / SortRadars converging on a group / assigning who tracks which contactPart III
Merge typesVertical (climber favored by God's G) / slow-speed (both nose-high, meet atop the loop) / high-speed nose-low (both nose-low, low rate both) / stern conversion (not a merge — placed on the 6 by outside cueing)Part I
MultipathLow-altitude technique exploiting ground clutter against a seekerPart III
Mutual support priorityPost-merge order of who you help, in strict priority: your threat, other threats, your wingman's threat, re-establish element, then the other elementPart II
NotchFlying perpendicular to a threat radar to zero closure ratePart II, III
No-escape zoneRange/aspect where a target statistically can't evade a shotPart III
OODA loopObserve–Orient–Decide–Act decision cyclePart I
PADS SetupUS Navy training-scenario format — Position, Altitude, Distance, Speed, with agreed allowable deviations (±30 m alt / ±185 m dist / ±10° bearing / ±19 km/h speed)Part I
The perchCovering aircraft holding an offensive position above/behind the engaged fighterPart IV
Plane of motion (POM)The direction an aircraft is actually traveling — distinct from its lift vector, though the two converge at high GPart I
Ps (specific excess power)Rate of energy gain/loss at a given speed/G point on the EM diagram; zero-Ps is the sustained-turn linePart I
Pursuit curve (lead/pure/lag)Nose position relative to a target's flight pathPart I
Quarter PlaneLast-resort break of excessive closure: roll wings-level then pull out of the bandit's plane of motionPart I
Radius Defence / Radius Defence FollowDefender's overbanked oblique nose-low pull to shrink radius and gain energy off God's G / the attacker's counter — extend, drive to the redefinition point, follow downPart I
RedefinitionAny defender action that changes the fight's character — vertical vs. horizontal, 1-circle vs. 2-circle, or a full role reversalPart I
ReversalA turn against the grain at the right moment, moving from defensive to neutral or better — wrong moment, worse. If in doubt, don't.Part I
RmaxThe volume of space around a target from which a missile shot can succeed — not a fixed number, moves with energy/aspectPart III
Weapon engagement zone (WEZ)The aspect-angle-dependent envelope a weapon is actually usable within — real-world USAF reference example: gun to ~760 m within 135° aspect, AIM-9P+ to ~1,370 m within 90°, AIM-9P to ~2,740 m within 45°Part I
Rule of Threes~900 m range, ~30° AA, steady closure — the three-part check before a gun shotPart I
RWS / TWS / STTRange-while-search / track-while-scan / single-target-track radar modesPart VI
Skate / short skate / banzaiAbort before Desired Out Range / abort before Minimum Abort Range / commit to mergePart III
Split-SPure nose-low maneuver: roll inverted, max-perform through the pull, idle throttle once pointed down to stay in the rate band; exits on the opposite cardinal headingPart I
Tail-end CharlieThe rearmost, least-covered aircraft in a groupPart IV
Tighten Down / Out-of-Plane / The JinkCash energy for turn rate / shift off the shared plane of motion / both combined as a genuine last resort — see also the three-method roll-based Jink variantPart I
Turn Circle Extension (TCX)Easing off the G for 2–3 seconds to shift your turn circle's post and align it with the bandit'sPart I
Vid hostileRadio call reporting a successful visual ID of a contact as hostile — usually the actual clearance to fire, distinct from a radar/IFF read alonePart II
Weapon deconfliction zone~10° cone around the engaged fighter; the support fighter never fires while the engaged fighter is inside it, factoring the weapon's full time of flightPart II

Load vehicle changes

Load vehicle changes

Status

Structured in training-manual order — airmanship, then formation flying, then weapons/killing, then strategy, then aircraft-specific application, then equipment reference — not by engagement chronology. Parts I–IV and VI are a working version, folding in Mike Solyom/The Ops Center's 11-video BFM series and 5-video Air Combat Maneuvering series, Echo Victor's "The ULTIMATE BFM Guide," Robert Shaw's Fighter Combat, and the other sources listed below. The only named gap remaining anywhere in Part I is Lag Reposition (see High-Aspect BFM). Part V's vehicle guide covers 133 aircraft across ten nations (USA, Germany, USSR, UK, France, Sweden, China, Japan, Italy, Israel), each with a researched Doctrine entry, and every card follows the F-4S compact/full template (quickref bullets + Combat Doctrine visible in Compact; Flight Performance, Matchup Notes, and other topic sections shown only in Full). A handful of reference tables — glossary, brevity, both maneuver catalogs, base bombing, and sustained turn rates — collapse behind a dropdown in Full mode to keep the page scannable. A hidden My vehicles editor, opened from a link at the foot of the page, lets the reader tick the aircraft they own — kept per named player, or in that browser only — and in Compact mode the vehicle guide then shows only those aircraft, while Full mode shows all of them with the ticked ones marked. A Training part just before the glossary adds a learning path, a coverage table, twelve drill cards taken from the training sources above (none invented — topics without a sourced exercise say so), and a link to the separate private Debrief Log page, which keeps the long-term record of deaths and names the next practice target; the Training part is hidden in Compact mode. Genuinely unsourced figures, after a real search attempt, stay marked ? rather than invented — see each affected card's own sections for the specific gap. Where two sources disagree on a figure, the companion fact-dump document carries the full sourcing/reliability reasoning; this guide states one best-judgment answer per fact rather than narrating the conflict.
